title: Solaris: Building a Multiplayer Video World Model in Minecraft
evidence: Sec. 4.1: the model works by "performing diffusion on a joint tensor of shape (P, H, W, C)" over the players' observations, with P = 2 in this work.
method: Adapts a single-player video diffusion transformer to two players via shared multiplayer self-attention; autoregressive action-conditioned latent video prediction trained with flow matching and Checkpointed Self Forcing.
evaluation: Minecraft, five held-out tasks (movement, grounding, memory, building, consistency); baselines frame-concat and no-pretrain, Self Forcing ablations; metrics FID and VLM-judge accuracy; TPU v5p training, no inference latency.
contribution: Builds a two-player action-conditioned video world model in Minecraft that generates both players' future views jointly, improving cross-player consistency (71.4% vs 49.5% VLM-judged) and FID over a frame-concatenation baseline.
flag: Predictive accuracy: reported directly, but as generation quality, not state error - FID and VLM-as-judge accuracy per task (Solaris VLM%/FID: movement 68.2/38.5, grounding 62.5/38.0, memory 37.5/55.1, building 20.8/83.6, consistency 71.4/99.4; frame-concat 77.1/68.9, 53.1/66.6, 37.5/74.4, 0.0/103.2, 49.5/129.4). No PSNR/FVD or pixel error; maintainer should decide whether FID plus a VLM judge is an acceptable predictive-accuracy metric. Frame-concat beats Solaris on movement accuracy. Joint state is only P=2 players and is pixel/latent-video generative (not non-generative). VLM judge model not identified in the text read. No inference latency or fps. The "safety mechanism" in Sec. 3.3 only aborts failed data-collection episodes and is not a criterion (a) mechanism. Not safety evidence; RQ5 capped at 2.

title: ODEBrain: Continuous-Time EEG Graph for Modeling Dynamic Brain Networks
evidence: "We propose ODEBRAIN, a Neural ODE latent dynamic forecasting framework to overcome these challenges" (Abstract)
method: Neural ODE over a latent state initialised from a GRU-GNN encoding of EEG spectral graphs plus CNN temporal features; a decoder forecasts future channel graphs; trajectory pooled for classification.
evaluation: TUSZ and TUAB seizure/abnormality detection, 19-node graphs; baselines latent-ODE, neural SDE, Graph ODE, DCRNN, BIOT; TUSZ AUROC 0.881, F1 0.496; graph similarity 0.63 vs 0.53; A6000, 0.516 s per batch.
contribution: A continuous-time latent dynamics model that forecasts future EEG connectivity graphs with a gated neural ODE, improving seizure detection and forecast-graph similarity over discrete and ODE baselines.
flag: Borderline include, thin on the Pillar 2 test. Headline results are DOWNSTREAM classification (AUROC, F1, accuracy). The only direct measure of predictive accuracy is a forecast-graph similarity score (0.63 vs 0.53 for latent-ODE; 0.55 vs 0.41 with 30 percent data masked, Table 7 and Fig. 6); the metric is not clearly defined as the Global Jaccard Index and the forecasting loss is never reported. If one similarity score against one baseline is not enough, this is E2. State is a graph of 19 EEG channels, not agents: domain is far from multi-agent systems, so 'multi-agent state' not claimed. Doubts: intro gains (6.0% F1, 8.1% accuracy on TUSZ) cannot be reproduced from Table 2 (F1 0.496 vs 0.470 latent-ODE; accuracy 0.877 vs 0.857); recall 0.563 in text vs 0.605 in Tables 4 and 8; AMAG named as a baseline but absent from Table 2. Latency: 0.516 s per batch, 164 function evaluations (Table 3), slower than latent-ODE 0.421 s and far from real time.

title: MetaMind: General and Cognitive World Models in Multi-Agent Systems by Meta-Theory of Mind
evidence: "The main contribution of this paper is MetaMind, a general, cognitive world model" (Sec. 1, Introduction)
method: TD-MPC2-style latent world model extended with inverse goal and belief predictors, self-reflection cycle loss, analogical inference of other agents' beliefs/goals, and a transformer aggregating them into a collective belief.
evaluation: SMAC, 13 maps; baselines MARIE, DCWMC, MAPPO, MBVD; win rates only, e.g. 3s_vs_5z 80.4% vs 72.4% MARIE; few-shot median 62.7% vs 25.9%; RTX 4090; no latency.
contribution: A decentralised latent world model in which each agent infers other agents' goals and beliefs by reusing its own inverse models, improving StarCraft multi-agent win rates and few-shot transfer over prior multi-agent world models.
flag: E2 under the maintainer's ruling: ONLY downstream results are reported (win rates, normalised win rate, a unitless 'inference cost' 12.3 vs 5.3). No world-model prediction error, no belief or goal inference accuracy, no multi-step error; the goal-identification theorems (Sec. 5) are not checked empirically and the Sec. 6.5 claim of accurately inferring others' goals has no metric. (b) itself is met: latent prediction over other agents' beliefs and actions. No component ablation, only an imagination-horizon sweep. Number doubts: abstract's 54% gain is not derivable from Table 1 (about 44% relative vs DCWMC on my average of 12 maps); text says 'up to 11.0%' on 3s_vs_5z but table gaps are 8.0 and 34.3 points; MARIE beats MetaMind on 4 of 13 maps; horizon H=15 in text vs H=30 in Table 3; the corridor cell (76.8) came from the text, table cell did not extract.

title: Social-JEPA: Emergent Geometric Isomorphism
evidence: "We identify and formalize the spontaneous emergence of geometric isomorphism" (Sec. 1, contributions)
method: Separate I-JEPA models are trained independently on different views of the same scenes; after training a linear map aligns their latent spaces, enabling probe sharing and representation migration.
evaluation: smallNORB, nuScenes camera pairs, ImageNet-1k; baselines MAE, SimCLR, DINO, MoCo v3, iBOT; cross-view alignment smallNORB MSE 0.036, R2 0.891; ImageNet R2 0.489; A100; no latency.
contribution: Shows that JEPA encoders trained independently on different viewpoints of the same world develop latent spaces related by a near-linear map, allowing probes and representations to be transferred between them cheaply.
flag: E1: multi-agent only nominally. The 'agents' are separately trained image encoders on different camera views or augmentations; there is no joint multi-agent state, no graph state, no interaction, and the prediction is masked-block latent prediction within one still image, not prediction of future state. Title on arXiv is longer: 'Social-JEPA: Emergent Geometric Isomorphism in Independently Trained World Models' (same paper). It would also fail E2 on the Pillar 2 test: NO direct measure of predictive accuracy - MSE, R2, DSC, NOS@10 and CKA measure cross-encoder alignment, Table 9 is downstream probe accuracy. Doubts: 'best overall balance' is not true per metric (MoCo v3 R2 0.987 vs 0.891 on smallNORB; MAE lower NOS@10 on ImageNet); Table 6 holds example values only; abstract's 'scant pixel overlap' robustness has no overlap metric; some Table 2 baseline MSEs (54.3, 93.6) look scale-inconsistent.

title: CounterScene: Counterfactual Causal Reasoning in Generative World Models for Safety-Critical Closed-Loop Evaluation
evidence: "Given a safe scene, CounterScene asks: what if the causally critical agent had behaved differently?" (Abstract)
method: Conditional diffusion world model jointly predicting all agents' trajectories with a causal interaction graph in attention; counterfactual guidance perturbs one selected adversarial agent to create conflicts in closed loop.
evaluation: nuScenes (100 val scenes, 10 s closed loop) and zero-shot nuPlan; baselines VAE, STRIVE, CTG, CTG++, CCDiff; long-horizon ADE 1.877, FDE 5.141, collision rate 22.7% vs 12.3% CCDiff; A100.
contribution: A diffusion world model over joint traffic-agent state with a causal interaction graph that generates safety-critical scenarios by counterfactually altering the most causally critical agent, raising collision rates at lower trajectory error than prior generators.
flag: Check whether this is what Pillar 2 wants: it is a scenario GENERATOR for offline/closed-loop testing, not a runtime mechanism, and its collision rate is a hazard it CREATES (higher is better), not one it prevents - do not read it as safety evidence; I did not claim (c). Predictive accuracy: ADE/FDE against recorded trajectories are reported with baselines and ablations (Tables 2, 4, 5), which I counted as a direct measure, but the authors use them as a realism/minimal-intervention proxy under counterfactual guidance, so it is not a clean forecast-accuracy test; no minADE. If the maintainer does not accept ADE/FDE here, this is E2. Other doubts: best-of-16 rollout selection uses the adversarial objective and may inflate collision rate; ego planner in nuPlan tests not named; Table 8 (26.0% CR at 10 s) and Table 9 (32.0%) disagree with each other; Table 3 values did not extract cleanly; at nuPlan 7 s CCDiff ties at 40.2% CR. Generative diffusion, no latency reported. Two driving datasets, not cross-domain.

title: HCLSM: Hierarchical Causal Latent State Machines for Object-Centric World Modeling
evidence: "The key insight is that structure must precede prediction." (Sec. 1, Introduction)
method: JEPA-style latent world model over up to 32 object slots with GNN edge-gated interactions, three-level dynamics (per-object SSM, event transformer, goal transformer) and a DAG regulariser.
evaluation: PushT, 206 episodes, 68M model on H100; no external baselines, one ablation (no-SBD vs two-stage); next-state loss 0.008 vs 0.002; Triton kernel 0.16 ms vs 6.22 ms on T4.
contribution: An object-centric latent world model that predicts next states over slot nodes linked by learned interaction edges, with hierarchical dynamics; evaluated only on PushT with a single internal ablation.
flag: WEAK include, could fairly be E2. A direct predictive measure IS reported but it is only the training next-state latent loss (0.008 two-stage, 0.002 without the slot decoder), so the one ablation shows the full method predicting WORSE; no rollout error, no held-out test stated, no external baseline (Table 1 is a feature checklist only). Authors admit: explicit causal adjacency learns no edges (weights collapse to zero), each object is split over about 10 slots, 40-60 percent of runs diverge to NaN, 2 of 4 runs survived, planners implemented but not evaluated, only the Small model trained. So the 'graph' is GNN edge weights over slots, the causal graph is nominal. Single scene, not multi-agent. Abstract SBD 0.0075 appears as 0.008 in Table 3. The 38-39x speedup is a kernel micro-benchmark on a T4, not end-to-end inference latency; the SSM '5 percent of forward time' claim has no table.

title: Learn2Fold: Structured Origami Generation with World Model Planning
evidence: Abstract: "a learned graph-structured world model serves as a differentiable surrogate simulator"; Sec. 3.3: "We formulate the transition as a sparse residual update" over crease-pattern edge states.
method: LLM proposes fold actions on a crease-pattern graph; a symbolic simulator discards invalid ones; a learned graph world model predicts residual edge-state updates and violation likelihood to rank candidates.
evaluation: OrigamiCode (25 categories, 75,000 trajectories); baselines Gemini, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, BrickGPT; LM/LM+WM/Full ablation; metrics step F1, Edge-IoU, success rate, goal distance; one RTX Pro 6000, no latency.
contribution: Plans origami folding sequences by pairing an LLM proposer with a symbolic validity check and a learned crease-graph world model for lookahead ranking, reaching 0.74 step F1 against 0.34 for the best prompted LLM.
flag: Predictive accuracy: NOT reported - no state error or violation-prediction accuracy for the world model; only downstream results (F1 0.7394 vs Gemini 0.3420; Edge-IoU 0.5820; Cat-SR 0.8912; ablation Traj SR IID 22.2/25.0/33.3 and OOD 20.7/17.8/27.7 for LM, LM+WM, Full), hence E2 under the maintainer's ruling. Model is predictive with a genuine graph state (single agent). The ablation is unflattering to the world model: adding it LOWERS step validity (70.8 to 54.2 IID) and OOD trajectory success (20.7 to 17.8), and IID goal distance for Full (0.855) is worse than LM alone (0.796), which the text does not discuss; standard deviations are near 45-55 points. The pre-execution rejection is done by the symbolic simulator, not the learned model, and is task validity not safety, so I set interceptor no. World-model architecture is not described beyond 'graph-structured'. Eq. 2 and Eq. 5 disagree on the mask; train/test split described inconsistently (80/20 vs 3,840 test prompts).

title: Toward Consistent World Models with Multi-Token Prediction and Latent Semantic Enhancement
evidence: "enforces latent consistency by aligning multitoken predictions with ground-truth hidden state trajectories" (Sec. 1, contributions)
method: LSE-MTP: multi-token prediction objective for a Transformer with a latent consistency loss and a semantic anchoring loss; auxiliary heads dropped at inference, standard next-token decoding.
evaluation: Path sequences on ER and urban-street graphs (n=100) and Manhattan taxi; baselines NTP, MTP K=2-8; state probe 0.967, valid trajectories 0.998, detour robustness 0.733; RTX 3090 Ti.
contribution: A latent-consistency training objective for multi-token prediction that makes a sequence model's hidden states track the true node state when navigating a graph, improving state probes and detour robustness over next-token training.
flag: BORDERLINE on (b), maintainer should rule. The model is predictive and is trained with a latent-prediction loss, and the ENVIRONMENT is a graph, but the modelled state is one traveller's current node in a single token sequence: no graph-structured state, no GNN, no multi-agent state. I read that as failing the graph-or-multi-agent-state test, hence E1; if 'latent prediction over paths on a graph' is accepted, it would be an include because predictive accuracy IS directly measured (current-state probe 0.967 vs 0.926 NTP, valid trajectories 0.998, next-step legal probability, distinction precision/recall in Table 4) with NTP/MTP baselines and lambda ablations (Tables 5-7). Gains are small and LSE-8TP is worse than NTP on distinction precision (0.285 vs 0.357). Cost: MTP adds 4.5 percent parameters, 17 percent lower training throughput, no added inference latency claimed; no absolute latency.

title: MultiWorld: Scalable Multi-Agent Multi-View Video World Models
evidence: "We propose MultiWorld, a unified framework for scalable multi-agent, multi-view world models" (Sec. 1, contributions)
method: Action-conditioned flow-matching video world model (Wan2.2-5B DiT) with a multi-agent condition module (identity embedding, action self-attention, adaptive weighting) and a VGGT-based global state encoder.
evaluation: ItTakesTwo game (100 h) and RoboFactory (2-4 robots); baselines Standard, Concat-View, COMBO; game FVD 179 vs 207 COMBO, PSNR 17.72, Action 89.8, RPE 0.67; robot FVD 96; no latency.
contribution: A video world model conditioned on the joint actions of several agents across several camera views, improving FVD and multi-view consistency over per-view and compositional baselines in a co-op game and multi-robot manipulation.
flag: Predictive accuracy IS directly measured (FVD, LPIPS, SSIM, PSNR, reprojection error, action-following) with baselines and ablations (Tables 1-5), so (b) minimum evaluation is met. Doubts: generative pixel-space diffusion model, the opposite of non-generative latent inference; the multi-agent state is joint ACTIONS plus a global scene latent, not an explicit per-agent state. Text claims best on FVD, PSNR, action and RPE in both settings but Table 1 shows COMBO higher game PSNR (17.82 vs 17.72) and Concat-View higher robot PSNR and action (authors call it not comparable). Table 4 with-AAW FVD 236 differs from Table 2 +MACM 228, unexplained. Only a 1.5x parallel speedup is given, no absolute latency. Training 8 A800 GPUs about 4 days. Not safety work; RQ5 capped.

title: DynoSLAM: Dynamic SLAM with Generative Graph Neural Networks for Real-World Social Navigation
evidence: a graph attention network predicts each pedestrian's next velocity from its history and social context, with neighbours inside radius R (Sec. III.D.1)
method: Graph attention network predicts per-pedestrian next velocity from history plus social context; Gaussian noise on the prediction gives sampled rollouts whose mean and covariance enter a SLAM kinematic factor.
evaluation: pyminisim social-navigation simulator, 6,000 self-collected episodes (5,500 train, 500 test), 1-15 pedestrians, 2.0 s horizon; robot and landmark RMSE, ATE, RPE, safety-distance error and prediction RMSE vs constant-velocity, single-agent MLP, deterministic GAT and a loss ablation; no hardware or latency.
contribution: A graph attention pedestrian predictor feeds covariance-weighted kinematic factors into dynamic SLAM, lowering safety-distance error from 0.037 to 0.033 against a constant-velocity model in simulation.
flag: Reports a direct predictive measure (prediction RMSE) with baselines and a loss ablation, so the criterion (b) minimum is formally met - but weakly: the proposed stochastic GAT ties the constant-velocity model at 1.21, the deterministic GAT is worse (1.355, given as 1.354 in the text), and the MLP is best (1.173), so the graph predictor is not shown to predict better. No ADE or FDE, no definition or units for prediction RMSE or safety-distance error. Localisation differences are third-decimal (robot RMSE 0.388 for four of five methods, ATE 0.183 vs 0.186) with no seeds, variance or significance tests, and the stochastic variant has the worst RPE (0.048) without comment. Despite "Real-World" in the title there are no real-world experiments and no closed-loop control: collision rates and navigation efficiency are future work (Sec. VI), and the MPC and PPO use of the predicted covariance is proposed but never implemented. The model is only nominally generative - isotropic noise on a deterministic head, which the authors concede "relies on manually injected perturbations" (Sec. VI) - so the multimodality claim is unsupported. No edge hardware, latency or FPS figures, and the covariance in the SLAM factor is a velocity covariance applied to a position displacement without time-step scaling, which the paper does not address.

title: MolWorld: Molecule World Models for Actionable Molecular Optimization
evidence: the world model "predicts how generation from each candidate context would expand the graph" (Sec. 3)
method: Latent world model over a molecule-transfer graph whose nodes are molecules and edges matched molecular pairs; a dynamics model predicts the latent expansion of a candidate action and a scorer ranks contexts for a SMILES generator.
evaluation: ZINC250 and PMV21 property optimisation (GSK3b, QED, JNK3, DRD2) and three docking targets; AUC@10, AUC@100 and isolated-node ratio vs nine baselines; five ablations; latent dynamics validation loss; AMD EPYC plus RTX A6000; no latency.
contribution: A latent world model over a matched-molecular-pair graph predicts the effect of each candidate edit and lifts property-optimisation AUC@10 on ZINC250 GSK3b from 0.8904 to 0.9576.
flag: Reports a DIRECT predictive-accuracy measure for the world model, though only in latent space: smooth-L1 validation error 0.0488 with matched contexts vs 0.2148 mismatched and 0.2083 for a mean-target baseline, a claimed 76.57% reduction, with mean cosine similarity 0.9421 (Appendix B.2.3, Table 4); encoder node-prediction loss 0.1048 vs 0.3617 with MMP edges removed (Table 3). Maintainer should decide whether latent-space regression error counts, since there is no next-molecule or property-change prediction accuracy. Downstream optimisation results are strong and well-baselined. Doubts: graph state is a molecular search graph, not agents, so the multi-agent reading of (b) is not met; no multi-agent aspect at all; scorer selection regret is defined but never reported; ablation numbers other than the STONED generator (PMV21 average AUC@100 0.5516 down to 0.2222) appear only in figures; no wall-clock or latency figures. My fetch covered roughly the first 100k of 116k characters, so the tail of the appendices is unverified.

title: IFPV: An Integrated Multi-Agent Framework for Generative Operational Planning and High-Fidelity Plan Verification
evidence: "ACSE introduces an opponent equipped with a customized world model" (Abstract), with trajectory prediction error reported as ADE and FDE in Table 2
method: Hierarchical LLM multi-agent planner (route proposer, analyst, planner, rule-based validator) plus offline Monte Carlo plan verification against a counterpart driven by a LoRA-tuned LLM world model with an entity-weighted loss.
evaluation: 2D asymmetric simulator, 100 Monte Carlo seeds; world-model ADE and FDE vs seven open LLMs; plan success and attrition vs Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek-V3, GLM-5, Qwen3-Max; module and loss ablations; one RTX A6000; no latency.
contribution: An LLM counterpart world model used for offline plan verification predicts multi-platform trajectories at ADE 0.18 and FDE 0.54, against 0.95 and 1.58 for the best baseline LLM.
flag: Reports a DIRECT predictive-accuracy measure with baselines: ADE 0.18 and FDE 0.54 (Table 2) vs 0.95 and 1.58 for InternLM2.5-7B, plus a loss ablation moving ADE 0.3113 to 0.1628 and FDE 0.6494 to 0.4036 (Fig. 4) - note the 0.18 vs 0.1628 inconsistency, and that units, test-set size and split are never stated. Downstream results are also present (61.00% overall plan success vs 49.33% for the strongest generator baseline). Doubts: the domain is adversarial operational planning, which the maintainer may consider out of scope on topic grounds; the world model is a generative LLM rather than a latent model; and verification is offline ranking with constraint-violation-driven repair, not a runtime interceptor, since the executing side "does not perform online re-planning" (Sec. 3.3). I could not reproduce the abstract's 31.8% suppression-rate figure from Table 4, and the abstract's 19.4% success and 41.7% attrition gains come from the Table 6 ablation under the weak validator, not from the verified results in Table 3. Appendix D and Sec. 3.4 give conflicting definitions of CLA, and the suppression rate is defined two different ways; PQS and cost weights are unreported; data only on request.

title: Deterministic Event-Graph Substrates as World Models for Counterfactual Reasoning
evidence: "This is closed-form linear algebra over the existing trajectory log; no physics simulator is invoked." (Sec. 4, Predictive)
method: Untrained symbolic world model: an append-only log of typed RDF deltas with deterministic replay; counterfactuals by forking the log at a tick; predictive answers by closed-form kinematic projection.
evaluation: CLEVRER validation (75,618 questions), ComPhy, GQA, bAbI and a new Twin-EventLog benchmark (500 specs); question-answering accuracy vs NS-DR, ALOE, Llama-3.1-8B and a Concordia-style agent; several ablations; no hardware, no latency.
contribution: A deterministic RDF event-log world model answers CLEVRER predictive questions at 69.5% and counterfactual ones at 59.9%, above the NS-DR oracle but below the learned ALOE model.
flag: Borderline E2 against include, and the maintainer should rule. There is NO direct measure of the model's predictive or counterfactual state fidelity - no trajectory error, no state divergence against an independent oracle - only downstream question-answering accuracy (CLEVRER predictive 69.50% per-question and 84.07% per-option vs NS-DR 68.7 and ALOE 87.5; counterfactual 59.85 vs ALOE 75.6). If predictive-question accuracy counts as predictive accuracy for Pillar 2, this flips to include. Also note the state is symbolic and not latent, and the model "is not trained at any stage" (Sec. 6). The Twin-EventLog 100% scores are circular: it "grades against the substrate's deterministic replay" (Sec. 5) and the model is "correct by construction" (Table 2). Multi-agent only nominally (Smallville awareness interventions). The claim that traversal "runs in microseconds" is asserted, never measured. Single author; the Concordia-style baseline is an admittedly cut-down reimplementation, and the Llama comparison uses n=300 against the substrate's full split.

title: SWoMo: Neuro-Symbolic World Model for Cataract Surgery Simulation
evidence: "a neuro-symbolic world model for cataract surgery simulation" (Abstract); the derived scene graph is only conditioning, where "Each node ... represents a connected component" (Sec. 2)
method: Rule-based Godot simulator supplies tool and anatomy motion; a video diffusion model conditioned on the simulated video and a derived scene graph renders realistic surgical frames.
evaluation: CATARACTS and Cataract-1k; FVD, FID, LPIPS, box IoU and F1 vs SG2VID, Endora, MOFA, LVDM, StyleGAN-V, MedSora; image and scene-graph ablations; downstream phase recognition; 4x A40 training; no latency.
contribution: A simulator-plus-diffusion pipeline generates controllable cataract surgery video, reaching FVD 265.4 on CATARACTS against 363.8 for the scene-graph-conditioned baseline.
flag: Recommend E1 after reading: the world state is a parametric vector (globe pose, pupil ellipse, tool pose), not a graph - the scene graph is a derived conditioning signal - and the setting is a single eye with tools, so there is no multi-agent state; the learned component performs sim-to-real rendering rather than forecasting future states. It also reports NO direct predictive-accuracy measure: FVD and FID are distributional video-quality scores and box IoU and F1 measure adherence to the conditioning, with the rest being downstream phase recognition (+1.1 accuracy, +2.3 F1 on CATARACTS; those table rows were garbled in my extraction), so E2 would apply as well. SG2VID beats it on Cataract-1k FVD (73.0 vs 123.0) and FID (14.9 vs 20.1); SWoMo-noIMG Cataract-1k FVD was missing from the table I could read.

title: Dreaming Of Others: Latent Teammate Modeling In World Models For Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
evidence: "we do not report empirical results" (Sec. 1); "This paper is a proposal intended to catalyze discussion" (Sec. 1)
method: Dreamer-style recurrent state-space model whose stochastic latent is split into environment and teammate parts; teammate latent decodes a partner next-action distribution and conditions actor and critic.
evaluation: None run. Only proposed: MPE, Overcooked-AI, Melting Pot via JaxMARL and BenchMARL, with proposed metrics of return, sample efficiency and zero-shot coordination. No baselines, no numbers, no hardware, no latency.
contribution: A workshop proposal to factor a Dreamer world model's latent state into environment and teammate components so an agent can imagine partner behaviour; no experiments are reported.
flag: Topic squarely fits (b) - latent prediction over multi-agent state - but this is a position/proposal paper with NO experiments: neither a direct predictive-accuracy measure nor any downstream result, and no baselines or ablations, so it fails the minimum evaluation (E2). Accepted as a WMW 2026 workshop poster, single author; worth re-queueing if an empirical version appears.

title: COGENT: Continuous Graph Emulators with Neural Ordinary Differential Equations for Long-Term Physical Forecasting
evidence: "the latent vector field f_theta is implemented as a graph neural network" (Sec. 3.3)
method: Latent neural ODE whose vector field is a GNN over a glacier mesh; GraphSAGE history encoder plus temporal Transformer; predicts at requested times without feeding predictions back.
evaluation: ISSM Pine Island Glacier simulations, 36 melt scenarios; 180-step rollout RMSE vs initial-state, single-step autoregressive and multi-horizon emulators; history, horizon and component ablations; 4x H100; no latency.
contribution: A continuous-time graph neural ODE emulator cuts whole-trajectory rollout RMSE by 26.3% against the best discrete graph emulator on 15-year physical forecasts.
flag: Reports a DIRECT predictive-accuracy measure (full-rollout RMSE, Table 1: aggregate 34.31 vs 46.56 for the best baseline and 94.62 single-step) with baselines and component ablations, so the criterion (b) minimum evaluation is met. Doubts for the maintainer: the graph is a finite-element mesh of one physical system, not agents, and the model is action-free forecasting rather than an action-conditioned world model, so E1 on scope is defensible. Baselines beat COGENT on final-step aggregate (66.74 vs 70.67). Some V_x baseline cells were illegible in my extraction; window-wise RMSE appears only in figures. No latency or inference-time figures at all.

title: The Theory of Mind Utility: A Formal Account of Mentalizing
evidence: "The reference simulation is a consistency witness rather than an empirically fitted model." (Appendix A.1); the Local Epistemic World Model is "a directed typed graph" of agents and belief states, distinguished from a learned dynamics model (Sec. 2.2).
method: Computational-level formal theory of mentalizing: generate-and-filter inference over candidate typed graphs of other agents' epistemic states, via backward inference, self-projection and mutual reconciliation with confidence thresholds.
evaluation: Theoretical; deterministic toy reference simulation (false-belief style scenarios) checking definitions compose, with internal 2x2 ablation (confidence 0.942 vs 0.752); no data, external baselines, hardware or latency.
contribution: Formal account of theory-of-mind inference as cost-bounded construction of local epistemic graphs over other agents, illustrated by a toy consistency simulation rather than empirical evaluation.
flag: NEITHER predictive accuracy NOR downstream results: the only numbers are confidence values from a hand-built toy witness that the authors say "tests compositional coherence, not parameter robustness or empirical fit". Recommend E1 because the model is not predictive in the world-model sense - the authors themselves separate their LEWM from "the reinforcement-learning sense of a learned, persistent model of environment dynamics" - it is a cognitive-science theory of belief attribution. If the maintainer reads a typed graph over several agents' belief states as (b), the exclusion becomes E2 (no empirical evaluation, no baseline). Internal halting on confidence thresholds is about the inference procedure, not an action veto. Witness parameters are inconsistent (tau_high 0.99 vs 0.90 in Table 2; decay 0.50 vs 0.8). Only first 100k of 110k characters read.

title: GraphWorld: Long-Horizon Planning with World Models for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
evidence: "we do not aim to extend the prediction horizon via explicit multi-step rollout" (Sec. 3); the latent world state is a set of node latents for surrounding agents plus ego over an ego-centric star interaction graph.
method: End-to-end driving planner with an ego-centric interaction graph over ego and K neighbours and a flow-matching latent world state, trained with a consistency loss to the next-step state, used as planning condition.
evaluation: nuScenes open-loop, Bench2Drive, NAVSIM v1/v2 closed-loop; vs UniAD, SparseDrive, World4Drive, DiffusionDrive; 6 s L2 1.34 m, collision 0.70% vs 0.87%, PDMS 90.1; 51 FPS, GPU unspecified.
contribution: Driving planner that conditions long-horizon planning on a single-step latent world state over an ego-centric agent graph, reporting lower open-loop collision rates than prior world-model planners.
flag: ONLY DOWNSTREAM RESULTS for the world model: no future-state or latent prediction error is reported and the Stage II world loss value is never given; all tables are planning metrics (L2, collision rate, PDMS/EPDMS, driving score). Hence E2 under the maintainer's ruling. The one borderline item is Table 7 agent motion prediction (minADE 0.55, minFDE 0.86, MR 0.112, EPA 0.512) - that is a predictive metric on other agents but from the motion head, not the world state; if the maintainer accepts it as predictive accuracy this flips to include. Also weak on (b): single-step latent, authors disclaim rollout, graph is ego-centric star. Inconsistencies: Sec. 5.4 claims best navhard EPDMS at 53.6 but Table 4 lists higher values for other methods (e.g. 80.4); Bench2Drive DS given as 51.55/SR 25.47 in Table 11 and text but 76.71/44.22 in Tables 2 and 13 as relayed; Adv-nuScenes 0.738% in text vs 0.742 in Table 8; text says 5 m radius is best but Table 15 favours 10 m. Collision avoidance is a planning outcome here, not a runtime filter, so (a) and (c) not met.

title: Dual-Channel Grounded World Modeling (DCGWM): Structural Prevention of Objective Interference Collapse via Heterogeneous External Grounding with Inward-Only Gradient Flow
evidence: "experimental validation is ongoing and will be reported in a future revision" (Abstract); the proposed JEPA latent is partitioned into a physical subspace and a behavioural subspace grounded on an external N-agent simulation.
method: Architecture proposal: JEPA world model with latent split into physically grounded and social-behaviourally grounded subspaces, each aligned by VICReg-style losses with inward-only gradients to avoid objective interference.
evaluation: None: no datasets, baselines, ablations, metrics, hardware or latency; Sec. 6 only proposes a three-condition falsification design (shared-latent JEPA, full DCGWM, partition removed).
contribution: Proposes a dual-channel JEPA world model whose physical and multi-agent behavioural latent subspaces are grounded separately with isolated gradients; argued conceptually, with no experiments yet.
flag: NEITHER predictive accuracy NOR downstream results: the paper has no experiments at all (position/architecture paper), so E2 regardless of the Pillar 2 ruling. Multi-agent state enters only as a training-time grounding signal from an external agent simulation; the model's own state is a continuous latent vector, not a graph. The conclusion says "We have proven dimensional collapse prevention" while Sec. 3.3 and 4.3 say prevention is not formally proven, and the central theorem rests on an unproven assumption; "Objective interference collapse is a conjecture" (Sec. 6). Re-check if a revision with results appears.

title: Learning a Normal World Model for Few-Shot Boundary-Calibrated Abnormality Detection
evidence: "This term combines prediction violation and predictive entropy." (Sec. 4.6, dynamic energy); the state is a context-conditioned soft hypergraph over the sensor variables of one engine.
method: Normal world model trained on healthy data only: next-state Gaussian prediction, hypergraph cross-sensor reconstruction and latent-manifold distance summed into an energy; K-shot abnormal examples only move the threshold.
evaluation: NASA C-MAPSS FD001-FD004; vs Gaussian, PCA, ridge, KNN, GRU/Transformer/TCN forecasters, GDN-lite; zero-shot AUROC 0.917-0.993, full 0.965-0.998; energy ablation; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Energy-based normal world model over a sensor hypergraph that flags turbofan degradation zero-shot and calibrates its decision threshold from a handful of abnormal windows.
flag: ONLY DOWNSTREAM RESULTS: all numbers are detection metrics (AUROC, AUPRC, F1, balanced accuracy) and Spearman rho of energy vs -RUL (0.51-0.69); no forecasting error (MSE/MAE) is reported for the dynamic branch, so by the maintainer's ruling this is E2. Also weak on (b): graph nodes are sensors of a single machine, not agents, and only one of three energy terms is a forecaster; the ablation shows the predictive term alone is poor (avg AUROC 0.753) and the hypergraph reconstruction term alone (0.980) beats the full model (0.971). KNN last-5 baseline beats the method on FD002 and FD004 AUROC. Several Table 1 cells are garbled or inconsistent in the source (FD003 zero-shot AUROC 0.9913 vs 0.9894 elsewhere; FD003 2-shot recall 0.0917 with F1 0.7772). Authors call it early verification on one dataset; no seeds or variance. The score is not connected to any halt or deferral.

title: Understanding Rollout Error in Graph World Models
evidence: "Yet how rollout error propagates in GWMs remains largely unexplored." (Sec. 1); a learned transition function predicts future graph states G_t=(V,E_t,X_t,A_t) under candidate actions and is rolled out H steps.
method: Analysis of rollout error in graph world models (fixed-edge vs dynamic-edge); Error-Aware GWM adds spectral regularisation, multi-horizon rollout consistency and critical-node weighting to the one-step loss.
evaluation: 7 synthetic 50-node topologies, agent calling-tree and skill-graph testbeds, Cora/Citeseer/Bitcoin-Alpha; vs MLP, GCN, MPNN, GPS, ActionNode GWM; NodeMSE@32 2.5e-4, 0/21 divergence vs GCN 10/21; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Characterises how rollout error grows with topology and edge dynamics in graph world models, and shows a regularised variant avoids divergence over 32-step rollouts where a plain GCN model diverges.
flag: DIRECT PREDICTIVE ACCURACY REPORTED (NodeMSE at H=1..48, divergence counts, DE vs FE 11.0x improvement p=1.5e-11) plus downstream agent task success (SR@20 0.417, not improved by the method) - meets the (b) minimum with baselines and ablations. Checks: mostly synthetic graphs; multi-agent state cell rests only on a small simulated agent calling-tree testbed (22-30 nodes, weak calibration r=0.311), so drop it if strict. Planning regret is figure-only. Table 2 as relayed shows MLP error falling from 0.1299 at H=1 to 3.0e-4 at H=32, which looks odd - verify against the PDF. Only first 100k of 114k characters read (tail appendix unread). No runtime interceptor, no latency, not a safety paper.

title: Agentic vs. Parametric World Models: Hybrid Planning for Reliable Language Agents
evidence: A parametric world model (MLP, GCN, MPNN, GPS; under 100k parameters) predicts action validity, state delta, reward, done, risk and value over a typed task graph G_t = (V, E, X, Z) (Sec. 3); Table 4 reports TransAcc/ValidAcc/DeltaAcc.
method: Hybrid-WM: small graph world model gives the LLM planner a predicted skeleton; a Jaccard consistency gate compares LLM and model state deltas and a risk gate re-prompts with only low-risk actions.
evaluation: Four graph-task benchmarks (calibrated simulator; 80 live GPT-4o-mini episodes) vs agent and parametric baselines, 11 ablations; SR 0.838 vs 0.668; hallucinated-state rate 0.079 vs 0.205; MPNN TransAcc 0.992.
contribution: A hybrid planner that checks an LLM agent's imagined state changes against a small graph world model, gating inconsistent or risky actions and cutting hallucinated state claims on graph-structured tasks.
flag: PREDICTIVE ACCURACY: reported directly for the parametric graph world model (Table 4: MLP 0.843/0.922/0.993, MPNN 0.992/0.995/1.000 TransAcc/ValidAcc/DeltaAcc) against backbone alternatives; NodeMSE is defined but no values were found. Headline results are downstream (success, hallucinated-state rate). Enters as method evidence on (b), RQ5 capped at 2. Check: (1) state is a graph but single-agent, no multi-agent state; (2) runtime_interceptor 'yes' is soft - above risk 0.65 (about 8% of steps) the drafted action is withdrawn and the agent re-prompted with low-risk actions only, and below Jaccard 0.30 one revision is requested; the paper itself says the agent is not hard-blocked and may override the skeleton, and no safety metric is claimed, so (a) is not credited; set to 'no' if a hard veto is required; (3) main Table 1 comes from a behavioural simulator calibrated on five live episodes that the authors say over-predicts hallucination and token cost by 3-4x; live runs have SR 1.000 for both arms; (4) Hybrid-WM hallucination rate differs across tables (0.079, 0.035, 0.014); (5) Claude-3-Haiku and Gemini rows are calibrated from published reports, not measured; (6) knowledge-graph test (n=12) favours agent-only, not significant; (7) world model trained on oracle transitions; WallTime units not stated, no hardware. PDF title reads 'Agent vs. Parametric World Models' (record says 'Agentic') - same paper. Read via text extraction of the PDF.

title: J-LAW: Joint Localization and Action-Conditioned World Modeling via Coupled Latent Factor Graphs
evidence: "Its maximum a posteriori (MAP) factor graph enforces consistency between these complementary sources" (Abstract); "Full metric localization improvement and closed-loop planning are considered for the future work." (Sec. V).
method: J-LAW: MAP factor graph over metric poses, predictive latents from a frozen action-conditioned JEPA predictor, and latent landmarks, with coupling, loop-closure and landmark factors; alternating block optimisation, IRLS variant.
evaluation: PushT recorded trajectories and 8 WildGS scenes vs open-loop rollout, pose-only, latent-only graph; PushT latent RMSE 0.033 vs 1.401 open-loop; WildGS mean drift 2.374 vs 2.488; no hardware or latency.
contribution: A factor-graph inference layer that jointly smooths robot poses and the latents of a frozen action-conditioned world model, reducing long-horizon latent drift on PushT with mixed results on real video.
flag: PREDICTIVE ACCURACY: reported directly (latent RMSE, latent endpoint error/drift) with baselines and ablations, so E2 does not apply; the issue is state. E1 reasoning (borderline, maintainer please check): single robot, no multi-agent setting; the 'graph' is a temporal factor graph used for inference over one trajectory's poses, latents and landmarks, not a graph-structured world state, and no new world model is trained (frozen LeWM predictor). If a factor-graph latent state is accepted as 'state is a graph' this is an include on (b). Doubts: WildGS gains are mixed (open-loop beats J-LAW at H=384, ties at H=512) and the authors call it not 'evidence of a general localization improvement'; best masked result uses ground-truth loops (non-deployable); permuted-coupling control (0.965) is nearly as good as paired coupling (0.951) and a direct proprioception predictor (0.945) is better; Table I 'relative reduction' figures (99.93%, 97.91%) are not explained by the RMSE columns as extracted; pose RMSE is only in Fig. 2. Read via text extraction of the PDF.

title: Towards World Model-Empowered Integrated Sensing, Communication, and Decision for Complex Unmanned Systems
evidence: "a swarm of N=5 UAVs collaboratively tracks multiple dynamic ground targets under limited wireless resources" (Sec. IV-A), with an RSSM world model whose action-conditioned latent rollouts evaluate candidate actions (Sec. III-C).
method: Vision framework: a shared RSSM-style world model with deterministic and stochastic latents couples sensing, communication and decision for heterogeneous unmanned systems, linked by a multi-granularity knowledge graph; PPO decides.
evaluation: Simulation, 5 UAVs tracking ground targets under Rayleigh fading vs modular SCD, no-world-model, edge LLM, deep RL; AoI about 30% lower than no-WM; RMSE gain 3.60 m; no hardware or latency.
contribution: A vision paper proposing a world-model-centred sensing, communication and decision loop for unmanned swarms, with a five-UAV tracking simulation showing lower age of information than a variant without the world model.
flag: PREDICTIVE ACCURACY: none reported (no prediction error or rollout fidelity); only downstream age of information and tracking RMSE, so E2 under the maintainer's ruling. Also close to E3: mainly a vision/framework article with one small case study; the AoI/variance sensing trigger has no stated weights or threshold, and how the knowledge graph forms a joint multi-agent state is not specified. Numbers are thin: 'approximately 30%' AoI reduction with absolute values only in Fig. 4(a); 'gain of 3.60 m' over the RL baseline without absolute SCD or RL RMSE (edge LLM 5.20 m at 4 dB is the only absolute figure). Only ablation is SCD without world model. Action selection by latent rollout is planning, not a runtime veto. Read via text extraction of the PDF.

title: Masked Generative-Contrastive Representation Learning for Cross-Dataset EEG-Based Emotion Recognition
evidence: "predicting structured targets in a latent space rather than reconstructing signal-level representations" (Sec. III.C.2); "Each EEG channel within the region is treated as a graph node." (Sec. III.C.1).
method: MGCRL: region-wise graph convolution over EEG channels, an I-JEPA style masked latent-prediction branch with EMA target encoder, and a stimulus-aware weighted contrastive loss; pretrain then fine-tune.
evaluation: Pretrain on FACED, leave-one-subject-out on SEED-IV/V/VII vs BIOT, TS-TCC, EEG2Rep, LaBraM; accuracy 41.47/34.99/34.73% vs best baseline 37.20/31.98/31.03%; no hardware or latency.
contribution: A masked generative-contrastive pretraining scheme for EEG emotion recognition that combines channel-graph convolution, JEPA-style latent prediction and stimulus-aware contrast to improve cross-dataset transfer.
flag: PREDICTIVE ACCURACY: none reported; only downstream emotion-classification accuracy, so E2 would apply even if (b) were granted. E1 reasoning: this is a masked representation learner, not a predictive model of dynamics; the JEPA branch predicts masked temporal embeddings inside one 1-second EEG sample, with no future state, action or agent. A literal reading of 'latent prediction over graphs' is arguable because of the channel-graph GCN, but removing the latent-prediction loss changes accuracy by only 0.52/0.54/0.14 points (Table II). Standard deviations (6-7 points) exceed the gaps to baselines and no significance test is given; the 'relative improvements' of 4.27/3.01/3.70% in the Conclusion are absolute point differences. Off-topic domain (biosignal classification). Read via text extraction of the PDF.

title: Branch-JEPA: Finite-Support Predictive Distributions for JEPA World Models
evidence: "Branch-JEPA replaces this point-valued transition with a context-weighted finite set of latent successors" (Abstract); "The online view contains the 50 observed focal states, observed neighbors, and static map" (Experiments, Data and implementation).
method: Branch-JEPA: JEPA transition returns K=6 weighted latent successors via branch predictors and a context-only router; trained by hard-assignment specialisation or full-set Energy Score; all branches kept at inference.
evaluation: Argoverse 2 validation (24,988 scenes, 5 seeds) vs K=1 JEPA, output-only branching, MDN: Energy Score 2.0766 vs 2.3827 MDN, 5.36 effective branches; OGBench verified route 19.2% vs 3.9%; 2.89 ms per batch-64.
contribution: A JEPA world model whose latent transition is a weighted finite set of successors, improving distributional trajectory forecasting on Argoverse 2 and route existence in OGBench graph audits over point-valued and MDN predictors.
flag: PREDICTIVE ACCURACY: reported directly (trajectory and endpoint Energy Score, expected ADE 2.7941 m, top-1 ADE, Brier .09194, N_eff) with baselines and ablations, so E2 does not apply; the issue is state. E1 reasoning: only the single focal agent's 60-step future is predicted; up to 16 observed neighbours and 48 map polylines are attention-pooled context (no GNN, no joint multi-agent future, future neighbours masked); OGBench states are single-agent vectors or images and the graph there is an evaluation artefact. If the maintainer counts neighbour-conditioned forecasting as multi-agent state this becomes an include on (b). NOTE: the unversioned pdf_url served an earlier version titled 'MoP-JEPA: Hard-Assigned Predictor Mixtures for Stochastic JEPA World Models' (OGBench and ETH/UCY only, no Argoverse); the arXiv abs page confirms the same id is now 'Branch-JEPA' (v3, 2026-08-03) and this row is drafted from the v3 PDF. Abstract numbers 5.36 branches, 19.2% and 3.9% were found in the body (Tables 1 and 3). Latency 2.89 +/- 0.59 ms is per batch of 64 on a datacentre GPU, not edge. Authors state the OGBench diagnostics are not closed-loop control.

title: GATS: Graph-Augmented Tree Search with Layered World Models for Efficient Agent Planning
evidence: "Predictions are cached to avoid repeated LLM calls. In practice, L3 is rarely invoked when L1/L2 have sufficient coverage." (Sec. 3.2); world model W(s,a) -> (s',p) with a search graph over canonical state keys (Sec. 3.3).
method: GATS: UCB1 tree search over a persistent graph of merged states, using a three-layer world model (symbolic STRIPS rules, count-based learned statistics, cached LLM fallback) with confidence-penalised values.
evaluation: 100 synthetic planning tasks plus 120-task stress test vs ReAct, LATS, oracle BFS; success 100% vs LATS 92.0% (b=10), stress 100% vs 88.9%; 0 planning LLM calls; no hardware or latency.
contribution: A graph-augmented tree search for a single LLM agent that replaces most LLM calls with a layered symbolic, statistical and LLM world model and reaches oracle success on synthetic planning tasks.
flag: PREDICTIVE ACCURACY: none reported directly (no next-state accuracy, calibration or per-layer error); only downstream success rate, optimality, node and LLM-call counts, so it would be E2 even if (b) were granted. E1 reasoning: the model is predictive, but the graph is the planner's search graph over one agent's symbolic states, not a graph-structured or multi-agent world state; maintainer may read this differently. Doubts: synthetic tasks are solvable by BFS (oracle also 100%); L1 hit rate is 100% so the learned and LLM layers are never exercised and the layer ablation is flat (all 100%); open-domain layer rates are 'projected', not measured; reproducibility section lists a mock backend; 5 seeds (Sec. 4.4) vs 3 seeds (Table 1 caption); LATS LLM calls 17/37 (Table 1) vs about 30/60 (Table 5); API-Bank is a non-discriminating check. Read via text extraction of the PDF.

title: Scalable and Efficient Joint Spiking Embedding Predictive Architecture for Large-Scale Dynamic Graphs
evidence: "formulates dynamic graphs as a temporal prediction problem" (Introduction); target node embeddings are predicted from context embeddings in representation space (Sec. 4.1-4.5).
method: SG-JEPA: GraphSAGE target encoder, PLIF spiking context encoder and nested spike-count predictor predict latest-snapshot node embeddings from earlier snapshots; InfoNCE loss with stop-gradient.
evaluation: Node classification on DBLP, Tmall, Patent vs 11 baselines; Macro-F1 74.17/61.89/83.84 at 40% labels; 5.2x and 2.8x per-epoch training speedup; no hardware or latency.
contribution: A spiking joint-embedding predictive architecture for large dynamic graphs that predicts future node embeddings in latent space and matches supervised spiking baselines on node classification at lower training cost.
flag: PREDICTIVE ACCURACY: none reported directly; only downstream node classification (Macro-F1 and Micro-F1) plus a normalised InfoNCE loss curve (Fig. 4), so E2 under the maintainer's ruling. Criterion (b) itself is met (latent prediction over a dynamic graph, not a world model with actions). Ablations exist (Table 4: IF/LIF, no stop-gradient, EMA, L1/L2/cosine). SG-JEPA is not best in every cell (SiGNN is ahead on Tmall 80% and all Patent splits; w/ L1 beats default on DBLP Macro-F1). No energy measurement despite the spiking framing; hardware not stated; memory only as circle size in Fig. 3. Read via a text extraction of the PDF: Table 3 Micro-F1 was partly illegible and two SpikeNet Patent cells (94.03, 94.20) look like extraction errors; I did not check the abstract's numbers separately against the body.

title: NaviAIS: A Scenario-Level Vessel Trajectory Prediction Dataset withVectorized Lane Priors and the NaviLane Forecasting Framework
evidence: NaviLane scores candidate trajectories with an interaction world model that predicts neighbour futures (Eq. 14) and a CFR-style energy with CPA and collision terms (Sec III, Eqs. 15-18).
method: Jointly encodes all vessels and vectorised lane map; decodes 128 anchor-conditioned candidates, refines them, then ranks with a neighbour-future world model, collision-aware energy, selector and reranker.
evaluation: NaviAIS AIS scenarios (4,000/1,000/1,000); nine baselines incl. TrAISformer, PECNet; three ablations; ADE@10 3.57, FDE@10 7.03, minADE@10 2.61 (units of 100 m); A100 training, no inference latency.
contribution: Scenario-level AIS dataset with vectorised lane priors and a multi-vessel trajectory forecaster that ranks anchor-based candidates using a learned neighbour-interaction world model and collision-aware energy terms.
flag: Title matches (record title has a typo 'withVectorized'). (b) met: predictive model over the joint state of all vessels in a scene, with an explicit neighbour-future 'world model' used for scoring. DIRECT predictive accuracy IS reported with baselines and ablations: ADE@10 3.57 vs best baseline 4.54-4.60, FDE@10 7.03 vs 8.85, RMSE 4.23, MaxDE 7.27, MHE 0.44; minADE@10 2.61, minFDE@10 4.85; ablations w/o refinement ADE@10 8.07, w/o World-CFR 4.10, w/o selector 3.97. Caveats: (1) the accuracy measured is the ego-trajectory forecast; the interaction world model's own neighbour-prediction accuracy is NOT reported separately, only its ablation effect (4.10 to 3.57); (2) not a safety paper - CPA/collision terms only rank candidates, no collision or hazard rate, no interceptor, so not (c) and RQ5 capped; (3) Table III looks unsound: PECNet's top-6 values equal its single-modal values exactly and DI-MTP's minADE@10/minFDE@10 equal its single-modal ADE@10/FDE@10, so the multimodal comparison may be against effectively unimodal baselines; (4) LSTM beats NaviLane at ADE@3 (1.06 vs 1.18), unmentioned in the text; (5) one day each for train/val/test, all January 2024, baselines at default settings; (6) macro-k 64 is slightly better than the default 128 on single-modal metrics. Non-generative inference not credited (anchor-based decoding of trajectories, not latent prediction). No inference latency. Extraction based on one full-document fetch summary.

title: Dreamer-CPC: Message Learning with World Models for Decentralized Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning
evidence: Each agent's world model learns "temporal dynamics of the environment from its local observation and action history as well as messages received from other agents" (Sec 2.2).
method: Each agent runs a DreamerV3 RSSM conditioned on received discrete messages; a recurrent message module with prior/posterior is trained in the world-model loss without cross-agent gradients; actor-critic trained in imagination.
evaluation: Two custom two-agent tasks (Observer, CatchApple); baselines IPPO-CPC, IPPO, no-comm DreamerV3, obs-shared DreamerV3; IQM return over 10 runs e.g. 39.85 vs 7.31; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Decentralised multi-agent Dreamer in which each agent's world model learns to emit and consume discrete messages, improving returns over IPPO-CPC on two small two-agent partial-observation tasks.
flag: Title matches. (b) is met loosely: a predictive world model in a multi-agent setting, but each RSSM is LOCAL (own observations plus received messages); no joint-state model is learned, so 'multi-agent state' holds only via message conditioning and the cell is credited weakly. ONLY DOWNSTREAM RESULTS: no direct measure of world-model predictive accuracy - no reconstruction, observation, reward or continuation prediction error, no mutual information or CPC accuracy; evidence is episode return only (Observer: 5x4 messages 39.85, CI 34.22-40.82, vs IPPO-CPC 6.81-7.31 and obs-shared 53.63; CatchApple: 28.53 vs 4.98-5.52 and 38.21). Recommend exclude-E2 under the maintainer's ruling. Other doubts: only two agents, both environments author-designed, no component ablations (only message shape 20x1 vs 5x4), CIs given for some conditions only, and the authors state they 'did not analyze what information the learned messages carry'. The abstract's '4 to 5 times' is the CatchApple return ratio vs IPPO-CPC (28.53/5.52 is about 5.2, 20.47/4.98 about 4.1). Not safety, coordination/communication only. Extraction based on one full-document fetch summary.

title: HP-JEPA: Hierarchical Partitioning for Multi-Resolution Graph Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning
evidence: HP-JEPA predicts "masked targets directly in latent space" (Abstract); "no cross-resolution, adjacent-resolution, or parent-child consistency term is included" (Sec 4.2).
method: Extends Graph-JEPA with several independent partition resolutions, each with online encoder, EMA target encoder and predictor; predicts hyperbolic-coordinate function of masked target tokens; learned resolution-weighted readout.
evaluation: Seven TUDataset graph-classification sets and ZINC-12K; baselines Graph-JEPA, GraphMAE, S2GAE, BGRL and others (mostly quoted); linear-probe accuracy e.g. PROTEINS 76.97 percent, ZINC MAE 0.472; no hardware reported.
contribution: Multi-resolution graph JEPA that tokenises each graph at several partition scales and predicts masked latent targets per scale, modestly improving graph-classification probes over Graph-JEPA on six of eight tasks.
flag: Title matches. (b) is met in form (latent prediction over graphs; graph-level, static, no dynamics, no agents). ONLY DOWNSTREAM RESULTS: no direct measure of predictive accuracy - no latent prediction error, link prediction or forecasting; all metrics are linear-probe classification accuracy and ZINC MAE; Theorem 1 and Propositions 1-2 are bounds, not measurements. Recommend exclude-E2 under the maintainer's ruling. Further doubts: gains over Graph-JEPA mostly sit inside overlapping standard deviations (MUTAG 91.70 vs 91.25 with std about 5); HP-JEPA is worse on IMDB-M (50.51 vs 50.69) and ZINC (0.472 vs 0.434), yet the text says it 'consistently outperforms' on the IMDB datasets; most baseline numbers are copied from prior work; there is no formal ablation table, the text cites nine resolution-bank configurations but Figure 4 shows fewer, from one pretrained seed; no hardware, runtime or latency. Extraction based on one full-document fetch summary.

title: NodeJEPA: Structure-Conditioned Latent Prediction for Node-Level Graph Self-Supervised Learning
evidence: NodeJEPA "trains a context encoder to predict the latent representations of the masked nodes" (Abstract).
method: Context encoder predicts EMA target-encoder latents of masked k-hop ego-subgraph nodes with a restricted message-passing predictor; cosine loss plus VICReg and SIGReg regularisers; PatchJEPA predicts METIS patch embeddings.
evaluation: Five node-classification graphs incl. ogbn-arxiv; baselines DGI, GraphMAE, BGRL, CCA-SSG, supervised GCN; six ablations; linear-probe accuracy e.g. 69.31 percent arxiv; one A100, training-time only.
contribution: Node-level graph JEPA that predicts latent representations of masked ego-subgraph nodes, reaching the best average self-supervised rank on five node-classification benchmarks at a much higher training cost.
flag: Title matches. (b) is met in form (latent prediction over a graph, static, no dynamics, no agents). ONLY DOWNSTREAM RESULTS: no direct measure of predictive accuracy is reported - no latent prediction error, loss value, link prediction or forecasting; every number is linear-probe or few-shot node-classification accuracy or a collapse diagnostic (effective rank). Recommend exclude-E2 under the maintainer's ruling on downstream-only papers and the v1.6 minimum evaluation for (b). If he includes it anyway as architecture evidence: gains are small (average rank 2.4 tied with PatchJEPA; loses to CCA-SSG on Coauthor-Physics 90.60 vs 93.06, p=0.002), the no-structure ablation B beats the full model on Photo (88.74 vs 87.87), which undercuts the structure-conditioning claim, and training on ogbn-arxiv takes 31582 s vs about 2000-2400 s for baselines. Non-generative inference cell credited only in the sense of latent-space prediction without reconstruction. No inference latency reported. Extraction based on one full-document fetch summary.

title: MASS: Multiplayer World Models with Authoritative Shared State
evidence: A learned Logic Engine predicts the next typed world state from current state and joint player actions; "No hand-written transition function runs during rollout" (Sec 1).
method: Transformer Logic Engine predicts next authoritative typed-record state for all players from joint actions; separate learned renderer draws per-camera frames; clients extrapolate during update stalls.
evaluation: Multiplayer Snake (2-8 players, up to 1,024 entities) plus other games; baselines MultiWorld, B-PV, B-SL, B-UN, CNN, U-Net, RSSM; state accuracy 97.9/90.8/86.8 percent at H=1/32/128; 45.55 ms/step.
contribution: Multiplayer world model that keeps one authoritative typed shared state for all players, predicts it with a learned transformer and renders views separately, giving cross-view consistency and measurable state-level rollout accuracy.
flag: Title matches. (b) met: predictive model over the joint state of all players (typed entity records, not a graph). DIRECT predictive accuracy IS reported, not only downstream results: Table B.2 semantic accuracy 97.9/90.8/86.8 and position accuracy 99.1/90.2/72.3 at H=1/32/128 (dense baselines at most 2.7 percent position accuracy); Table 2 LPIPS 0.098 vs MultiWorld 0.277, Event F1 0.552 vs 0.065; Table C.1 exact match e.g. Breakout 84.5 percent at H=1 falling to 3.2 percent at H=128, Tile Merger 0.0 percent. Baselines and typed-vs-dense carrier ablation present. Not safety: a games/simulation paper with no interceptor; RQ5 capped. Doubts: (1) the abstract claim of 10,000 recurrent steps with 1,024 players was NOT found in the body as read - Table C.2 covers 2, 4 and 8 players to H=4096 and the 1,024-entity results appear qualitative; (2) latency figures are inconsistent - 45.55 ms per logic step (said to fit a 20 Hz tick) vs 740.7-867.4 ms in Table C.2 with the unit undefined, renderer 189.6-842.4 ms on one H100; I did NOT credit the latency/jitter-aware cell because the latency is far from sub-15 ms and stall handling is plain client-side extrapolation - maintainer may differ; (3) long-horizon accuracy decays sharply (position recall 1.000 to 0.224 by tick 128; judge score 100.0 at H=1 to 1.2 at H=600); (4) the SRSC metric uses an LLM judge; (5) X-view 0.000 holds by construction. The fetch reported some appendix content as not present, so 1,024-player throughput is unverified.

title: CausalNav: Reliability-Certified Causal World Models for Control under Physical-Parameter Shift
evidence: "reduces exactly to its base controller" when the reliability certificate fails (Sec 4.1); the proposition is "not a probabilistic control-safety guarantee" (Sec 4.4).
method: Action-conditioned causal transition model over eight identified state coordinates; H=8 planner advice added to PPO logits only when reliability certificate, margin and argmax-agreement gates pass.
evaluation: CartPole-v1 and discretised Pendulum-v1 under mass/length shift; nine controlled-adaptation baselines; returns over 10 seeds, one-step NRMSE 0.56, structure F1 0.59; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Single-agent causal world model whose planner advice is gated by a predictive-reliability certificate and otherwise abstains to the base controller, tested on CartPole and Pendulum under physical-parameter shift.
flag: Title matches. BORDERLINE on (b): the model is predictive, but it is single-agent and the 'graph' is a learned dependency graph among 8 scalar state coordinates of CartPole/Pendulum, not graph-structured or multi-agent state; I read that as not meeting (b), hence E1. If the maintainer reads (b) as met, the minimum evaluation is satisfied only thinly: a DIRECT predictive-accuracy measure IS reported (one-step NRMSE 0.56 +/- 0.38, CartPole only, Table 3; structure precision 0.53, recall 0.70, F1 0.59) alongside downstream returns, but Pendulum has no trained transition model and no prediction error. Not (a): the gate only adds planner advice to logits and by the paper's own proposition preserves the base controller's greedy action, so it cannot override, veto or halt; abstention is of the planner, not of an action. Results are weak: paired differences vs the routed expert are non-significant (CartPole ID -12.17, p=.766; shift +11.95, p=.768; Pendulum 0.00 by construction, certificate passes on 0/10 Pendulum seeds). Baselines are 'controlled adaptations', not native reproductions. Extraction based on one full-document fetch summary.

title: Population-Scalable Multi-Agent World Modeling across Scene Geometries
evidence: Cross-view consistency comes from "a shared world state" rather than "dense interactions among observation streams" (Sec. 4); Sec. 6 admits "the current evaluation is primarily qualitative."
method: Khora: shared world-coordinate entity table (STBoard) updated by a kinematic proposal plus learned residual per agent action; a diffusion-transformer renderer generates each agent's view from the projected state.
evaluation: Game-like maps, 2/4/8 views, runtime to 80 agents; 4 views PSNR 25.28, FVD 38.68 vs 73.49 without cross-agent state; Solaris at 2 views only; 107.16-116.73 ms per step, 37.33-34.27 FPS; GPU unnamed.
contribution: Khora keeps one shared entity-state table for all agents and renders each view from it, holding step latency near 107-117 ms from 1 to 80 agents.
flag: Fetched title is "Population-Scalable Multi-Agent World Modeling" without the record's "across Scene Geometries"; content matches, treated as the same paper. Borderline on v1.6: the only predictive metrics are video-quality scores (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FID, FVD), the authors call the evaluation primarily qualitative, and state-prediction error of the residual dynamics is never reported; E2 is defensible. Solaris beats Khora on FID (4.37 vs 7.71) and FVD (11.43 vs 36.55) at 2 views, undiscussed. Generative pixel renderer, so not non-generative. Latency is measured but not a constraint and uses one GPU per view, so latency/jitter and edge cells not credited. Environments unnamed; needs a per-map static prior. Humans appear only as raters in a user study of unstated size.

title: PBD-AG: Persistent Baseline-Delta Active Graphs with Uncertainty-Aware Inspection for Long-Horizon Service Robots
evidence: "graph uncertainty schedules active inspection of already-discovered fixtures" (Sec. 3.4); existence beliefs are updated with fixed hand-set log-odds increments, with no learned predictor of future graph state.
method: Persistent hierarchical scene graph for one service robot: frozen fixture baseline plus object deltas, visibility-gated existence updates, persistent IDs, and uncertainty-scored inspection view selection.
evaluation: OmniGibson/BEHAVIOR, 3 scenes x 3 seeds; coarse F1 .868 vs DynaMem-adapted .757, ConceptGraphs-adapted .696; dynamic IDF1 .833, event recall 11/12, false absence .014; no hardware or latency.
contribution: A baseline-plus-delta scene-graph memory with visibility-gated updates keeps object identities over long horizons for a single service robot, reaching 0.833 IDF1 on dynamic sequences.
flag: E1 on both grounds named in the Pillar 2 ruling: the model is not predictive (scene-graph memory maintenance with hand-set update rules, fixed scoring policy) and it is single-robot. Deferral of fixtures with no feasible view is inspection scheduling, not safety deferral. Conclusion cites paired acquisition experiments that I could not find as quantitative results. Physical-robot demo is qualitative only.

title: A Unifying Perspective on Causal World Models: From Observations to Representations to Structure
evidence: "CWMs should be understood as structured decision models rather than as monolithic predictors" (Sec. 4); the conclusion defers practical algorithms and empirical testing to future work.
method: Position paper defining causal world models as a tuple with relational latent states and a causal graph, plus a component-wise identifiability framework; no algorithm.
evaluation: None: no experiments, metrics, baselines, hardware or latency.
contribution: A perspective paper that formalises causal world models with a relational, graph-structured latent state and sets out component-wise identifiability conditions, without experiments.
flag: Topic matches (b) (graph-structured latent state) but there is no evaluation of any kind and no proved theorem evaluated; it reads as a position/perspective paper, so E3 is an equally defensible code. Single-agent MDP; entities are scene objects, not agents. Useful only as background vocabulary.

title: WONDER: A Radio World Model-based Negotiation Framework for Multi-Agent UAV Coverage Optimization
evidence: The JEPA-based radio world model "predicts each trajectory's" ... "incremental impact relative to the trajectories already committed" (Sec. IV-B).
method: JEPA radio world model predicts the latent change in seven coverage metrics for a candidate UAV trajectory given committed trajectories; a PPO election actor commits one trajectory per negotiation round.
evaluation: 62 ray-traced city scenes (11 test), 10 UAVs, 6 eval seeds; balanced score 0.870 vs MAPPO, STACCA, Flocking, MAGI; without JEPA encoder 0.659; offline recall 99.62% at Kc=3; no compute latency.
contribution: A JEPA world model that scores candidate UAV trajectories by predicted radio impact, conditioned on teammates' committed plans, lifts a multi-UAV coverage score to 0.870 against 0.659 without it.
flag: Predictive-accuracy evidence is thin: no regression error for the predicted metric change, only ranking recall (99.62% offline, 4.92 points above a DR variant) plus the encoder ablation; maintainer should decide whether recall satisfies the v1.6 predictive-metric test, else E2. Abstract says "0.162 coverage advantage over STACCA" but Sec. VI-B gives 0.162 as a score advantage in one representative scene. Each method trained with a single seed. Not safety; connectivity is a reward penalty, not a runtime block. Communication topology is an input, state is not an explicit graph.

title: Offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with a Physics-Informed World Model for Cooperative Mixed Traffic Control
evidence: "the physics model is not treated as the state transition function in this paper" (Sec. 3.2); a 7-member probabilistic ensemble predicts the next global traffic state and reward from the CAVs' joint histories.
method: Offline model-based MARL: transformer history encoder and per-cell cross-attention infer global density and speed from CAV beliefs; ensemble dynamics with soft LWR/CTM physics loss; pessimistic imagined rollouts.
evaluation: SUMO on-ramp merge, 15% CAV penetration, 1e6 offline transitions, 5 seeds; true-state MAE 0.09543 vs 0.41197 without physics; ATT 116.96 s vs 145.81 no control, 107.93 online MAPPO; no hardware or latency.
contribution: A physics-informed ensemble world model over the joint state of connected vehicles cuts true-state prediction error by 76.84% and supports offline multi-agent policy learning for ramp merging.
flag: Includable under (b) only: no safety metric at all (no collisions reported), outcomes are travel time and delay. State is cell-level traffic density and speed, not a graph. Uncertainty truncation acts on imagined rollouts in training, not at execution. Number of agents never stated. Paper is internally inconsistent on the policy optimiser (MAPPO in Sec. 3.4, MAIQL in Sec. 4.2). Simulation only.

title: When Graph-JEPA Learns the Wrong Thing: Diagnosing and Repairing Category-Conditional Collapse
evidence: "Masked-aspect retrieval against the full corpus nevertheless recovers 0.00 of 14.4 recoverable bits" (Abstract); Sec. 3 describes a Graph-JEPA predicting the latent embedding of a masked aspect of a paper subgraph.
method: Graph-JEPA (heterogeneous GIN encoder, EMA target, transformer mixer, latent predictor) on a scientific-paper graph; diagnoses category-conditional collapse and repairs it by changing target frame and loss.
evaluation: 58,149-record heterogeneous graph; 4,000-query masked-aspect retrieval in bits vs chance; baseline 0.00, repaired 14.377 of 14.379 bits; oracle 13.865, BM25 14.335; one L40S GPU; no latency.
contribution: Shows a Graph-JEPA can score 0.871 on linear probes yet recover 0.00 of 14.4 retrieval bits, and that changing target frame and loss restores 14.377 bits.
flag: Graph is a static citation-style graph of paper aspects, not agent or temporal state: latent prediction is masked-node, not forward-in-time, so (b) holds only on the broad reading. No multi-agent content, no action, no latency. Only the first 100k of about 170k characters read (appendices unread). Useful mainly as a warning that probe accuracy can hide JEPA collapse.

title: RiskWorld: Object-Centric Latent World Modeling for Autonomous Driving Risk Identification
evidence: RiskWorld "rolls relation-aware object states into the future using RSSM-style latent dynamics" (Abstract); it "remains a risk monitor rather than a closed-loop planner" (Discussion).
method: Object-centric RSSM latent world model on frozen V-JEPA2 features; masked relation attention over ego and up to 64 object tokens; latent rollout decodes position, distance and temporal risk without image generation.
evaluation: RiskBench, 6,916 CARLA scenarios, causal per-frame test; F1 63.0%, false alarm 2.1% vs FLaRA* 61.8, BADAS* 48.8, Range-10m 53.6 (FA 15.2); six ablations; planner collision rate 24.2% obstacles; no hardware or latency.
contribution: An object-centric latent world model rolls ego and road-agent states forward without generating images and identifies risk sources at 63.0% F1 with a 2.1% false-alarm rate on RiskBench.
flag: Closest record in this batch to the review's latent-interception idea, but it only scores risk: nothing halts or overrides the planner, hence interceptor no. (c) is arguable: primary outcome is risk-source F1 and false alarms against baselines, with planner collision rate secondary; drop (c) if the primacy test requires a hazard rate. Margin over FLaRA* is only 1.2 F1 points and collision-scenario recall is 40.4%. Interaction structure is attention over tokens, not an explicit graph. No hardware, latency or FPS reported, so RQ1 latency relevance is unsupported. Simulation (CARLA) only. RQ5 capped at 2 per protocol.

title: Clinical Graph-JEPA: Predictive Patient-State Knowledge Graphs for Cognitive Decision Support
evidence: "The evaluation is explicitly of a refiner" (Sec. 4.2); a context encoder predicts the latents that an EMA target encoder assigns to masked nodes or BFS patches of the admission graph (Sec. 3.2, App. A.7).
method: Graph-JEPA over per-admission patient knowledge graphs: typed graph transformer predicts EMA-target latents of masked nodes or patches; frozen encoder plus InfoNCE readout ranks candidate relation triples.
evaluation: MIMIC-IV, 4,000 admission graphs, plus ACI-Bench (207); note-free vs note-grounded and note-placement ablations; leave-one-out MRR 0.477 vs 0.364, Hits@10 0.917; no hardware or latency reported.
contribution: A graph JEPA over patient-state knowledge graphs recovers held-out clinical relations (MRR 0.477 with entity-grounded note features vs 0.364 without), positioned as decision support rather than autonomous decision-making.
flag: Borderline (b): latent prediction over a graph is genuine (graph transformer, EMA target), but what is predicted is MASKED latents of the current graph, NOT future patient state, despite the word Predictive in the title. Multi-agent only nominally: four LLM specialist agents propose edges during graph construction; the model state is one patient graph. Baselines are only the paper's own variants (no external link-prediction baseline). Batch-mask AUC is slightly WORSE with notes (0.805 vs 0.811). External ACI-Bench gain is tiny (MRR 0.481 vs 0.475). Graph-QA uses just 20 questions. Fig. 1 schema guard assigning revision actions conflicts with App. A.12, which says no Keep/Review/Prune actions are assigned; no clinician deferral step, so (e) not met. No hardware or latency figures at all. Recovery is against an LLM-drafted graph, not adjudicated labels.

title: Neurosymbolic Alignment for Physiologically-Safe Clinical Language Models
evidence: "the HGNN scorer is used only during alignment, and inference uses the aligned LLM alone" (Sec. I)
method: Iterative on-policy ORPO preference alignment of Mistral-7B using scores from a heterogeneous GNN over a static 847K-node physiological knowledge graph; scorer is discarded at inference.
evaluation: Synthetic CSB benchmark (2,500 scenarios), 5 seeds; vs SFT, RAG, DPO, ORPO, KG-LLM, DrugBank-Rule, GPT-4; CSS 90.8 vs 69.5, physician-rated hallucination 5.1 vs 14.1 percent; 8x A100, no inference latency.
contribution: Knowledge-graph-scored preference alignment makes a clinical LLM more physiologically consistent on a synthetic benchmark (CSS 90.8 vs 69.5 for ORPO), with no runtime verifier.
flag: The so-called Physiological World Model is a static knowledge graph plus HGNN plausibility scorer: no rollouts, no temporal prediction (authors list missing temporal physiology as a limitation), single model, no multi-agent state. Safety enters only through a training signal, so (a) fails; the selective deployment verifier and its <5 ms overhead are future work, not evaluated. E4 would also be defensible (single-input guardrail-style alignment). Evaluation circularity: the HGNN contributes to CSS and PC, and RSS uses the DrugBank-Rule baseline as checker. Synthetic data only. Text says six specialties, Table XIV lists seven; Table IV has missing cells; GPT-4 hallucination rate not reported.

title: HyperWorld: Hypergraph-Structured State Serialization Improves Learned Textual World Models
evidence: "it isolates the quality of the learned dynamics rather than the sophistication of search" (Sec. 3.4); a LoRA-tuned LLM maps a hypergraph-serialised state and an action to ADD/REMOVE fact effects or INFEASIBLE.
method: Textual world model: LoRA-fine-tuned Qwen2.5 (0.5B-3B) predicts symbolic state effects and feasibility from state+action, comparing hypergraph serialisation of the fact set against raw text, sentences and triples.
evaluation: 410 TextWorld games, IID and larger OOD test; vs raw, sentence, triple serialisations; OOD effect exact match 0.914 vs 0.838 (1.5B), rollout F1 0.989 at H=5; planning success 76.7% vs 56.7%; one RTX 5090, no latency.
contribution: Shows that serialising state as hyperedges per entity makes small LLM world models more accurate and seed-stable at next-state effect prediction, especially on larger out-of-distribution text games.
flag: DIRECT PREDICTIVE ACCURACY REPORTED (effect exact match and fact F1 per model size, IID and OOD, feasibility accuracy, multi-step rollout state F1) plus downstream planning success - meets the (b) minimum with baselines and a data-fraction ablation. BORDERLINE on graph state: the hypergraph is a text serialisation of a relational fact set, not a graph network, and the setting is single-player TextWorld with no multi-agent state; if the maintainer requires an actual graph-structured model or several agents this is E1. Doubts: gains vanish at 3B IID (triples 0.956 vs 0.952); raw observations give the best feasibility accuracy (0.965 vs 0.944); rollout margins are tiny (0.989 vs 0.983); seed means for 1.5B baselines (0.826, 0.805) differ from Table 1 single-run values (0.850, 0.838) unexplained; planning is 30 games and the 93.3% figure comes from removing the confidence term after seeing results on those games. Feasibility output is a soft planner score term, not a veto, hence interceptor no. arXiv id 2609.00002 is unusually low - title matched on fetch.

title: Self-Supervised Pretraining of Molecular Graph Encoders with LeJEPA
