evidence: "the benefit of pretraining is real at the level of the learned representation but does not robustly survive finetuning" (Abstract); the prediction term makes views of the same molecule agree, with no predictor network.
method: Predictor-free LeJEPA pretraining of molecular graph encoders: global and local subgraph views pulled to the global-view centroid, SIGReg isotropic-Gaussian regulariser, RDKit descriptors on global views.
evaluation: Antibiotic screen (39,312 compounds) and ogbg-molhiv; vs descriptor models, Chemprop, random-init, Morgan fingerprints; frozen-probe ROC-AUC 0.788 vs 0.665; fine-tuning gain 0.005; 4 GPUs, no latency.
contribution: LeJEPA pretraining of molecular graph encoders improves frozen-probe representations (ogbg-molhiv ROC-AUC 0.788 vs 0.665 random-init) but the benefit largely disappears under fine-tuning.
flag: Recommended E1 because the model is not predictive in the review's sense: predictor-free multi-view agreement on static molecules, no dynamics, no actions, no agent state; world models appear only as motivation. It IS a JEPA-family method on graphs, so if the maintainer admits Tactile-JEPA (2609.24385) or Clinical Graph-JEPA (2608.22583) on a literal reading of latent prediction over graphs, this one should be judged consistently. Internal inconsistency: Table 4 pooled p-value 0.004 vs text 0.095. Mostly a negative or mixed result.

title: GAVEL: Graph World Models for Verified and Efficient Long-Horizon LLM Task Planning
evidence: "Each action is applied only if its preconditions hold. Otherwise rollout stops at the first violation." (Sec. IV-F); transition function f(G, a) returns the predicted next scene graph or invalid.
method: Typed scene-graph world model with symbolic transition function rolls out LLM plans before execution, rejects invalid actions, applies graph-derived repairs, feeds residual failures back to the LLM; belief-based task ordering.
evaluation: BEHAVIOR-1K, 100 single and 500 multi-task instructions, symbolic executor checked in OmniGibson; vs LLM-only, SayPlan, EPoG; success 91.8 vs 76.4 percent; planning 15.5 s; ordering about 17 ms.
contribution: A scene-graph world model verifies and repairs LLM task plans before execution, lifting BEHAVIOR-1K success from 76.4 percent (SayPlan) to 91.8 percent with fewer LLM calls.
flag: Check three things. (1) The world model is a hand-specified SYMBOLIC precondition-effect transition over a graph, not learned or latent; only the room-belief network (RSN) is learned. (2) Minimum evaluation for (b): no predictive-accuracy metric for the transition model itself; nearest are RSN AUC 0.904 and Brier 0.057 (true room ranked first in only 47 percent of 832 queries) and cost-model R2 0.93, none with a baseline; headline metrics are task success, not prediction accuracy. (3) runtime_interceptor set to yes because the verifier vetoes and repairs plan steps before execution, but this is plan-time validation inside a planner loop, not an execution-time monitor, so (a) NOT claimed; no safety metric is reported. Single robot, no multi-agent state. Paper does not say what happens when verification still fails after 5 calls. GPU model unspecified. Table I row labels were garbled in extraction; values assigned per the text's order. Simulation only.

title: Few-Shot Demonstrations Elicit the Use of In-Context World Representations in LLMs
evidence: "is nearly orthogonal to the world representation subspace" (Sec. 4.2); world model is defined as a world property linearly recoverable from internal representations and causally used for prediction, studied on static token-labelled graphs.
method: Interpretability study: linear probes and activation interventions test whether LLMs form and use in-context representations of a latent static graph, and how few-shot demonstrations change their use.
evaluation: Random-walk graph tracing on 5 grid topologies, 6 LLMs; zero-shot, random-probe and random-subspace controls; probe AUROC about 0.69-0.78; also ARC-AGI, Mind2Web, Othello; GH200 GPUs, no latency.
contribution: Probing study showing few-shot demonstrations make LLMs causally use an in-context latent graph representation they already encode, with probe AUROC near 0.7-0.78 unchanged across shot counts.
flag: Not a world-model or latent-prediction METHOD: it is a mechanistic-interpretability analysis of existing LLMs. The graph is static (no transition dynamics; paper says it does not cover the simulator sense of world model) and there is no multi-agent state. If the maintainer reads (b) as including evaluations of internal graph world representations it could be reconsidered, but nothing here predicts future state. Most main-text results are plots only; exact numbers found only in Appendix E.3 for Qwen3-4B on the 4x4 lattice. Abstract claim of 6 models from 4 families relies on appendix E.1. Practical-task gains (ARC, Mind2Web, Othello) have no numeric values in text.

title: Tactile-JEPA: Topology-Aware Self-Supervised Representation Learning for Distributed Tactile Sensors
evidence: "The target encoder parameters are maintained as an exponential moving average (EMA) of the context encoder weights." (Sec. III-B); the model predicts embeddings of masked taxels from visible ones, with masks sampled on the taxel connectivity graph.
method: I-JEPA-style masked latent prediction for tactile skins: taxel connectivity graph drives local (Dijkstra) and global mask sampling; transformer context encoder, EMA target, 4-block predictor, MSE latent loss.
evaluation: Sparsh-skin, tactile socks, DECO-50 bimanual policy; vs end-to-end, BYOL, MAE, DINO, mask ablation; force RMSE 14.05 vs 15.00 cN, theta-RMSE 5.48 vs 6.92 deg; 4x A100, no latency.
contribution: Topology-aware JEPA pretraining for distributed tactile sensors predicts masked taxel embeddings using graph-sampled masks, lowering force error 6.3 percent and in-hand orientation error 20.8 percent versus prior self-supervised baselines.
flag: WEAK (b), maintainer may well prefer E1: prediction is spatial in-filling of masked sensor latents within one time window, not forward prediction of a world state; the graph is a sensor layout used ONLY for mask sampling (encoder is a plain transformer, not a GNN); single robot or person, no multi-agent state. No predictive-accuracy metric as such, only downstream probe metrics, so the v1.6 minimum for (b) is arguable. MAE beats it on the only policy task (0.4400 vs 0.4634 RMSE); object-classification gain is nil (83.27 vs 83.26). n=3 seeds, no multiple-comparison correction. Claim of 65-75 percent faster pretraining than DINO has no supporting table. No inference latency despite a control-loop-rate claim.

title: Relationally Grounded Latent World Models for Autonomous Driving
evidence: "the scene graph explicitly emphasizes relative orientation and proximity between traffic participants" (Sec. III-B); "All scene-graph, text-embedding, and alignment components are used only during training and discarded at inference" (Sec. II-D)
method: LAW latent driving world model whose visual latents are cosine-aligned to a frozen text embedding of an actor-centric scene graph (ego, vehicles, cyclists, pedestrians); branch dropped at inference.
evaluation: nuScenes open-loop planning; retrained LAW, unstructured-text variant, loss-weight ablations; avg L2 0.661 to 0.622 m, collision 0.456 to 0.217 percent; 4x H200 training, no latency reported.
contribution: Aligning a latent driving world model to a multi-actor scene graph during training cuts open-loop nuScenes collision rate from 0.456 to 0.217 percent with no added inference cost.
flag: Borderline (b): the latent state is a set of visual latents, NOT a graph; the multi-agent scene graph is only a training target encoded as text by a frozen Qwen embedding model. Maintainer should decide if relational supervision counts as multi-agent state. Open-loop only, no closed-loop sim, single runs with no seeds or variance. Collision rate is a planner metric, not an interceptor outcome. Temporal (future-latent) alignment alone worsens collision (0.476, 0.659). 52.4 percent collision reduction is against the authors' retrained LAW, not the published checkpoint. No inference latency measured.

title: Beyond Static Graph World Models: Learning Stochastic Latent Dynamics over Evolving Topologies
evidence: Sec. 4.1 (paraphrase): the Graph Dynamics Model is an RSSM-style latent model with per-node and graph-level deterministic and stochastic states and a sampled recurrent adjacency matrix that is part of the latent state.
method: Stochastic latent graph world model: per-node and graph-level categorical latents plus a recurrent sampled adjacency (Hard Concrete edge edits); predicts next graph, reward, continuation and action mask.
evaluation: Four graph environments, train 15-25 nodes, test 20-1000; vs Vanilla GWM, EA-GWM, G-RSSM; GDD e.g. OD 0.449 vs 0.916, SAR 0.917 vs 1.122; ablations; 10 seeds; no latency.
contribution: A stochastic latent world model whose state includes a sampled, evolving adjacency predicts graph transitions better than static-topology graph world models and holds up from 20 to 1000 nodes.
flag: Single agent acting on a graph (node-selection actions), not multi-agent, so no multi-agent cell. Prediction-only evaluation under a random policy: no control or planning result. Multi-step results and adjacency BCE appear only in figures, no numbers in text; rollout range stated as 2-5 steps in text but 1-5 in Fig. 7 caption. Removing graph-level state improves GDD on OD and SAR. GDM ties or loses to Vanilla GWM in CF at 200 nodes (1.249). No latency or hardware beyond GPUs with 16 GB. Evidence is paraphrased by the fetch tool, check wording.

title: MA-WAM: Multi-Agent World-Action Model for Test-Time Planning
evidence: Sec. 3 (paraphrase): the Routed World Model's dynamics model predicts the next joint observation of all agents and its reward model predicts per-agent rewards; candidates are ranked by predicted cumulative return. "The policy remains fixed, and selection stays within its sampled candidates." (Sec. 1)
method: Frozen flow policy proposes 8 joint-action sequences; a frozen routed mixture-of-experts world model rolls out joint observations and rewards, ranks candidates, executes the first joint action, replans.
evaluation: 30 offline MARL settings (MAMuJoCo, SMAC, MPE), 5 seeds; 13 baselines; planning beats reactive on 26 of 30 (+22.0%); rollout MSE 0.037-0.199 at H=8; scoring 13.4 ms, total 428 ms on RTX 3090.
contribution: Test-time planning for offline multi-agent RL: a routed world model over joint observations scores sampled joint-action plans in about 13 ms and improves return on 26 of 30 settings.
flag: Fetch covered about 100k of 136k characters: Appendix A.8 and B (formal model, pseudocode, routing equations) NOT read. The 12-13 ms figure is world-model scoring only on RTX 3090 or A100 (not edge); candidate generation dominates at 415-462 ms. Selects the best candidate, never vetoes or halts, so no interceptor. Centralized execution only. Same-state counterfactual ranking is weak (Top-1 0.275 vs 0.125 chance; 4Ant-Medium at chance), much weaker than the snippet Spearman 0.81. Dynamics trained by MSE regression in observation space, not latent.

title: Metro-WM: Long-Horizon Latent Planning with Realisable Sub-Goals
evidence: "METRO-WM replaces the prediction of Eq. 2 with a shortest-path search over prior experience." (Section 5)
method: Frozen single-agent JEPA world model (LeWM or PLDM) with CEM-MPC as micro planner; non-parametric macro planner does shortest-path search over a graph of encoded frames from recorded episodes.
evaluation: PUSHT, OGBench-CUBE, TWOROOM, REACHER; 50 query episodes x 3 seeds; baselines flat LeWM/PLDM, Hi-LeWM, Hi-LeWM-C; metrics success rate and mean planning latency; no prediction-error metric.
contribution: Replaces learned latent sub-goal prediction in hierarchical JEPA planning with shortest-path search over a graph of recorded experience, raising long-horizon success by 4 to 37 points at up to 10.9x lower planning time.
flag: Title matches. Read via arxiv.org/pdf/2609.31868v1 in ONE fetch (tool-summarised whole PDF; no offset re-reads because the host then rate-limited everything). E1 reasoning: single-agent manipulation/navigation, no multi-agent state; the graph is an episodic memory over recorded frames (vertices = encoded frames, temporal and bridge edges), not a graph-structured world state, and the macro level explicitly removes prediction. Predictive accuracy: NOT reported - only downstream results (success rate, latency, offline compute); closest items are a realisability residual r(z) (median 0.9 CUBE, 2.3 PUSHT) and a latent gap ratio, neither a prediction error. So E2 would apply as well if the maintainer reads the experience graph as graph state. No runtime veto/halt/defer and no human takeover; the fallback to direct goal-seeking when graph progress is exhausted is a planner fallback, not an interceptor. Headline numbers found in body: +16.67 PUSHT, +18.00 CUBE, +37.33 TWOROOM, +4.00 REACHER points over Hi-LeWM-C at d=75; 2.2-10.9x faster; 13-56x less offline compute. Caveat on the 'outperforms an oracle' claim: METRO-PLDM is below the oracle on PUSHT (44.00 vs 72.00) and METRO-LeWM slightly below (62.67 vs 64.00). GPU used for online latency is not stated (sweep ran on 8x A100 80GB).

title: CyberWorld: World Models for Sample-Efficient Autonomous Cyber Defense
evidence: "a Dreamer-style world modeling framework" (Abstract); graph arm uses "graph-attention message passing" over the host adjacency (Sec. 3.2)
method: DreamerV3-style RSSM world model for a network defender; state is per-host node features, optionally encoded by GAT over static host graph; change-weighted state loss, class-balanced reward loss.
evaluation: CyberWheel, 15-100 hosts, 4 scripted attackers, 3 seeds; vs PPO, GNN-PPO, rule control; steps to beat control e.g. 3,600 vs 25,875 (GNN-PPO) vs 3.08M (PPO); A100; no latency.
contribution: Dreamer-style latent world model over a host-network state lets a cyber defender beat a rule-based control in thousands rather than millions of environment steps, with a graph-encoded variant compared.
flag: Graph state is one of five representation arms and is not clearly better than the vector arm (worse on 2 of 4 attackers at N=15; 43 GB vs 10 GB at N=100); the paper is mainly about sample efficiency. Single centralized defender vs scripted attackers, authors explicitly avoid multi-agent coordination. Predictive fidelity (state-bit and reward loss) only in Fig. 5, no numbers in text, so the v1.6 predictive-accuracy minimum is weak. Has reconstruction heads (not non-generative). PPO comparison not budget-matched. Seconds-per-step only in figures.

title: Scanning While Imagining: A Scene-Graph World Model for Robotic Ultrasound Navigation
evidence: Sec. III-A/III-B (paraphrase): SonoGraph-WM is an action- and goal-conditioned Transformer that predicts the next K=10 anatomical scene graphs and probe poses from H=10 past graph-pose pairs, without synthesising ultrasound images.
method: Scene-graph world model: Transformer predicts future anatomical scene graphs (up to 7 nodes, 3 relation types) and probe poses; receding-horizon planner imagines 8 branches recursively and replans each step.
evaluation: CADS CT, 24 patients (4 held out); relation F1 93.6-94.9%, node F1 82.7-93.1%, bbox mIoU 31.6-42.4%; navigation 77.5%, 75.0%; KUKA phantom 14/19; no baselines; no latency.
contribution: Predicts future anatomical scene graphs and probe poses instead of images, and uses recursive imagination over those graphs to steer a robotic ultrasound probe to target views.
flag: BORDERLINE E2: quantitative predictive metrics exist but NO baseline and no component ablation (authors say evaluated without isolating individual design contributions); only an execution-horizon comparison (1 vs 5 vs 10 steps). Single robot, graph is anatomy not agents. Predictions are symbolic graphs, not latent, so the non-generative cell is arguable. Planner returns NO_GOAL_REACHED when no branch qualifies, which is planner-internal, not an interceptor. Inputs are annotation-derived graphs; B-mode perception untested. Evidence is paraphrased by the fetch tool, check wording.

title: Phenomenon-Graph JEPA: Label-Efficient Representation Learning for Contactless Cardiorespiratory Sensing
evidence: "It is not a graph neural network, and no messages are exchanged at inference" (Sec. 3.2)
method: JEPA pretraining for radar, rPPG and depth physiological streams; the graph is two typed cross-stream prediction edges among four sensor nodes; output is activity and pose classification.
evaluation: OMuSense-23 (50 participants) and WESAD (15); vs matched supervised, wrong-edge and all-pairs graphs; label-efficiency +3.91 pp (C1), macro-F1 36.25 vs 28.68 at 1.11% labels; RTX 2080 SUPER.
contribution: Label-efficient JEPA pretraining across contactless cardiorespiratory sensor streams; improves over supervised training on one corpus, with no gain from the typed pairing over wrong or all-pairs edges.
flag: Not a world model: no actions, no dynamics of an environment, no agents; the graph is a fixed set of two sensor-pairing edges used only in pretraining. Has a 10-20 s future-window latent prediction term, but over a single biosignal stream. Typed graph did not beat wrong-edge graph (-0.74 pp, n.s.). Clear E1 on reading.

title: MA-JEPA: Joint-Embedding World Models for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
evidence: "MA-JEPA learns latent dynamics by predicting future observation embeddings." (Abstract); "Neither the joint predictor nor the centralized critic is used during execution." (App. D.6)
method: JEPA-style multi-agent world model: per-agent latent states, centralized joint predictor (agent self-attention, causal Transformer) predicts next observation embeddings; CTDE policies trained in imagination.
evaluation: SMAC v1, 8 maps, 3 seeds, 100k-400k steps; vs DMAWM, MAPPO, QMIX, MAT; win rate e.g. corridor 66.0 vs 50.0; gradient ablation 77.0 vs 69.8-73.9; A100, no latency.
contribution: Shows a non-reconstructive joint-embedding world model over joint multi-agent latent state can match a reconstruction-based multi-agent world model on SMAC win rate at low sample budgets.
flag: No predictive-accuracy metric: only win rates and a gradient ablation, so the v1.6 minimum for (b) is met only via the maintainer ruling (experiments present). World model is training-only, not used at execution. Results text says matches or exceeds DMAWM on four maps; Table 1 means give five. Third ablation map not named. No latency figures. Only 3 seeds.

title: WorldGraph: Graph-Native World Modeling
evidence: Abstract: "graph evolution itself constitutes the world dynamics"; Sec 3.1 builds latent node-level states from multi-hop and random-walk views plus a history-aware encoder.
method: Graph-native world model: state-aware graph transformer with history encoder gives latent node states; a transition policy trained with transition-aware GRPO samples graph edits predicting node, edge and graph-level changes.
evaluation: GWM-Zero, 8 temporal graph datasets, 13 baselines (GCN, TGN, Graph-JEPA, C-SWM, GWM-E); avg +10.77% over best baseline; TGBN-Trade Add F1 0.970, Rem F1 0.661; ablations; 4x V100, 66.89 s/epoch, no inference latency.
contribution: Treats the evolution of a graph as the world dynamics and learns to predict node, edge and graph-level transitions as sampled edit sequences, outperforming static, temporal and world-model graph baselines.
flag: Offline prediction on temporal graph benchmarks; not multi-agent in the acting sense and no safety content. Inference samples edit sequences with a policy, so I did not claim non-generative inference. Baseline count inconsistent in the paper (13 in Sec 4.1, eleven in App F.2). Table 1 was not read in full, only selected values; the 10.77% headline is the paper's own average. Only training time per epoch is reported (App H.1), no inference latency. Quotes relayed by fetch tool, not checked verbatim.

title: Graph World Models for Constrained Epidemic Policy Planning
evidence: Sec 2.2.3: "a positive rho_exec certifies the learned rollout, not the unknown true environment"; the GF-RSSM keeps per-region latent states and aggregates neighbours over a mobility graph (Eq. 6).
method: Graph-factored recurrent state-space world model over a time-varying mobility graph of regions, frozen for planning; graph-temporal ADMM optimises interventions with budget projection and smooth STL robustness.
evaluation: Synthetic 5-region and US state semi-synthetic simulator; vs Action-LSTM, VARX, no-graph, MPC, PPO, MAPPO: admission RMSE 0.221 vs 0.311 no-graph; admissions 29.89 vs 64.14 per 100K; budget feasibility 100%. No hardware or latency.
contribution: Learns a graph-factored latent world model of epidemic spread across mobility-linked regions and plans budget-feasible interventions through it, with a 29% forecast error reduction over the same model without the graph.
flag: Constraints live inside the planner (projection, STL term), not a runtime shield, so (a) is not met; STL is only checked on the learned rollout and nothing happens if it fails. Regions are graph nodes with per-region action blocks but the paper does not call the setting multi-agent, so the multi-agent state cell is not claimed - maintainer may differ. Learned planner has higher regret than oracle dynamics in all 9 configurations; coordination ablation gains under 1% and called incremental by the authors; a best feasible constant policy slightly beats it on the synthetic objective. Framed as decision support, no handoff mechanism. Real-context results are model-relative projections. Quotes relayed by fetch tool, not checked verbatim.

title: DeepRewind: Predicting and Repairing Premature Commitments in Deep Research Agents
evidence: Abstract: "A binary controller blocks risky commitments"; Sec 3: "A NOT-COMMIT decision leaves the base agent free to gather more evidence."
method: Control layer on Open Deep Research: a prompted LLM world model predicts changes to a typed research-state graph and reversibility per candidate commitment; a gate commits or defers; a monitor rolls back invalidated commitments.
evaluation: DRBench and LiveDRBench, 100 tasks each, 4 backbones, 3 seeds, vs ODR and 4 ablations; premature commitment 31.7% to 13.1%; recall +3.6, precision +3.1 points; latency +14%, tokens +6.5%; no hardware.
contribution: Gates a deep-research agent's commitments with a predicted research-state graph and rolls back those later invalidated, cutting premature commitments by more than half at 14% extra latency.
flag: Single agent, so check E4: I judged it sequential (gate plus rollback over a trajectory), hence not E4. The hazard is premature epistemic commitment, not a safety hazard in the usual sense - maintainer to judge whether (a) is met. For (b) the paper admits (Limitations) it does not evaluate accuracy or calibration of the world model's predicted graph transitions, so (b) alone would fail the v1.6 minimum; inclusion rests on (a). World model is a prompted GPT-4o, i.e. generative. Predicts reversibility of commitments but no time-to-irreversibility, so that cell is not claimed. Abstract says 59.1% relative reduction; Table 4 (31.7 to 13.1) gives about 58.7%. Quotes relayed by fetch tool, not checked verbatim.

title: Do-JEPA: From Masking to Intervention in Latent World Models
evidence: Sec 3.1: action-conditioned latent predictor over object slots z_t in R^(K x d); Sec 3.3: "planning uses only the factual prediction". Gated message passing learns soft edge gates between slots (Eq. 5, 7).
method: JEPA-style action-conditioned latent predictor trained on paired factual and reference-action futures to learn the action effect; a sparse mask locates where the action enters and gated message passing learns slot-to-slot edges.
evaluation: Synthetic SCMs, state/vision/LeWM Push-T, CausalWorld vs MASK (C-JEPA), AUG, OBS; edge AUROC 0.975 vs 0.624; LeWM effect RMSE -28.4%; CausalWorld effect RMSE -20% under shift; A100 GPUs, no latency.
contribution: Replaces masking with intervention in JEPA world models: training on paired action and reference futures makes the latent predictor learn action effects and a sparse propagation structure across object slots.
flag: BORDERLINE (b): graph is only learned soft gates between object slots, present in the synthetic and state Push-T models; the LeWM backbone uses one global latent (K=1) with no gates, and nothing is multi-agent. Maintainer may prefer exclude-E1. Mixed results: CausalWorld factual RMSE 51-53% worse (beyond the paper's own preregistered tolerance), AUG control beats it on vision Push-T, planning success within +/-3 pp of base. Needs an exactly restorable simulator. Only the first 100000 of 121990 characters were read (late appendix unread). Quotes relayed by fetch tool, not checked verbatim.

title: World-as-Graph: Relational World Modeling Through Latent Space Graphs
evidence: Sec 2.2.2: the "memory-driven future predictor" will "autoregressively evolve the learned object-level memory states"; Sec 2.2.1 builds a time-varying latent KNN graph over object slots.
method: JEPA-style object-centric world model: slots become nodes of a dynamic latent KNN graph; relation-aware masking, temporal GNN encoder and memory GRU predict future object latents autoregressively.
evaluation: CLEVRER VQA and PushT CEM planning vs OC-JEPA, C-JEPA, DINO-WM; CLEVRER 91.37% vs 89.40%, PushT 90.70% vs 88.67%; latent MSE 4.83 vs 6.66 (x1e-3); one NVIDIA H20, no inference latency.
contribution: Models the world as a sequence of latent graphs over object slots and predicts future object states in latent space, improving on C-JEPA in visual reasoning and matching it in planning at far lower memory.
flag: Graph nodes are object slots, not agents; single-robot PushT only. Main metrics are downstream (VQA accuracy, planning success); direct predictive accuracy is only a latent-MSE case study (Sec 3.4) - check that satisfies the v1.6 minimum. Headline "up to 30.03 pp" is against OC-DINO-WM, gain over C-JEPA on PushT is 2.03 pp and DINO-WM (91.33%) still beats it. Efficiency figures are training time and memory (410 vs 6712 MiB), not inference latency. Quotes relayed by fetch tool, not checked verbatim.

title: World Requirement Model: Learning Requirement-Change Consequences from Typed Artifact Graphs
evidence: Sec 3.4: "Input nodes and edges remain intact, permitting relation additions but not node/text edits or edge deletion." State is a typed directed multigraph of requirement artifacts; action is a candidate edit.
method: State-action-successor model over a typed artifact multigraph (8 node, 10 relation types); Qwen2.5+LoRA node encoder, typed propagation and graph attention; heads score impact, conflict, violation, defect risk.
evaluation: WRM-Bench, 282 synthetic LLM-labelled cases, 28 test; vs hashed-text MLP, TF-IDF, BM25, GLM prompts: impact MAP 0.724 vs 0.626, nDCG@10 0.831 vs 0.747, violation F1 0.693 vs 0.617. No hardware or latency.
contribution: Learns to predict the downstream consequences of a requirement change as scores and relation additions over a typed artifact graph, beating text and prompt baselines on a small synthetic benchmark.
flag: Weak evidence: only 28 test cases, labels are synthetic LLM judgments, paper admits checkpoints were selected on the scored cases and backbones are unmatched; no matched ablations (baselines only). Predicts consequence scores and added relations rather than a full successor state - check it is predictive enough for (b). Not multi-agent, logical domain only. Runtime and analyst effort unmeasured. Quotes relayed by fetch tool, not checked verbatim.

title: Software World Models: From Consequence Prediction to Decision Value
evidence: "We instead model the software system the agent changes, rather than only the environment it observes." (Sec 1); state is a typed System-Surface Graph with latent per-component execution state.
method: Software World Model: fine-tuned code LLM, optionally with relational-GCN graph tokens, predicting the blast set and check feedback of a code change over a typed system-surface graph; trained by exploration and GRPO.
evaluation: Synthetic multi-service systems and two real library ecosystems; baselines typed reachability, CWM, Qwen-AgentWorld, GNN-only; blast-set F1 0.571 vs 0.431; ranking regret 0.593 vs 1.430; one A100-80GB; no latency.
contribution: A fine-tuned code model predicts which components a software change will break over a typed system graph, cutting candidate-ranking regret from 1.43 to 0.59 against graph reachability and reducing broken consumers.
flag: Graph-state consequence predictor in a logical/enterprise domain, close to the review's software-agent side, but generative (LLM emitting JSON), one-step only (no rollout), and single coding agent - services are components, not agents, so no multi-agent cell. Not a runtime gate: predictions rank candidates and trigger paid checks; no hard veto, so runtime_interceptor no; maintainer may want to look at Proposition 1 (cost-threshold check/migration rule) as a near-deferral mechanism. Paper admits cheap exhaustive checks (return 0.826) beat the learned belief plan (0.757), and that some differences are within seed variation; synthetic return gain is +0.052 with SD 0.052. Supervised recipe F1 0.608 exceeds the GRPO 0.571 headline. Model size unclear (3B agents vs 0.5B predictor in Table 13). Tables 5 and 13 garbled. Human oversight is only recommended in the ethics statement, not evaluated.

title: BeliefGraph-JEPA: Structured Latent World Models for Action-Conditioned Time Series
evidence: "a structured latent world model that factorizes driver influence into typed latent-effect states" (Abstract); a relation-aware GNN routes these states to target nodes (method section).
method: BeliefGraph-JEPA: JEPA-style latent predictor over a typed relational graph of actions, exogenous inputs, latent-effect families and targets, with recurrent per-family belief states and a gated residual for direct drivers.
evaluation: VitalDB, greenhouse, wastewater, district heating; baselines persistence, Chronos-2, TimesFM 2.5, DAG, TFT plus internal ladder; nMAE 0.0495 vs TFT 0.0576 (PreDist); loses on wastewater; one A100; no latency.
contribution: A JEPA-style world model with a typed graph of latent effect states forecasts action-conditioned industrial and clinical time series, matching or beating TFT on three of four systems with 2-3M parameters.
flag: Graph is over variables (actions, effects, targets) of ONE physical system, not over agents; no multi-agent state. All four domains are physical/clinical processes, so no cross-domain cell. Evaluation is retrospective forecasting conditioned on logged future actions; no planning or control (stated as future work). Gains over TFT are small and TFT wins on wastewater nMAE and on Shanghai glucose. Has an observation decoder, so 'non-generative' holds for the latent prediction objective only; maintainer may tighten. PreDist carries a dagger footnote I did not see explained. Text read to 100k of 116k characters (cut in Appendix K.2). Small model (2.0-3.1M params) but no inference latency reported.

title: Independent Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Counterfactual Semantic-Social World Models
evidence: "agents can learn more effectively by prospectively comparing the consequences of candidate actions" (Abstract); the SSWM predicts task progress, distances and interaction events per candidate action (Sec III).
method: CASTLE: frozen pretrained local RSSM plus a semantic-social transformer predicting H-step consequence tokens per candidate ego action; tokens bias IPPO actor logits with a coefficient annealed to zero.
evaluation: JaxMARL MPE Tag/Spread/Adversary, 30 seeds; baselines IPPO, IQL, DPO, Dreamer; normalized score avg 95.70 vs 85.09 best baseline; held-out pretraining 87.44; one L40 GPU; no latency.
contribution: Pretrained counterfactual world models that predict the social consequences of each candidate action give independent multi-agent learners a temporary prior, raising normalized MPE scores from 85 to 96.
flag: Borderline on two counts. (1) State: at runtime each model sees only its own agent's local history; joint simulator state is used only offline to build counterfactual labels, so 'multi-agent state' is nominal - the model predicts interaction outcomes, not a joint state. (2) Minimum evaluation: no numeric predictive-accuracy value in the text; prediction quality appears only in Fig. 2 (distance ranking correlation, event error by horizon), which I could not read; ablations (Sec IV-E, Fig. 4) are also figure-only. If figure-only evidence is insufficient this is E2. The logit bias is soft and annealed to zero by update 244, not an override. Held-out and in-domain (R) variants lose to plain IPPO on Tag (72.4 vs 78.1); headline gain needs target-task data. Text says KL decreases monotonically yet reports a mid-training peak. Evidence quote from abstract.

title: Learning in Dreams, Winning in Reality: A Continuous Dyna Loop for a Ten-Hero MOBA
evidence: Closely paraphrased from the world-model section: each of the 206 units is one token plus a global token, and the actions of all ten heroes enter the model at every tick to predict the next game state.
method: 0.66M-parameter transformer world model over per-unit tokens of a ten-hero MOBA, trained autoregressively; PPO policy trains inside it in a continuous Dyna loop with KL anchor and drift guard.
evaluation: PufferLib MOBA vs shipped net, holdout seeds; radiant wins 70.2% (421/600) from 33.7%; 200-tick hero position error 9.7 cells vs 28.5 no-change, 22.8 pre-Dyna; A40 GPUs, 135k steps/s.
contribution: A tiny symbolic world model over all 206 units of a ten-hero MOBA, refreshed continuously with real games, lifts a dream-trained policy from 34% to 70% wins and shows model exploitation is invisible in-dream.
flag: Single-author paper; evidence field is a paraphrase, not a verbatim quote, so check wording. State is joint multi-agent (per-unit tokens with attention) but explicitly not a graph. Prediction is in symbolic state space, not latent, so non-generative cell not claimed; maintainer may disagree. Anchor, drift guard and promotion gate act on training, not on live actions, so not (a). Fidelity is poor for events (stuns 2% precision, hero deaths 20% recall). Dire side wins 0/300 throughout. Real-game count inconsistent (about 46,000 in text vs 10,700 in Table 1). Tables 2, 4, 6 garbled in extraction. Throughput given but no per-decision latency.

title: Multi-Agent Egocentric World Model with Fine-Grained Embodied Interaction
evidence: "ME-World performs joint multi-agent generation by denoising all streams in a shared token sequence" (Sec 1, Introduction).
method: ME-World: fine-tuned video diffusion transformer jointly denoising several agents' egocentric streams in one token sequence, conditioned on all agents' body and head poses and a shared environment memory.
evaluation: CoMind real and Blender synthetic two-agent clips (100 each); baselines GEN3C, EgoSim, MultiWorld, Solaris, MetaWorld; S_env 0.468 vs 0.421, PSNR 19.85, FVD 637.9; 4 A100 training; no latency.
contribution: A video diffusion world model generates consistent first-person futures for two interacting agents by denoising their streams jointly, beating adapted multi-agent baselines on shared-world consistency (0.468 vs 0.421).
flag: Weak fit: pixel-generative video diffusion (35 denoising steps, 77 frames), the opposite of the review's non-generative latent target; shared state is implicit pooled memory, not a graph or explicit joint state; only two human agents; no planning, control or safety use (planning is listed as future work). Metrics are video quality and consistency, not state-prediction error. Ablation Table 4 was garbled in extraction so ablation numbers are unverified. No inference time or FPS reported. Include only as architecture background; maintainer may prefer E1.

title: CivWorldBench: Evaluating Language World Models in Structured Multi-Agent Sandbox Worlds
evidence: "Isolating world-model capabilities therefore requires prediction tasks with verifiable hidden states and intervention outcomes" (Sec 1); worlds are multi-civilization Freeciv games.
method: Benchmark on the Freeciv engine testing language models as world models: association forecasts, hidden-belief inference and intervention prediction over recorded multi-agent game states with paired counterfactual rollouts.
evaluation: 475 worlds, 1,900 decision points; 11 LLMs vs FLOOR/EXPERT/CEILING references; SWFI index best 29.47 (Claude Opus 5) vs EXPERT 51.18; ablations on history, thinking, notes; no latency reported.
contribution: A Freeciv-based benchmark shows language models that forecast multi-agent world quantities well still fail at hidden-state inference and intervention prediction, with the best model at 29 of 100 on the composite index.
flag: Benchmark paper evaluating LLMs as world models, not a new world model; includable under (b) only via the 'or evaluates' wording. State is the joint state of several civilizations but no graph representation. Generative LLM predictors, so no non-generative cell. Prompt counts disagree within the paper (18,499 in intro, Table 2 sums to 20,759, App G.4 says 22,763). Only first 100k of 162k characters read; appendices H.4 onward (process study detail, agent-play protocol) not read. EXPERT is an LLM with manual and tools, not a human. Compute: about 3,600 GPU-hours, no per-inference latency.

title: Relational Learning as World Modeling
evidence: "TabWM uses them as context to predict the sparse structured edits caused by a new action" (Abstract); state is a relational database of tables, rows and primary/foreign-key links (method section).
method: TabWM: in-context tabular world model predicting an action's consequence as sparse structured edits over a relational database state; adapts from K observed transitions without weight updates; recursive rollouts rank plans.
evaluation: Synthetic WORLDREL worlds plus real-derived topology/values; baselines Flat-GBM, Flat-TabPFN, Qwen3 8B/14B/32B; Edit F1 0.687 vs 0.407 at K=64; planning Spearman 0.622; no hardware or latency reported.
contribution: An in-context relational world model predicts action consequences as sparse edits to a linked-table state, reaching Edit F1 0.69 on unseen worlds against 0.41 for a 32B LLM.
flag: Borderline on (b): state is a relational database with key links (a relational graph in the RelBench sense) but the paper does not call it a graph and there is no multi-agent state; maintainer to rule whether this counts. Single-actor, no safety content. Inconsistent numbers: Sec 5 says Edit F1 0.029 to 0.705, Table 1 gives 0.043 and 0.687, abstract/held-out table 0.016 to 0.685. Evaluation worlds are synthetic generators; real data only supplies topology and value distributions. Evidence quote taken from abstract. No hardware or latency.

title: Dynamic Graph World Modelling: Learning Future Dynamics from Temporal Context
evidence: "We instead predict future latent states, which capture structural changes" (Sec. 3.4); described as "an action-free relational transition model rather than a full planning system" (Sec. 2).
method: DyG-WM: JEPA-style dynamic-graph world model; from historical snapshot and event views with path signatures, predicts future latent node and relation representations of an EMA target encoder.
evaluation: 12 DyGLib link-prediction datasets and DBLP, Tmall node classification vs 11 baselines (TGN, DyGFormer, DVGMAE); best average AUC rank 2.67 transductive, 2.83 inductive; three ablations; A100; no latency.
contribution: A JEPA-style dynamic-graph world model that predicts future latent node and relation representations from temporal context, achieving the best average AUC rank across twelve link-prediction benchmarks.
flag: Clean (b) fit on graph state but action-free, no agents, no safety content; benchmarks are social/interaction graphs. 'Best average rank in every link-prediction setting' holds for AUC only: on transductive AP DyGFormer ranks ahead under rnd (2.42 vs 2.67) and hist (3.67 vs 3.83). Predictive accuracy is measured via downstream link prediction, not latent error. Ablation gain from the predictive objective is modest (Enron 71.69 to 74.99) with overlapping std. Efficiency claim (Fig. 4) has no numeric timings. Read chars 0-100000 of 179826: Table 9 (inductive AP) and later appendix not read.

title: Constrained Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning in Imagination
evidence: "CA-MAMBA extends MAMBA, a multi-agent worldmodel learner, to predict each agent's cost" (Abstract); per-agent RSSM latents coupled by attention messages over a neighbourhood (Sec. 3.2-3.3, paraphrase).
method: CA-MAMBA: MAMBA multi-agent RSSM world model with per-agent cost head; policies trained on imagined rollouts under one Lagrange multiplier updated from measured episode cost; no runtime shield.
evaluation: SMAC with casualty cost (24 configs) and Safety-Gymnasium MAMuJoCo vs MACPO, MAPPO-Lagrangian; lower cost on 23 of 24 at 100k steps; multiplier and communication ablations; RTX 3090; no inference latency.
contribution: Adds a cost head and measured-cost Lagrange multiplier to the MAMBA multi-agent world model, giving lower cost than MACPO and MAPPO-Lagrangian on 23 of 24 SMAC configurations at 100k interactions.
flag: Included on (b) only: constraint is a Lagrangian in training, NOT (a). No single joint latent - per-agent latents coupled by attention messages. Safety picture is mixed and should not be oversold: on MAMuJoCo d=25 its cost is far HIGHER than baselines (17.4 vs 0.2 Ant 2x4; 16.6 vs 0.0 HalfCheetah) though under the limit, tight limits are missed (HalfCheetah d=5 cost 18.2), no config meets zero-casualty on SMAC, and fixed beta=1 beats the learned multiplier on 8m. Model under-predicts cost in 17 of 18 runs (gap about 33-35 percent); transition TV error 0.45-0.73, too large to certify the bound per the authors. Only 2-3 seeds, not bit-reproducible. Read chars 0-100000 of 149607: appendix proofs and full SMAC tables (App. L, M) not read; per-config SMAC values not checked.

title: DriveWorld3D Evidence Constrained 3D World Modeling and Generative Simulation for Real-World Autonomous Driving
evidence: "The system has not yet been implemented or validated on a vehicle." (Research status note, p.1); "Table entries are placeholders for future experiments, not predictions or measured results." (Sec 7.6)
method: Design proposal: unified 3D driving world state (road surface, occupancy, dynamic entities, road-relation graph) with evidence/provenance tracking, action-conditioned future prediction, CVaR trajectory ranking and offline NeRF/3DGS generative simulation.
evaluation: None performed. Experimental protocol only (baselines B0-B6, planned metrics incl. false-free rate, collisions, P50/P95/P99 latency); results table reads 'Not evaluated' in every cell.
contribution: Unimplemented architecture and preregistration-style protocol for an evidence-constrained 3D driving world model with action-conditioned prediction and risk-sensitive planning; reports no experiments or results.
flag: Recommend exclude-E2: the paper states it is not implemented and reports no results at all, so there is neither a direct predictive-accuracy measure nor downstream task results. Criterion (b) is only nominal (traffic participants and a road-relation graph are in the proposed state; no equations for the predictor beyond a sampling statement). Trajectory filtering and a minimum-risk fallback are described but sit inside the planner and are untested, so not (a). Company-authored (Robostreet Inc.) position/design paper, 10 pages, references are mostly corporate web pages; no arXiv id printed in the text itself (id only from filename). Latency is listed as a planned metric only.

title: Quantum-JEPA: Quantum Born Priors for Latent-Action JEPA World Models
evidence: "HEP18 is a controlled four-agent task on HighwayEnv" (Sec 5.3); "We use twelve bits, three per agent." (Sec 5.3)
method: Latent-action JEPA world model: a conditional quantum circuit Born prior (or classical prior) samples binary latent actions; a shared predictor maps them to alternative future representations, trained with a sampled energy score.
evaluation: Stochastic MovingMNIST, 4-agent HighwayEnv intersection (HEP18), D3IL; vs Variational JEPA, Latent-CVAE, classical priors. HEP18 Entangled-QCBM: coverage 99.73%, validity 93.38%, TV 0.188, minADE 0.20 m, ES 34.36. No latency.
contribution: Latent-action JEPA whose quantum or classical prior samples correlated per-agent latent actions; on a four-agent intersection the entangled prior recovers 99.7% of 18 coordinated futures at 0.20 m minADE.
flag: Reports DIRECT predictive-accuracy measures (coverage, validity, TV, minADE, energy score of predicted trajectories against the true futures) with baselines and ablations, not downstream task results, so E2 does not apply. Doubts: (1) multi-agent state is only one of three tasks; HEP18 is a small constructed 4-agent task with 18 enumerated, uniformly likely futures and all 18 seen in training, so it tests mode recovery and coordination, not open-ended dynamics. (2) Paper is primarily about quantum priors; the best HEP18 numbers belong to classical priors (Softmax-Categorical validity 98.00%, Mixture-4 minADE 0.19 m) and the authors concede no consistent quantum advantage. (3) Re-pairing agents drops joint validity 93.38% to 12.71%, the main evidence the prior carries the coordination. (4) Real-QPU run (AGate-100, 12 qubits, 8 observations) lowers validity to 76.88-86.69% vs 98.41% ideal. (5) Three training seeds; D3IL diagnostic is admitted not to be a blind test. No latency, edge or safety content; MovingMNIST and D3IL are single-agent. Predictions are in representation space but futures are sampled, so I did not tick non-generative inference. Appendices A-J skimmed via grep only (J read in part).

title: LiveAct: Towards Real-Time Multi-Agent World Models with Heterogeneous Action Interfaces
evidence: "We presented LiveAct, a multi-agent video world model for" (Sec 5 Conclusion); "All agents read from the same shared visual state Xk" (Sec 3.4)
method: Action-conditioned video diffusion world model (Wan2.2 5B) generating a joint visual future for several controlled agents; language-gated per-agent attention and schema-token action encoding, distilled to a 4-step causal streaming generator.
evaluation: 108 held-out clips, 4 games and 2 multi-robot sources; 5 baselines plus ablations. Games/robots: FVD 338.5/270.2, PSNR 20.17/20.51, SSIM 0.743/0.871, Attr-Acc 0.898/0.942; 17.70 FPS at 512x448, single unnamed GPU.
contribution: Multi-agent video world model that binds each action stream to its agent via language-conditioned gates; best FVD, PSNR and attribution among five baselines on games and multi-robot manipulation, streaming at 17.70 FPS.
flag: Reports DIRECT predictive-accuracy measures against ground-truth future video (FVD, LPIPS, PSNR, SSIM, motion magnitude error) plus action-following metrics, with five baselines and ablations, so E2 does not apply. Doubts: (1) state is pixel/latent video of a shared scene, a generative diffusion model, not a graph or explicit joint agent state; multi-agent is genuine (2-4 controlled agents) but the contribution is the action interface. (2) Abstract says latency is evaluated; the body gives only throughput (17.70 FPS, Stages 1-3: 2.77/1.66/17.70) measured on 'a single GPU' whose model I could not find; no per-frame latency, jitter or deadline figures, so I did not tick latency/jitter aware. (3) Evaluation is one 81-frame prediction at seed 0 per clip, no confidence intervals. (4) Two baselines are altered or reproduced by the authors (MultiWorld forced to one view, WanToFight-style reimplemented because code is unreleased), which weakens the comparison. (5) Distillation worsens robot NRMSE 0.430 to 0.558. Games plus robot simulation are both physical-style visual domains, not cross-domain in the review's sense. Industry co-authored (Kling Team). No safety content. Supplementary read only in part (efficiency and ablation tables).

title: Inside-JEPA: From Prediction to Relational Grounding in Latent World Models
evidence: "The state zt = (rt , st ) concatenates all entity" [latents and relational channels] (Sec 3.1); "and a predictor P forecasts it" (Sec 3.2)
method: JEPA world model whose latent state holds one latent per entity plus soft relational channels for every ordered entity pair; an inverse-dynamics loss on those channels grounds them without relation labels.
evaluation: Blocks2D, Something-Something V2 (Something-Else boxes), RH20T; five arms vs prediction-only JEPA. Relational AUROC gain +.065 to +.103; forecast AUROC on changing relations .599 vs .621 observed; planning top-5 .425 vs .244.
contribution: JEPA world model with pairwise relational channels in its latent state; inverse-dynamics supervision grounds them (+.065 to +.103 AUROC) and lets action-conditioned forecasts of relational change reach .599 against .621 observed.
flag: BORDERLINE on (b), maintainer to decide between include and exclude-E1. For: the state is entity nodes plus ordered-pair relational channels (the authors call it pairwise like a scene graph) and the predictor forecasts the future state given an action, so it is predictive, not static masked prediction. Against: entities are at most 4 objects and hands in single-actor manipulation video, not agents; the predictor is a two-layer MLP on the flattened state, no graph network; the paper never calls its state a graph. Predictive accuracy: a DIRECT measure is reported (AUROC of forecast relational channels on entries whose relation changes: .599 true action, .511 permuted action, .621 observed future, copy baseline; RH20T only .518), but the headline metric is grounding/interpretability (matched relational AUROC of the encoder channels), not prediction, and the forecast horizon is one step of about 3-4 s. Only one baseline family (their own prediction-only arm and controls); authors admit no other relational method was run. Absolute AUROCs are modest (.63-.67 vs supervised ceiling .998). 3-5 seeds. Planning is one-step action ranking, not control. No hardware, latency, multi-agent or safety content. Appendices not read beyond grep.

title: FlockWorld: Toward Population-Scale Multi-Agent Video World Models through Artificial Life Simulation
evidence: "We introduced FlockWorld, an environment for population-scale multi-agent video world modeling," (Sec 6); "jointly generates multiple agents" [views using temporally causal cross-agent attention] (Sec 1)
method: FlockDiT: 27.5M-parameter action-conditioned latent flow-matching transformer jointly generating synchronized egocentric videos for 2-30 camera agents in a 100-boid flocking simulation, with block-causal cross-agent attention.
evaluation: 28 held-out episodes, 10 s rollouts; vs independent single-agent floor and VAE ceiling, 7 ablations. P=10: detection rate 28.5% vs floor 19.2% (ceiling 96.5%), position error 2.51 px; diffusion forcing SSIM 84.3. A40/A100.
contribution: Boids-based testbed and joint multi-agent video world model for up to 30 camera agents; joint generation detects more true agents than independent rollouts (28.5% vs 19.2%) and diffusion forcing most improves rollout fidelity.
flag: Reports DIRECT predictive-accuracy measures against the recorded ground-truth trajectory (detection rate, position error, detections per frame, SSIM, cross-view displacement and motion error) with a floor baseline and ablations, so E2 does not apply on that ground. Doubts, several serious: (1) absolute accuracy is poor: the model recovers 22-32% of visible boids against a 96.5% ceiling, and several settings over-render about 2.5x the true count; the authors say consistency metrics are confounded by density. (2) Single training run per condition, fixed seed 42, no variance across seeds or hypothesis tests (stated in limitations); intervals are across 28 episodes only. (3) Toy 2D rule-based boids; actions are simulator accelerations replayed during rollout, so action and state diverge. (4) Venue is the NeurIPS 2026 Creative AI track; abstract wording is hedged ('results suggest'). (5) State is per-agent egocentric pixels via a VAE, generative, not a graph. No latency or real-time figures (50-step Euler sampler), no safety content. Maintainer may judge this too weak an evaluation; if so E2 is the fallback. Appendices read only for compute and limitations.

title: More Is Better? Exploring Latent Correspondence in Federated Hypergraph Learning
evidence: Sec. 6 (Implementation Details): "FedASTRA uses two masks, a local EMA target, and parameter-only FedAvg"
method: FedASTRA: federated hypergraph node classification without cross-client hyperedge identifiers; learned heat-diffusion scales on local incidence plus masked-view latent prediction of an EMA target, parameter-only FedAvg; identifiability and complexity theory.
evaluation: 8 static datasets (CoraCA, DBLP4k, IMDB4k, Trivago, Cora, CiteSeer, Facebook, ogbn-papers100M), K=3/6/9 clients; 7 federated hypergraph and 4 federated graph baselines; accuracy, Macro-F1, traffic; RTX A6000.
contribution: Federated hypergraph learner that avoids matching hyperedges across clients, using adaptive heat diffusion and masked latent prediction on static local hypergraphs, with identifiability bounds and node-classification gains over identifier-free baselines.
flag: Recommend E1 under the 2026-11-12 ruling: the latent prediction is masked-view prediction of an EMA target on a STATIC hypergraph (JEPA-style regulariser added to a supervised cross-entropy loss, Eq. 22); no future state, no dynamics, no agents acting. The word 'dynamics' in App. C.9 refers to diffusion and EMA-target training dynamics, not environment dynamics. Predictive accuracy of a world model: not applicable - the only metrics are downstream node-classification accuracy and Macro-F1 (e.g. CoraCA 75.17 vs 68.64 Fed-HGNN; ogbn-papers100M 50.07/29.73 vs 40.38/21.44 Fed-HyperGCN) plus communication traffic; masked prediction is ablated only via downstream accuracy (Table 12, CoraCA 67.26 to 74.27). 'Clients' are federated data silos, not interacting agents. Abstract numbers (50.07, 29.73, 59.60 MiB) found in Table 3; note FedASTRA is the slowest and most memory-hungry method in Table 18 (1069.7 s, 19.53 GiB), which the abstract's Pareto claim does not mention. The ogbn-papers100M run is a single execution. Long file (238k chars): read abstract, intro, Sec. 5-7, App. D.4, E.3, E.4; did not read the proofs in App. B-C.

title: Bayesian Offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Latent World Models
evidence: Sec. 6.3: "World model prediction performance is measured by the joint normalized root mean square error (JNRMSE), which jointly characterizes observation and reward prediction errors."
method: Bayesian offline MARL for Dec-POMDPs: GRU infers a latent global state from joint observation-action histories; 7-member probabilistic ensemble world model refined by multi-agent posterior information loss (MPIL); SAC under CTDE on imagined rollouts.
evaluation: Multi-agent splits of D4RL HalfCheetah, Hopper (3 agents), Walker2d (2 agents), 12 datasets, 5 seeds; baselines BC, OMAR, MOMA-PPO; normalized return, JNRMSE, per-dimension MAE/R2 before vs after refinement; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Bayesian latent world model for partially observable offline multi-agent RL, refined by a posterior information loss that bounds policy regret, cutting next-observation prediction error and giving best returns on 8 of 12 multi-agent MuJoCo datasets.
flag: Predictive accuracy: a DIRECT measure is reported, so not E2. Table 9 (appendix) gives per-dimension next-observation and reward MAE and R2 before vs after MPIL refinement (e.g. Hopper reward MAE 0.0280 to 0.0024, Walker2d dim 1 R2 0.5628 to 0.9598; HalfCheetah MAE cut 42-63 percent); Fig. 3a gives JNRMSE but only as a figure. Doubts: (1) the comparison is the paper's own initial vs refined model (an ablation); no external world model (e.g. MOMA-PPO's) is compared on prediction error, and Table 9 does not state the dataset type, seed count or variance. (2) Multi-agent state is thin: the 'agents' are 2-3 actuator groups of ONE MuJoCo robot with overlapping observation slices (Table 7), and the model predicts the concatenated joint observation through a single GRU latent - no graph, no per-agent structure. (3) Rollout length is 1 (Table 5), so no multi-step prediction is tested. (4) Returns are mixed: loses to BC on Hopper-expert and Walker2d-expert and to MOMA-PPO on two HalfCheetah sets. (5) Regret theorems rest on a bounded concentrability coefficient and an assumed K/N contraction rate. Preprint; AI-use statement declares generative AI assisted writing and derivation checking. Not a safety paper, no runtime interceptor (expected for P2). Did not read proofs in App. A.3 in detail.

title: FORCE: Factorized Object Relations for Counterfactual Editing in Video World Models
evidence: Sec 3.3: the per-pair relation latent is "held fixed for the entire rollout"; Abstract: "a relation can be removed, changed, transferred or introduced directly."
method: Video world model: slot attention on frozen DINOv2 gives entities; an 8-d relation latent per ordered object pair sets a central force; a fixed integrator rolls state forward; relations are editable.
evaluation: Simulated 4-object spring scenes, 800 held-out clips, 5 seeds; controls: edit-direction prior, wrong pair, re-derived relation, oracle. Dfixed held-out 0.189-0.372; relation AUC 0.826. No hardware or latency.
contribution: Factorises a video world model into objects and per-pair relation latents so a relation can be removed, changed, transferred or introduced and the counterfactual rollout predicted, shown on simulated spring scenes.
flag: BORDERLINE (b): state is passive objects plus pairwise relation latents (an implicit interaction graph), not agents and not an explicit graph; maintainer may prefer exclude-E1. Toy 4-object simulator only. Metric is counterfactual edit fidelity (Dfixed), low in absolute terms (0.19-0.37); no competing method run, only controls and ablations; a distance-only statistic selects pairs as well as the learned latent (AUC 0.845 vs 0.812). Quotes relayed by fetch tool, not checked verbatim.

title: GURU: A Hierarchical Neuro-Symbolic Multi-Agent System for Verification-Aware Automation of Mission-Critical Digital Engineering and Operations
evidence: Sec. 3.5: "A violation blocks the action, demotes the proposal, invokes a defined fallback, or escalates to the human, according to the rule's severity."
method: GURU: hierarchical neuro-symbolic agent platform; learned models (incl. a per-object orbital JEPA time-series world model) propose and rank, a symbolic rules engine gates actions before execution, validated physics decides.
evaluation: Five applications (CFD, ParaView control, space conjunction risk, reentry avoidance, 200-aircraft simulation); CFD convergence under 1 to 74 percent, conjunction F1 0.628 vs four baselines, collision-world fraction 0.021 to 0.039; no gate latency.
contribution: Company system paper describing a propose-check-decide agent architecture where a symbolic rules engine vetoes learned proposals, with heterogeneous results across CFD automation, orbital conjunction screening and simulated 200-aircraft teams.
flag: Recommend E2 (with an E1 argument on criterion b). (b): the JEPA world model IS predictive (encoder of past orbital state window, predictor of future-window embedding, horizon up to 72 h) but its state is a SINGLE object's time series; two objects are only combined afterwards into a pair embedding for a conjunction classifier, and the paper says the pipeline never builds the pairwise graph. No graph or joint multi-agent state, so (b) fails on reading. Predictive accuracy: NO direct measure of the world model's latent prediction error anywhere; only downstream results (conjunction F1 0.628 +/- 0.008 vs Llama-3.2-1B 0.622, PatchTST 0.621, Qwen2.5-0.5B 0.603, Chronos-2 0.577, differences within seed variation by the authors' own admission; maneuver AUC 'near 0.98' taken from prior work on a 2D UMAP projection). The 200-aircraft work is PPO plus MPPI with no world model. (a): a runtime rules-engine gate is described, but its only quantitative evidence is an ablation imported from the authors' PRIOR paper on an older mesh generator (boundary-layer capture 98 to 85 percent - a quality metric, not a safety rate); the avoidance result is one constructed synthetic encounter with perfect state and privileged future trajectories; in the multi-aircraft study collisions ROSE (0.021 to 0.039) and separation is a cost, not a checked constraint. The paper's own Table 5 marks the OOD gate, refusal path and reactor actuation gate as 'designed', not implemented; conjunction Stage 3 is 'in refinement' and Stage 4 not built. Human approval is described, not evaluated. Self-published company paper (MSBAI) promoting a product (OrbitGuard); the text file shows no arXiv id. The architecture spans physical and software (ParaView) domains but the gate is not evaluated as a safety mechanism in either, so no cross-domain cell. Long file (246k chars): read abstract, Sec. 1 opening, 3.5, 4.3, 6.1-6.6, 7.5, 8, 10.2-10.5, 11 (part), 12; did not read Sec. 2, 3.1-3.4, 4.1-4.2, 4.4, 5 (CFD/ParaView detail), 7.1-7.4, 9, 10.1, 13-14.

title: Seeing Beyond the Next Step: World-Model-Guided Human-Like Navigation in Multi-Agent Scenes
evidence: Paraphrase (Method; Appendix E): a frozen State Transition World Model predicts each surrounding entity's next ego-frame relative position change and relative velocity, conditioned on a candidate anchor; verbatim (Abstract): "At deployment, both world models are removed and the policy acts in a single forward pass."
method: Two frozen anchor-conditioned world models (per-entity state regressor; EDM denoiser for future segmentation maps) score candidate anchors to refine a Qwen3-VL-2B LoRA navigation policy via GRPO; removed at deployment.
evaluation: Unity ETH/UCY scenes, 5 held-out scenarios, 3 runs; baselines GBM, CCP, CEDRL, forecaster+MPC; GSR/SRVR/GD; WM ADE 0.185 m, mIoU 87.0%; 65 ms per decision, RTX 6000 Ada.
contribution: Training-time dual world models (per-pedestrian state and semantic-map prediction) distil lookahead into a single-pass VLM crowd-navigation policy, reaching 66-88% goal success on five simulated ETH/UCY scenes at 65 ms per decision.
flag: Title matches (read from /pdf/2611.07730v1; first 100k of 117k chars plus the tail, which is only the NeurIPS checklist). PREDICTIVE ACCURACY: reported directly, not only downstream - Appendix E Table 6 state model position ADE 0.1846 m, RMSE 0.2481 m, velocity MAE 0.3354 m/s, heading error 20.77 deg; Table 5 semantic model pixel acc 99.28%, mIoU 87.00%, Dice 89.08%. DOUBT 1: those accuracy figures are not compared against any other forecaster, so the v1.6 'predictive metric AND baseline or ablation' test is met only via downstream ablations (w/o Dual World Models: Zara01_Group GSR 16.7 vs 77.8; w/o State branch; w/o Semantic branch) and Table 3 forecaster+MPC alternatives (Constant Velocity, Social-LSTM, Social-GAN, Trajectron++), which are downstream GSR/SRVR/GD, not prediction error. An Appendix O leave-one-scene-out ETH/UCY forecasting benchmark is mentioned but I could not see its content - check whether it supplies a predictive baseline; if not, E2 is arguable. DOUBT 2: multi-agent state is per-entity explicit low-dimensional prediction from RGB, no graph or joint-state architecture is described, and it is not latent; the semantic model masks pedestrians (ignore label). DOUBT 3: world models are training-time only; no runtime interceptor, no human takeover; simulation only, no real robot (Limitations). Table 7 ADE/FDE (Zara01 0.2064/0.3897) is policy motion fidelity versus human trajectories, not world-model accuracy. Latency: 65 ms policy, 1.2 s OnlineWM variant; 65 ms is on a workstation GPU, not edge, and no deadline is imposed. Numbers come from a model-summarised read of the PDF; spot-check before citing.

title: The Delta Gap: Cellular World Models for Perturbation Response Prediction Are Far Harder Than Global Correlation Implies
evidence: Sec. 3.1: "A perturbation response model f takes as input a perturbation label p and outputs a predicted post-perturbation expression"
method: Evaluation critique of single-cell perturbation-response predictors (GEARS): score on control-subtracted delta rather than global Pearson; post-hoc random-walk and kNN corrections; delta-aligned training loss with amplitude calibration.
evaluation: Replogle K562 (509 held-out perturbations) and Norman (107); GEARS vs mean-delta baseline, MLP, simplified flow matching; delta Pearson 0.076 vs 0.267 baseline, 0.179-0.218 after fixes; 3 seeds, RTX 4060; no latency.
contribution: Shows that gene-perturbation response predictors scored by global correlation look accurate while barely predicting the perturbation-induced change, and proposes delta-space evaluation with partial corrections.
flag: Recommend E1: 'world model' is used by analogy. The state is one pseudo-bulk gene-expression vector of a cell population and the 'action' a perturbation label; the model is a one-shot map from label to mean expression, with no temporal dynamics, no agents and no joint multi-agent state. A graph appears only as an inductive bias (GEARS GNN over a gene co-expression graph; RWR smoothing), not as the predicted state. Predictive accuracy IS measured directly (delta Pearson, top-20 DE Pearson, direction accuracy) against baselines, so this is not an E2 case; the exclusion rests on scope. If the maintainer reads a gene graph as graph state, it would be a bioinformatics outlier. Candid doubts: single-author, self-published preprint; the Norman dataset is called A549 lung adenocarcinoma throughout, whereas the Norman et al. 2019 Perturb-seq screen is, to my knowledge, K562 - if so the headline 'zero-shot transfer across cell lines' claim is unfounded (from memory, not checked here: no web). Internal inconsistencies: Eq. 11 defines the gap as a ratio but Table 2 prints differences (-0.901, -0.329); GEARS one-step delta Pearson is 0.076 in most places but 0.069 in Sec. 4.5; Limitations says only GEARS was evaluated as a deep model though Table 4 lists MLP and flow matching; cell counts differ (60,400 in Table 1 vs 'full 310K cells'); data downsampled to 30 cells per condition for an 8 GB GPU; RWR significance from n=3 seeds (Cohen's d 7.42). The trivial mean-delta baseline (0.267) still beats every corrected variant on Replogle (best 0.218). Related-work paragraphs repeat themselves, suggesting machine-assisted drafting. Read Sec. 1-4.6 and scanned Sec. 4.8-5.3; did not read supplementary figures.

title: Evaluating LLM-Generated World Models for Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning
evidence: Sec. 6: "Among the 134 Lane-1-valid game candidates, mean permutation-invariant F1 is 0.366 and the median is 0.178"
method: Benchmark of five LLMs generating formal multi-agent world models (partially observable stochastic games as JSON or Python) from text; three evaluation lanes: mechanical validity, structural agreement with a reference, semantic checks.
evaluation: 44 scenarios (games, situational, cultural), 410 first-pass generations; 5 LLMs compared; validity 134/135, 104/135, 125/140; structural F1 0.366/0.432/0.553; exact match 28/134; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Benchmark showing that LLM-generated multi-agent world models (stochastic games) almost always execute yet rarely match a reference transition structure, so executability is not evidence of faithfulness for safety reasoning.
flag: Borderline include on (b): the paper EVALUATES world models whose state is the joint state of several players (POSG with joint-action transition function), but they are symbolic models written by an LLM, not learned or latent predictors; maintainer should decide whether that is in Pillar 2 scope (else E1). Predictive accuracy: a direct fidelity measure of the world model is reported rather than downstream results - structural F1 against authored reference POSGs over action-conditioned successors, terminal states and transition probabilities, unrolled to depth 3 (per-LLM F1 0.171 to 0.498). It is reference agreement, not prediction error on observed trajectories, and the paper explicitly does NOT measure downstream planning. Baseline/ablation: only a cross-LLM comparison and an anonymised vs country-named prompt contrast; no baseline method or ablation in the usual sense, so the v1.6 minimum-evaluation test is arguable (E2 if the maintainer requires one). Other doubts: only the 9-game track has true references; situational and cultural F1 use criteria-derived feature references and are not comparable; Lane 3 human annotation 'is specified but not yet run', so semantic and bias results are programmatic and preliminary; small hand-crafted benchmark, 3 generations per pair, 1 per cultural cell; the one significant correlation (rho -0.677, p .045) is on nine games. Inconsistencies: cultural Lane 3 checklist is 136/140 in Table 1 but 133/140 in Sec. 6; 11 situational scenarios are described but results cover S1-S9 (135 candidates); Table 4 structural n is 107 while Lane 1 pass is 104. Short workshop-style preprint; no runtime interceptor and no safety outcome measured. Read main text in full and scanned appendix headings; did not read App. A-C in detail.

title: Modelling Competitive Behaviors in Autonomous Driving Under Generative World Model
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science (including subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics)
evidence: "we pretrain a generative world model to predict the environmental dynamics of self-driving scenarios" (Abstract)
method: Generative cross-attention world model (transition, observation, candidate action predictor, QCNet-style) pretrained on driving logs; CCE-MASAC with optimistic Bellman update and magnetic mirror descent learns coarse correlated equilibria inside it.
evaluation: Four held-out Argoverse 2 scenarios, 3 seeds; vs MASAC, MAPPO, QCNet, GameFormer; CCE-gap curves and discounted rewards in figures only (table in appendix); no hardware or latency.
contribution: Models competitive multi-vehicle behaviour as a general-sum Markov game, learning coarse correlated equilibria with CCE-MASAC inside a pretrained generative world model of joint traffic dynamics on Argoverse 2 scenarios.
flag: File is a proceedings volume; chapter at pp. 19-36 read in full (appendices A-F are referenced but not in the file). The world model is predictive over joint multi-agent state, so (b) is met in kind, but NO direct measure of the world model's predictive accuracy is reported (no ADE/FDE, no prediction error): evaluation is only downstream - CCE-gap (exploitability) and discounted cumulative rewards, shown as training curves in Figs. 3-4 with the numeric table deferred to Appendix F, plus trajectory visualisations. Per the maintainer's ruling this is exclude-E2. Other notes: generative (not latent non-generative) model; evaluation happens inside the learned model itself on only four hand-picked scenarios; the paper's own limitations say constraints are not modelled; not a safety mechanism; the main body contains no numeric results at all.

title: World Model Learning for Highly Autonomous Proactive Planetary Robot Teams
evidence: "presents new concepts for multi-level robot decision and learning autonomy" (Abstract)
method: Conceptual paper on world-model building for planetary multi-robot teams: shared world models via multi-agent model-based RL, federated learning, map merging and anticipatory networks, for icy-moon (Europa) rovers.
evaluation: None. No experiments, datasets, baselines or metrics; an illustrative Europa navigation example, an architecture figure, a table of concepts and generated sample images. No hardware or latency.
contribution: A concept paper proposing that planetary multi-robot teams learn and exchange world models through multi-agent model-based and federated reinforcement learning, illustrated for icy-moon exploration without experimental evaluation.
flag: File is a whole proceedings volume; chapter located at pp. 339-352 and read in full. Unevaluated position/concept paper: topic matches (b) nominally (multi-robot shared world model) but there is no implemented model, no predictive-accuracy measure and no downstream results either - only concepts, a block diagram and a table of ML concepts. Neither a direct predictive measure nor downstream task results are reported. Could arguably also be E3 (overview-style chapter). Hence exclude-E2.

title: Object-Centric Dreamer
evidence: "employs a graph neural network (GNN) to predict the dynamics of a given environment" (Abstract)
method: Object-Centric Dreamer: frozen slot extractor (SLATE or DINOSAUR) feeds an object-centric RSSM whose Graph GRU predicts per-object latent dynamics over a complete graph; GNN actor-critic trained in imagination.
evaluation: Shapes2D, Robosuite, ViZDoom, Atari Pong, 3 seeds; vs DreamerV3 variants, ROCA, OCRL, OC-CA, OC-SA, OCARL; steps to 0.9 success (e.g. 0.14M vs >2M), success rate, return; no latency.
contribution: Object-Centric Dreamer replaces DreamerV3's recurrent state model with a graph-GRU over slot-based object latents, improving sample efficiency on multi-object Shapes2D tasks but not beating DreamerV3 on Robosuite, ViZDoom or Pong.
flag: File is a proceedings volume; chapter at pp. 153-164 read in full. The model is predictive with a graph-structured latent state (complete graph over object slots), so (b) holds in kind, but the graph is over objects in a single-agent scene, not agents - multi-agent state cell not credited. NO direct measure of world-model predictive accuracy is reported: only downstream results (steps to reach 0.9 success or a return threshold, final success rate and episode return); the only non-task metric is foreground ARI of the frozen extractor (95%/90% Shapes2D, 59% Robosuite), which measures segmentation, not prediction. Per the maintainer's ruling this is exclude-E2. Also: conclusion claims it 'outperforms both object-centric and monolithic model-based baselines' but Table 2 shows DreamerV3 is equal or faster on Robosuite, ViZDoom and Pong; no ablation of the GNN beyond the 'DreamerV3: slate' comparison; compute is quadratic in slots; no hardware or timing reported.

title: Object-Centric World Models Meet Monte Carlo Tree Search
venue: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
evidence: Sec 4.2: the dynamics model is a GNN with edge and node models, similar to C-SWMs, taking the factored (slot) state and action; Sec 7: 'the computational complexity of ObjectZero becomes quadratic with respect to the number of slots'.
method: ObjectZero: EfficientZeroV2 with frozen SLATE/DINOSAUR slot extractor, GNN dynamics over a fully connected object-slot graph predicting next slots, GNN reward/value/policy heads, Gumbel MCTS planning.
evaluation: CausalWorld Object Reaching and Robosuite Block Lifting; baselines EZ-V2, DreamerV3, ROCA, OCRL, OC-SA, OC-CA; success rate and return curves only (3 seeds); no ablation, hardware or latency.
contribution: ObjectZero plans with MCTS over a GNN latent dynamics model on object slots, matching EfficientZeroV2 and beating object-centric baselines on two single-robot manipulation tasks.
flag: ONLY DOWNSTREAM RESULTS: no direct measure of world-model predictive accuracy (no prediction/reconstruction error); results are return and success-rate curves in Fig 2 with no numeric values in the text, and no ablation - hence E2 under the maintainer's rule. Graph is an object-slot graph within a single agent (no multi-agent state); predictive of next latent state, so (b) is met only via the graph reading. Sec 3.2 says the consistency loss is negative cosine similarity, Sec 4.2 says MSE - unreconciled. Gain over EZ-V2 is nil ('comparable'/'nearly equal'). No runtime interceptor, as expected.

title: World Models as Constraints: Heterogeneous Rail Robot Coordination via CA-JEPA and LLM-Based Planning
evidence: "If a candidate plan exceeds the feasibility threshold, it is rejected and structured feedback (e.g., dominant violation type and risk magnitude) is returned to the LLM for adjustment before any execution occurs." (Sec. 4.4 PEEFA Loop)
method: CA-JEPA: JEPA world model with disentangled dynamics and constraint (topology graph, comm graph, time budget) latents; constraint-conditioned latent rollouts predict violation risk; PEEFA loop gates LLM-proposed multi-robot plans.
evaluation: PyBullet rail sim (RailBench, 200k transitions), RWARE; vs MAPPO, MADDPG, TarMAC, vanilla JEPA; success 87.1%, violations 12.9%, FAR 4.3%, AUROC 0.862, ECE 0.042; no hardware or latency.
contribution: CA-JEPA rolls out a constraint-conditioned joint-embedding world model over multi-robot rail state to score LLM-proposed plans, rejecting risky ones before execution and cutting violations and false accepts against MARL baselines.
flag: File is the PAKDD 2026 proceedings volume (copyright line says 2027); chapter at pp. 196-208 read in full. Strong fit: latent (non-generative) prediction over joint multi-robot state with graph constraints, used as a pre-execution veto on LLM plans. Direct predictive measure IS reported, but for violation-risk prediction (AUROC 0.862, OOD AUROC 0.821, ECE 0.042 vs vanilla JEPA 0.089, FAR), not latent-state prediction error; plus downstream success/violation rates with baselines and a 9-row ablation. Doubts: (1) FAR for the full model is 4.3% in Table 1 but 5.2% in Table 3, and CA-JEPA without PEEFA is 7.8% in Table 1 vs 8.4% in Table 3; (2) Table 3 'w/o all constraint enc. (= Vanilla JEPA + PEEFA)' scores 74.2% success, below vanilla JEPA without PEEFA at 79.2% in Table 1 - unexplained; (3) PEEFA gain quoted as 4.3% in Sec. 6.2 and +3.6% in Sec. 6.4 (relative vs absolute points); (4) Table 1 says all methods trained 2M env steps, unclear how an offline world model plus LLM planner is 'trained online'; (5) LLM not named, number of robots, threshold tuning, model size, hardware and inference latency not reported; (6) simulation only, no real robots, no code/data link seen; 'cross-domain' is rail to warehouse (both physical) so the cross-domain cell is not credited, and on RWARE success is 4.6 points below MAPPO; (7) abstract gives no numbers. The interceptor is plan-level (macro-action sequences before execution), not per-step; no human handoff. Very regular results tables with a short method section - maintainer may wish to sanity-check plausibility.

title: Hypergraph normal world modeling for normal-only logical visual anomaly detection
evidence: "Thus, fitting is statistical rather than gradient-based, and inference is fully determined once the normal-world parameters, calibration statistics, and threshold are fixed." (Sec. 3.7)
method: Per-category Gaussian statistics of frozen DINOv2 patch tokens, pairwise relations and fixed spatial hyperedges; standardized energies summed into an image-level anomaly score.
evaluation: MVTec LOCO AD, five categories; six reproduced global and patch-memory baselines; component ablation; logical AUROC 0.7276 vs 0.7204 DINOv2-L CLS. No latency or hardware figures seen.
