contribution: Normal-only logical anomaly detector that scores single images against hypergraph statistics of frozen DINOv2 tokens, reaching 0.7276 average logical AUROC on MVTec LOCO.
flag: Not predictive: 'world model' here is a set of static per-image feature statistics on a fixed spatial hypergraph over patches of ONE image; no dynamics, no future-state prediction, no agents (falls under the 2026-11-12 static-graph ruling). No predictive-accuracy measure of a world model, only image-level anomaly AUROC/AUPRC. Gain over the non-hypergraph variant is 0.7173 to 0.7276 with no variance reported, and the method loses on all-sample AUROC (0.6943 vs 0.7235 patch-kNN). Baselines are the authors' own reproductions, not published SOTA numbers. Did not read Sec. 4.5-6 (interpretability, counterfactual tests, discussion) in full.

title: Robust model-based MARL via masked cross-agent completion under observation loss
evidence: "The RSSM model encodes the state variables of multi-agent systems into a globally unified latent state representation" (Section 4.1, Architecture)
method: RSSM multi-agent world model with cross-agent Transformer observation and action fusion and reward-trend smoothing; masked fine-tuning lets it reconstruct observations of agents that lose sensing, feeding decentralised policies.
evaluation: SMAC (8 maps) and MAMuJoCo, 3 seeds, versus RMIO, MAMBA, MAG, MAPPO, QMIX, FACMAC; 2s3z AUC 93.8, reconstruction loss 0.071 versus 0.174 without observation fusion. No latency in body.
contribution: RMIOv2 adds cross-agent Transformer fusion and masked fine-tuning to a recurrent multi-agent world model so that agents losing observations can act on reconstructed ones, tested on SMAC and MAMuJoCo.
flag: DIRECT predictive measure IS reported: reconstruction loss Lrec for missing-observation completion (Table 1: 2s3z 0.071, 3s_vs_5z 0.073, 1c3s5z 0.443, corridor 0.871, each against three fusion ablations; Table 2 across mask rates), plus downstream win rate, step return and robustness AUC. Caveats: Lrec is 'dimensionless', is given numerically only against the paper's own ablations (the RMIO comparison in Fig. 9 is a normalised curve), and measures reconstruction of the CURRENT masked observation from history and peers more than multi-step future prediction; no rollout-horizon error is shown. Headline comparisons with external baselines are in Figs. 7-8 and Appendix A (online supplement, not in this file), so I could not read their values. Abstract carries no numbers to check. The pmask=0 column in Table 2 has Lrec of 4.96-15.4, two orders above the rest, worth a glance. Under observation loss the method needs inter-agent communication of recent observations and actions at inference. Simulation only, 3 seeds; overhead figures are in Appendix D, unseen. Extends the authors' RMIO and GAWM; check those are not queued as duplicates. Not safety work, no interceptor (expected); RQ5 capped at 2. Read: abstract, introduction, Section 4.1-4.2 opening, all of Sections 6-7; skimmed past Sections 2-3, 4.1 detail and Section 5 algorithms.

title: CauCity-WM: an intervention-consistent generative world model for counterfactual urban dynamics and risk-aware decision making
venue: Journal of King Saud University - Computer and Information Sciences
evidence: Abstract: "This defines a unit-level counterfactual semantics for a graph-conditioned diffusion world model rather than treating causality as an auxiliary prediction head."
method: CauCity-WM: graph-conditioned latent diffusion transition over urban sensor/zone graph; abducts an episode disturbance and reuses it plus the diffusion noise path in factual and counterfactual rollouts; sparse intervention Jacobians; CVaR-regularised planning.
evaluation: METR-LA, PEMS-BAY, PEMS04/08, LargeST, NYC TLC, Citi Bike plus SUMO; baselines DCRNN, Graph WaveNet, STAEformer, UniST, OpenCity, Diff-SCM, VCIP, DreamerV3, TD-MPC2; MAE, E-MAE, PEHE, CRPS, coverage; A100, 96 ms per 12-step rollout.
contribution: Graph-conditioned diffusion world model for urban traffic that shares disturbance and noise between factual and counterfactual rollouts, reporting lower forecasting MAE and counterfactual-effect error than adapted causal and forecasting baselines.
flag: Predictive accuracy: DIRECT measures reported with baselines and ablation (Table 5 forecasting MAE, e.g. METR-LA 2.47 vs OpenCity 2.58; Table 7 E-MAE 2.61 and PEHE 3.29 vs Diff-SCM 3.22 and 4.07, sign accuracy 0.846, 90% coverage 0.896; Table 12 ablation; Table 11 CRPS/NLL), so the (b) minimum is met on paper. Abstract numbers all found in the body (Tables 7 and 10). CREDIBILITY CONCERNS the maintainer should weigh: (1) received 29 Aug 2026, accepted 11 Sep 2026 - 13 days; (2) the published article still points to an anonymised code link (anonymous.4open.science), which I could not check; (3) every table shows the proposed model best on every dataset and metric with uniformly small, smoothly ordered SDs and a perfectly monotone baseline ranking, a pattern that looks too tidy - treat the numbers as unverified; (4) counterfactual ground truth is semi-synthetic (a response kernel the authors designed is injected into real data) or SUMO, so E-MAE/PEHE measure recovery of the authors' own generator; (5) text says both 'seven real urban forecasting benchmarks' and 'eight public observational datasets'; GeoLife is listed in Table 2 but has no result column in Table 5; (6) the abstract's 'reduces average MAE' gives no figure. State is a graph of traffic sensors/zones, not agents: graph state yes, multi-agent no. Not a runtime interceptor: the CVaR term and constraints sit inside the planner (SUMO violations 1.9% vs DreamerV3 4.1% is a planner outcome, not a shield). Generative (diffusion), slowest but one of the models in Table 13 (96 ms per 12-step rollout, A100-80GB); authors say below 0.1 s. Simulation and offline data only.

title: Scalable physics-informed multi-agent reinforcement learning for building energy system control
evidence: "we integrate the learned dynamics model as a differentiable world model for policy optimization" (Abstract)
method: Physics-consistent GNN (causal convolutions plus heat-diffusion graph layer) predicts multi-zone temperatures; used as differentiable world model for multi-agent SAC with kappa-hop truncated critics, one agent per zone.
evaluation: 6-zone simulation (114 days) and 18-zone real building (42 days), 15-min control; autoregressive MAE 0.31-1.18 C and 0.59-1.40 C; ablated vanilla GNN 0.45-1.26 C; energy savings 15.7% and 35-70% vs existing controller.
contribution: A physics-consistent graph neural network predicts coupled zone temperatures in multi-zone buildings and serves as a differentiable world model for neighbourhood-truncated multi-agent reinforcement learning, validated in an 18-zone real building.
flag: Meets (b) with a DIRECT predictive-accuracy measure: per-zone autoregressive temperature MAE (Tables 2, 3) and an ablation without physics constraints (Table 5: e.g. zone 1 0.39 to 0.70 C, zone 3 0.58 to 1.14 C). Not safety work; no interceptor; comfort bounds are soft reward terms and real-building temperature violation was slightly WORSE than baseline (0.49 vs 0.32 C). Inconsistencies: abstract says 'below 1.4 C' MAE but Table 3 zone 17 is exactly 1.40; text says zone 6 MAE is 0.86 C but Table 3 gives 0.59 for zone 6 (0.86 is zone 7); global critic dimension given as 126 in text but 138 in Table 1. The predictive baseline is only the authors' own ablated model (no external predictor compared); 4 of 18 zones malfunctioned and savings are also reported excluding them. No latency or hardware figures for inference. Graph is thermal adjacency between zones (agents = zones), so multi-agent is real but benign.

title: Latent dynamics graph convolutional networks for model order reduction of parameterized time-dependent PDEs
evidence: Sec. 2.4: "the meshless decoder of LDNets is replaced with a graph convolutional network defined on the mesh"; a latent dynamics network advances a low-dimensional state by explicit Euler steps.
method: Encoder-free reduced-order model: a small network integrates a global latent state in time, and a graph convolutional decoder maps it to the full field on the finite-element mesh.
evaluation: Advection-diffusion (two cases), lid-driven cavity, Coanda bifurcation; baseline GCA-ROM, LDNet quoted from its paper; latent-size ablation; metrics relative error and NRMSE; no hardware, timing or speed-up reported.
contribution: Learns low-dimensional latent dynamics for parameterized time-dependent PDEs with a graph-convolutional mesh decoder, cutting mean relative error to 5.1e-3 against 1.9e-2 for a graph autoencoder baseline with half the parameters.
flag: Predictive accuracy: reported directly with a baseline - mean/max relative error, Square Advection n=10 5.06e-3/4.16e-2 vs GCA-ROM 1.86e-2/1.13e-1; Moving Hole n=15 8.81e-3/1.02e-1 vs 3.54e-2/1.92e-1; cavity NRMSE 6.79e-3 (n=3); Coanda mean 4.57e-3, max 3.62e-2. Include is borderline and rests on a literal reading of (b): the 'graph' is a finite-element mesh (1352-10024 nodes) used by the DECODER; the predicted latent state itself is a global vector of dimension 3-15, not a graph, and there are no agents, actions or control - a scientific-computing surrogate. If the maintainer requires the predicted state to be the graph, or an acting system, this is E1. It decodes to the full field, so not non-generative. LDNet (non-graph) is more accurate on the cavity (1.39e-3, quoted not rerun). No hardware, wall-clock or speed-up figures despite the model-order-reduction framing. Journal version (J. Comput. Phys.) read via arXiv; last 23k characters of the PDF text (references/appendix) not read.

title: Enhancing multi-agent reinforcement learning via world model assisted single-agent population policies in multi-UAV cooperative-competitive scenario
evidence: Sec. 4: "each team of agents employs a common hypernetwork-based hierarchical world model to interactively reason about the mental states and trajectories of both their team and the opponents."
method: Hierarchical recurrent latent world model infers opponents' intention and strategy latents and predicts both teams' future trajectories and rewards; used as surrogate fitness for a CEM population and to generate imagined data for MAPPO-style MARL.
evaluation: 4 vs 4 UAV air combat in gym-jsbsim; SMAC (8 maps); baselines MAPPO, MADDPG, HAPPO, ERL, PDERL, CEMRL, PGPS, ROMMEO, PR2, AORPO, MAMBA, MAZero; reward curves, win rate, 5 seeds; RTX A4500; no latency.
contribution: World-model-assisted cross-entropy evolutionary MARL that imagines opponents' intentions and trajectories to evaluate population policies, reporting about 40-fold faster convergence than model-free MARL in simulated 4 vs 4 UAV combat.
flag: Predictive accuracy: NOT reported. Only downstream results (average reward curves in the UAV game, SMAC win rates in Table 4), so exclude-E2 under the maintainer's ruling. The world model does predict joint multi-agent trajectories (the loss includes a multistep trajectory prediction error) so (b) is met in form, but no trajectory, reward or opponent-intent prediction error is ever given; the only look at the model itself is a qualitative t-SNE of inferred opponent latents (Fig. 3). UAV results are figures only: the headline 'accelerates learning by 40 times' (converges at 0.4-0.5M vs about 20M samples) and 'reward around +50' are read off Fig. 2 curves with no table, and the baselines never reach positive reward, so the speed-up compares convergence to different optima. 'Nearly 10 times' vs the no-ES variant is likewise from a curve. SMAC Table 4 is mixed, not uniformly best: 5m_vs_6m 71.87 vs MAZero 90.12 and RODE 90; 2c_vs_64zg 78.12 vs MAZero 90; 3m 93.75 vs MAZero 100; baseline numbers appear to be taken at very small step budgets (5e4-1e6) and one MAZero cell is missing. Ablations (Fig. 6) remove ES guidance, RL guidance and quality-assured mutation; none varies the world model's accuracy. Adversarial air-combat application (red vs blue UAV teams); no safety mechanism, no collision metric, no runtime interceptor. Simulation only.

title: A latent ODE approach to full-cycle biventricular cardiac motion modeling from cine MRI
evidence: "should be viewed as prognostic evaluation within UK Biobank rather than as a deployment-ready HF prediction model" (Sec. 5); the model is a covariate-conditioned VAE with latent ODE over one subject's cardiac mesh sequence.
method: Covariate-conditioned VAE with SpiralNet++ mesh encoder/decoder and neural-ODE latent dynamics over the cardiac cycle; residual latent embedding feeds a Cox model for incident heart failure risk.
evaluation: UK Biobank cine MRI, 72386 subjects, 367 HF events; vs Linear+ODE, GNN+Fourier, GNN+Transformer, MeshHeart, PCP-HF; Euclidean error 1.366 mm, C-index 0.785 vs 0.704; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Latent-ODE mesh model of the full cardiac cycle whose latent residual improves heart-failure risk prediction over clinical scores in UK Biobank; medical imaging, no agents or acting system.
flag: TITLE DIFFERS: arXiv paper is titled "A Latent ODE Approach to Spatiotemporal Modeling of Cine Cardiac MRI" (Brueggemann et al.), record says "...full-cycle biventricular cardiac motion modeling from cine MRI". Content (latent ODE, biventricular meshes, cine MRI) matches, so I treated it as the preprint of the same work, not as a wrong paper - maintainer should confirm, else this is E6. Recommend E1: state is a 64-d latent vector for a single heart; the mesh is a fixed-topology graph of 5806 vertices but there are no agents, no actions, and the model reconstructs/interpolates a periodic cycle rather than forecasting a system's future. A literal reading of (b) as latent dynamics over a graph could capture it; I do not think that is the intent. Direct accuracy IS reported (Euclidean 1.366 mm, angle 12.561 deg vs MeshHeart 1.614 mm) alongside downstream C-index, so E2 would not apply. Component ablations are figure-only.

title: TIMAR: Transition-informed representation for sample-efficient multi-agent reinforcement learning
evidence: Abstract: "leverages the joint transition model, i.e., a surrogate world model that captures the dynamics of the multi-agent system, to learn effective representations among agents through a self-supervised learning objective."
method: TIMAR: auxiliary self-supervised loss; a Transformer joint transition model predicts K-step future latent observation representations of all agents from joint observations and actions, matched to an EMA target encoder; added to MAT and QMIX.
evaluation: MA-MuJoCo (8 configs), SMAC (4 maps), vision-based Multi-Agent Quadcopter Control (2 tasks); baselines MAPPO, HAPPO, MAT, finetuned QMIX, MA2CL; episode return and win-rate curves, 5 seeds; no latency.
contribution: Transition-informed auxiliary objective that trains MARL encoders by predicting all agents' future latent observations with a Transformer joint transition model, improving sample efficiency of MAT and QMIX on three benchmarks.
flag: Predictive accuracy: NOT reported. Only downstream results (episode return on MA-MuJoCo and MAQC, win rate on SMAC, value loss and Q value in Fig. 8), so exclude-E2 under the maintainer's ruling for (b) papers with downstream-only evidence. The joint transition model is a latent predictor over joint multi-agent state (non-generative, BYOL/SPR style, no decoder), so (b) is met in substance, but its prediction error is never measured and it is used only as a training-time auxiliary loss, discarded at execution. All results are learning curves (Figs. 4-9); there is no results table with numeric values, so no metric value can be quoted. Ablations cover hyperparameters H, lambda and K on HalfCheetah 6x1 only; no ablation removes the transition model versus a non-predictive SSL loss other than the MA2CL baseline comparison. Larger K hurts performance, which the authors attribute to overfitting of the transition model. Text is inconsistent on the acronym (JTM vs JMT). No safety content, no runtime interceptor, no hardware timing.

title: Spatiotemporal interaction and world-model-enhanced multi-agent reinforcement learning for USV formation control in dynamic marine environments
evidence: "WM-PIL improves sample efficiency by generating uncertainty-filtered imagined samples." (Sec. 3.5)
method: MATD3 with pairwise relation aggregator in the critic, an ensemble Transformer world model over joint observation/action generating variance-filtered imagined transitions, and BYOL-style auxiliary temporal prediction.
evaluation: 3-USV formation simulator (Director); vs MATD3, MADDPG, GCA-MADDPG, TIMAR; 5 seeds; hit rate, formation error, obstacle clearance, steps; single-seed ablation; Tesla V100, no latency.
contribution: Multi-USV formation-control MARL that trains a joint-state Transformer world model for uncertainty-filtered imagination, raising converged hit rate from 0.684 to 0.853 over MATD3 in simulation.
flag: ONLY DOWNSTREAM RESULTS: the world model is a real latent predictor over the joint state of 3 agents, but the paper never reports its prediction error (no MSE, no rollout-horizon accuracy, no ensemble-uncertainty calibration); all metrics are training hit rate (AP 0.872, CRHR 0.853), formation error, clearance and completion steps. Recommend E2 on the maintainer's downstream-only ruling. WM contribution is isolated only in a single-seed ablation (A1 to A2: CRHR 0.639 to 0.738) which the authors themselves call non-definitive. Robustness tables are single fixed-scenario trajectories. Collision avoidance is one reward term, not the primary measured outcome, so (c) is not met; no runtime interceptor. Simulation only, 3 homogeneous USVs.

title: M-JEPA: Predictive Self-Supervised Learning for Molecular Graphs with Scaffold-Shift Evaluation on Tox21
venue: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling
evidence: Mechanism as read (paraphrase, Methods): a student encoder and predictor regress the EMA teacher's embedding of a masked connected subgraph of a molecular graph; "ESOL is used here as a proxy for objective selection" (Results, Phase 1).
method: JEPA pretraining on molecular graphs: context encoder plus predictor MLP regress EMA-teacher embeddings of masked connected subgraphs (ZINC); GINE, D-MPNN, SchNet3D backbones; no dynamics or actions.
evaluation: ESOL proxy RMSE 2.117 JEPA vs 3.746 InfoNCE (n=40 each); Tox21 scaffold split ROC-AUC 0.546 to 0.609, ECE 0.279 to 0.190 vs supervised scratch; no inference latency.
contribution: Latent-prediction (JEPA) pretraining on molecular graphs beats a compute-matched contrastive objective on an ESOL proxy and improves Tox21 scaffold-split AUC and calibration over supervised training from scratch.
flag: BORDERLINE (b): latent prediction over a graph, but STATIC masked-subgraph prediction on molecules - no temporal dynamics, no agents, no actions, not a world model; maintainer may prefer E1. Predictive-accuracy metric is downstream RMSE/AUC, not latent prediction error. No controlled ablations (paper says EMA/mask ablations not run). Internal inconsistencies: 2 vs 5 pretraining epochs, 10M vs 100,000 ZINC molecules, Wilcoxon one- vs two-sided, 80 runs but 12 paired units. Tox21 baseline AUC near 0.55 is weak. 'Safety-relevant' wording refers to toxicity, not system safety.

title: Physics-informed GCN-LSTM framework for long-term forecasting of 2D and 3D microstructure evolution
evidence: Results, Predicting long-horizon microstructures: "The graphs use a fixed 4-neighbor spatial connectivity and are passed to a GCN-LSTM model, which predicts the latent representation of the next timestep"
method: Convolutional autoencoder compresses phase-field frames; latents become a 4-neighbour grid graph (4096 nodes in 2D); GCN-LSTM predicts next latent; Cahn-Hilliard and mass-conservation loss terms; decoder with mean-composition projection.
evaluation: Bi-Sb spinodal decomposition phase-field data, 2D (9 compositions) and 3D (2); train t=0-20k, forecast 20k-40k; four ablations, no external baseline; MSE, SSIM, mass conservation; CPU, forecast 22-39 s.
contribution: Physics-informed GCN-LSTM that forecasts phase-field microstructure evolution in an autoencoder latent arranged as a grid graph, reaching validation MSE 5.1e-5 and SSIM 0.9994 in 2D with mass conserved.
flag: Predictive accuracy: DIRECT measure reported (Table 1 and 3 validation MSE/SSIM; Table 4 forecast at t=23,000: full model MSE 0.009231, SSIM 0.9110), with ablations but NO external baseline. Borderline on topic, maintainer should decide: this is a materials-science PDE surrogate (Cahn-Hilliard spinodal decomposition); the 'graph' is a fixed regular 4-neighbour lattice over CNN latent pixels of one scalar field, not a relational or multi-agent state, and there are no agents or actions. It meets (b) only on the literal reading (latent prediction of future state on a graph); if the maintainer wants graph state to mean entities/agents, this is exclude-E1. Doubts: (1) in the Table 4 forecast the full model is WORSE than the autoencoder ablation (MSE 0.006820, SSIM 0.9324) and the GCN ablation (0.006896, 0.9199); the paper argues for the full model on training time and mass conservation instead. (2) GCN ablation was trained only to epoch 12, so that comparison is not like for like. (3) Forecasting is described as 'one-shot': the model predicts one latent and the decoded frame is compared to several future ground-truth frames, so the 'long-horizon' claim (to t=39,000) is not an autoregressive rollout; forecast SSIM about 0.91 is far below the 0.999 validation figure. (4) Table 4 covers one composition (X=0.30) at one timestep. (5) 3D model trained on CPU for 52 h, only 2 compositions, loss for X=0.50 described as partially converged. No safety content, no runtime use, no latency constraint.

title: Robust graph-coupled state-space identification under missing observations: mask-aware EM with uncertainty quantification for panel systems
evidence: "We model inter-unit coupling in latent space through a Laplacian-driven diffusion term embedded directly in the transition operator." (Sec. 2.3)
method: Linear latent state-space model over 117 regions coupled by a fixed kNN graph Laplacian; mask-aware EM with Student-t observation noise and spectral-radius stability projection.
evaluation: NUTS2 socio-economic panel, 2016-2022 window; masked-entry reconstruction at 5-20% MCAR/MAR vs two Gaussian state-space baselines; MAE, RMSE, 80/95% interval coverage. No hardware or latency.
contribution: Graph-Laplacian-coupled latent state-space identification for partially observed panels, reporting near-nominal 95% interval coverage (0.953-0.957) but no point-accuracy gain over Gaussian baselines.
flag: BORDERLINE (b). Direct accuracy measure IS reported, but it is held-out masked-entry reconstruction by a smoother (uses past and future data), not forecasting: at 10% masking proposed MAE 3.45/3.55, RMSE 10.94/11.16, Cov95 0.953/0.957 (MCAR/MAR) vs Gaussian B1 MAE 3.45/3.49, RMSE 10.60/10.93, Cov95 0.798/0.796 and B2 Cov95 0.992/0.993. Point error is NOT better than the plain Gaussian baseline; the only gain is coverage. Multi-step forecast errors and CRPS are promised in Sec. 2.9 and Method 5 but no forecast numbers appear anywhere, so no future-state prediction metric exists; if the maintainer requires forward prediction this is E2. No ablation removing the graph coupling. Nodes are EU regions (economic panel), not agents; no safety content. Internal inconsistencies: transition written as I(x)A + L(x)C in Sec. 2 and (A(x)I) - (L(x)G) in Sec. 3; stability by projection in Sec. 2.7 vs penalty in Sec. 3.4; Laplacian called symmetric in Sec. 4.7 but built as row-normalised from a directed kNN graph; nu updated in M-step vs fixed degrees of freedom; smoothness energy falling to ~0 looks like over-smoothing. Single author; ChatGPT use disclosed; data and code not public.

title: Adaptive and transparent decision-making in autonomous robots through graph-structured world models
evidence: "This graph-structured world model aids in the prediction of future states and supports graph-based planning algorithms." (Section 3, Proposed method)
method: Contrastive hindsight learning gives a reachability latent space; offline states are clustered into graph vertices with transition edges; an LLM relabels rewards; value iteration plans, LLM explains.
evaluation: D4RL Maze2D, AntMaze, Kitchen, Adroit versus BC, CQL, IQL, ATAC, COMBO, VMG, Diffusion-QL: normalised totals 475.8, 498.1, 243.6, 175.3; loss and radius ablations. Simulation only, no latency.
contribution: Builds a graph-structured world model from offline robot data in a reachability latent space, uses an LLM to relabel rewards to user intent, plans by value iteration and explains the plan in language.
flag: Recommend exclude-E2: ONLY DOWNSTREAM task results are reported (D4RL normalised scores in Tables 2-4 and task-completion ratios in Table 3); there is no direct measure of the world model's predictive accuracy (no latent-displacement or transition prediction error, no graph-edge validity check). E1 is also arguable: this is a SINGLE agent, and the graph is an abstraction of that agent's state space (vertices are clusters of states), not a graph-structured or multi-agent state; the latent displacement predictor is predictive, so I kept (b) as borderline. No runtime interceptor; the LLM explains plans and tells the user when a goal is infeasible (Fig. 6) but there is no deferral or takeover, so no human-handoff cell. Explainability is shown by two worked examples only, no user study. Details: Section 4.3.4 says self-imitation is tested by 'removing Lcontrast' (should be Limit); hindsight offset h 'sampled from {1, 10}'; seeds and variance are not reported in the tables; several baseline cells are blank; method loses to VMG on 4 of 9 maze tasks and gains are concentrated in Kitchen. No abstract numbers to verify. Read abstract, Sections 3.1-3.4.1, 4, 5, 6; did not read Sections 1-2, 3.4.2-3.4.3 detail or appendices.

title: Adversarial Trajectory Attack Targeting Autonomous Driving Planners with Residual-based Defense
evidence: Sec. V-E2: "Table 11 shows that enabling defense reduces the collision rate from 0.9033 to 0.1143."
method: AVATAR: PPO adversary vehicle perturbing a local goal fed to a quintic planner. Defense: log-likelihood-ratio detector on multi-horizon MTR prediction residuals of surrounding agents switches ego to conservative IDM fallback planner.
evaluation: Waymax closed loop, 5 core plus 25 extra WOMD scenes, 4 victim planners, 3 attacker seeds x 50 rollouts; no-defense baseline, 8 anomaly detectors; safety score, collision rate, AUC, FPR/TPR, efficiency; no latency.
contribution: A prediction-residual likelihood-ratio monitor that switches a driving planner to a conservative fallback under adversarial-vehicle attack, cutting simulated collision rate from 0.90 to 0.11 at 9.25% object-level false positives.
flag: NOT a Pillar 2 criterion (b) paper: it neither proposes nor evaluates a world model. The only world-model content is LatentDriver used off the shelf as one of four victim planners, and MTR used off the shelf as the trajectory predictor behind the detector; no predictive-accuracy metric of either model is reported (only detector AUC 0.9227 vs 8 generic detectors, and downstream safety/efficiency). On Pillar 2 grounds alone this would be exclude-E1. I recommend include because it squarely meets (a) and (c): a runtime monitor plus fallback switch between nominal planner and execution, with collision rate against a no-defense baseline (overall 0.9033 to 0.1143; safety score 0.2660 to 0.9422; time to first collision 2.97 to 6.30 s) and false-halt cost reported (FPR 9.25%, TPR 85.03%, fallback active in 37.66% of benign steps, 10.47 switches per benign rollout, benign efficiency 0.9420 to 0.9052, under-attack efficiency 0.8540 to 0.5786). Maintainer should decide whether it belongs under Pillar 1 instead. Caveats: simulation only; n=3 attacker seeds so several 95% CIs exceed [0,1]; VS scenario stays weak with defense (BC 0.5778); detector Gaussians fitted on the same attacker family (leave-one-scenario/planner-out AUC 0.87-0.99 partly addresses this); no defense-aware adaptive attacker; no inference-time or latency figure for the detector despite calling it real-time (the 200 ms latency test applies to the attacker's observations); fallback has no formal guarantee. Abstract numbers (1.0 to 0.27, 0.27 to 0.94, 100 scene-victim pairs) all found in body. Extended version of an ACSW 2025 workshop paper. Header carries a template placeholder DOI (10.1109/ACCESS.2024.0429000) and 'VOLUME 11, 2023': author's accepted version, not final. Long file (294k chars): I read abstract, intro, Sec. IV defense, Sec. V-E defense results, Tables 8-12 and discussion; I skimmed and did not fully read the attack results (Tables 1-7), related work and appendices.

title: A Relational-Latent World Model for Long-Horizon Dyadic Interaction: Results on the ACII-DaiKon 2026 Challenge
venue: 2026 14th International Conference on Affective Computing and Intelligent Interaction Workshops and Demos, ACIIW 2026
evidence: Sec. IV-H: "Under autoregressive rollout with no fresh input the trained tracker retains 80% of its k=0 predictive power at k=4 (0.494 -> 0.395)"
method: Heterogeneous graph-attention encoder over a per-turn two-speaker graph plus three-stream GRU state tracker yields a 384-D dyadic latent; small heads read influence, turn-taking and rapport. Simulator-pretrained, fine-tuned end to end.
evaluation: ACII-DaiKon 2026 validation split, 3 seeds; baselines Hume audio model, feature MLP, random init, frozen backbone; CCC, macro-F1, latency MAE, latent rollout CCC; 21 ms per turn A100, 137 ms one CPU core.
contribution: A 7.49M-parameter graph-recurrent latent model of two-speaker conversation whose autoregressive latent rollout keeps 80% of influence-prediction CCC at four turns ahead and runs in 21 ms per turn.
flag: Predictive accuracy: DIRECT measures are reported (Influence CCC 0.495 vs 0.39 baseline, Rapport CCC 0.697 vs 0.65, Turn-Taking macro-F1 0.547 vs 0.61 i.e. worse than baseline, latency MAE 1.89 s vs 1.53 s worse; autoregressive latent rollout CCC 0.494 at k=0 to 0.395 at k=4 vs random-init and identity controls), so not E2 on that ground. Doubts: (1) the 'agents' are two HUMAN speakers in recorded audio; nothing is an autonomous or acting system, the LLM planner-critic use is stated intent only and no closed loop is evaluated - multi-agent only nominally (dyad). (2) The paper itself reports that a capacity-matched feature MLP with no graph or recurrence matches it on Influence (0.496 vs 0.494) and Turn-Taking (0.546 vs 0.547); the frozen backbone never reaches baseline; a multi-step linear probe shows no forecasting advantage over raw Whisper at k>=1 (0.210 vs 0.231 at k=4); the JEPA and EBM auxiliary objectives were switched off because they did not help. The world-model claim therefore rests on one rollout experiment. (3) Validation split only, no official test scores; best-epoch selection is admitted to overstate Rapport by up to about 0.09 CCC, larger than the +0.047 headline gain. (4) Most ablation tables are in supplementary material not in this text. (5) Single author from a small organisation, workshop challenge paper; pretraining corpora are synthetic and undescribed. (6) 'Suited to on-device, edge deployment' is asserted from an A100 and a single-CPU-core timing (p95 197 ms); no edge hardware tested, so I did not credit the edge cell. Rapport per-country CCC for Germany is given as 0.122 (3-seed) and 0.082 (single checkpoint); the text explains the difference. Abstract numbers all found in body. Timings are against a 250 ms dialogue budget, not a safety deadline.

title: Coordinated World Model Learning for Deep Space Robot Teams
evidence: Sec. 7: "the research presented in this article belongs to the Concept Phase with feasibility studies conducted for simple test service and laboratory robot teams."
method: Conceptual framework: a robot world model defined as a 4-tuple (meta-model, real-time instance, decision engine, generalization algorithm); team world models merged by sharing and consensus under changing communication graphs; multicriteria task allocation.
evaluation: Illustrative worked examples of a 3-4 robot icy-moon team and one Matlab map-coverage simulation over 405 s shown as figures; no baselines, ablations, accuracy metrics, hardware or latency.
contribution: A concept-phase formal framework for shared world-model building by planetary multi-robot teams, illustrated with a simulated icy-moon mapping example and no quantitative evaluation.
flag: Predictive accuracy: NONE reported, and no downstream metrics against a baseline either. The only 'results' are Figs. 5-6 (map coverage progress and per-robot data-transfer quantities at five time steps of one simulated run) and hand-worked utility examples. The authors themselves call it Concept Phase and say ablation studies are future work. E1 is also defensible: the 'world model' here is a knowledge base of maps, object libraries, rules and labelling functions (SLAM-style shared map with knowledge fusion), not a learned predictive or latent dynamics model; MA-MBRL, federated learning and Dreamer-like methods are named as candidate ingredients but none is implemented. Abstract promises 'arguments' that the approach minimizes robot damage risk and a reliability/cost comparison of single- vs multi-robot missions; I found no quantitative comparison in the body. Single author, heavy self-citation ([19],[20],[22]). Background image generated with DreamShaper. Read: abstract, Secs. 1-2, parts of 4-5 including the simulation, Secs. 7-8; skimmed Sec. 3 and Sec. 6.

title: TrajJEPA: A Joint-Embedding Predictive Model For Multi-agent Trajectory Prediction
venue: 2026 9th International Conference on Advanced Electronic Technology, Computers and Software Engineering, AETCSE 2026
evidence: Sec. IV-B1: "TrajJEPA achieves minADE20/minFDE20 = 0.70/0.87, outperforming both MART (0.73/0.90) and the previous best-performing"
method: Unified spatio-temporal Transformer over an agents-by-time token grid; whole agents' histories are masked in training and their latents predicted against stop-gradient targets (JEPA loss) alongside multi-modal coordinate decoding.
evaluation: NBA SportVU (10 players plus ball, 2 s history, 4 s horizon); baselines STAR, GroupNet, MemoNet, MID, NPSN, LED, DynGrpNet, MART, ViTE; minADE20/minFDE20, parameters, MACs; ablations; no latency or hardware.
contribution: Agent-level masked latent prediction added to a compact Transformer trajectory forecaster, reaching 0.70/0.87 minADE20/minFDE20 at 4 s on NBA player tracking against 0.72/0.91 for the prior best.
flag: Predictive accuracy: DIRECT measure reported (minADE20/minFDE20 at 1-4 s vs 9 baselines, plus ablations), no downstream task at all, so the (b) minimum evaluation is met. Doubts: (1) the JEPA part is an auxiliary training loss; the output is still decoded coordinates, and the 'target' is the same encoder with stop-gradient (no EMA target encoder), so calling it a world model or latent predictor is generous - it is a trajectory forecaster with a masked-latent regulariser. No actions, not action-conditioned. I did not credit the non-generative cell for that reason; maintainer may differ. (2) The JEPA gain is small: full 0.701/0.871 vs no-JEPA 0.717/0.907 and mask-only 0.716/0.898, single run, no seeds or variance. (3) Abstract and Sec. IV say state of the art 'across all time horizons', but Table I shows 1.0 s minADE 0.18 vs ViTE 0.17. (4) Abstract claims 'highly competitive computational efficiency' but Table II gives 289.1M MACs vs ViTE 23.1M and MART 43.3M (about 12x and 7x more); only parameter count (0.87M) is best; no inference time measured. (5) Baseline numbers are copied from the ViTE paper, not rerun. (6) Single dataset of human players and a ball, no vehicles or robots, no graph (attention over tokens), no safety content. Minor low-tier conference, authors use personal qq.com addresses. Removing time positional encoding gives 1.848/1.954, the only large ablation effect.

title: World-Model-Enhanced UAV Intelligent Inspection Method for Converter Station Valve Halls
venue: 2026 9th International Conference on Computer Information Science and Application Technology, CISAT 2026
evidence: "The world model is defined as a dynamic state container for valve-hall inspection rather than merely a three-dimensional map." (Sec. III-A)
method: Single UAV: multisensor fusion writes equipment evidence into a temporal graph state store; RAG LLM diagnoses from it; deterministic rule verifier rejects unsafe LLM outputs and gates every flight action.
evaluation: Field records and trial flights, 7:1:2 split; baselines visible-only to multisensor+world-model, 5 ablations. F1 95.4%, risk accuracy 93.4%, hallucination 1.9%, localization error 0.09 m. No hardware or latency.
contribution: Valve-hall UAV inspection pipeline in which a graph-structured evidence store grounds an LLM diagnoser and a rule gate vets its outputs and reinspection actions; reports defect F1 of 95.4%.
flag: Pillar 2 (b) NOT met: the 'world model' is an evidence/state store (geometry, equipment, defects, rules, history), not a predictive or latent-prediction model, and there is one UAV, so no multi-agent state; no predictive-accuracy metric exists (not applicable) - hence E1 on Pillar 2 grounds. Only downstream perception/diagnosis results are reported. It does have a runtime gate (Sec. III-C, V: unsafe outputs 'rejected and replaced by a safe action'; 'Every action must pass the safety-gating module'), so I marked (a) and interceptor yes; but if judged under (a) it fails the minimum evaluation (E2): safety-constraint violations are 0 for ALL arms in Table V including fixed-route and rule-triggered baselines, and the 'without rule validation' ablation reports F1/risk/hallucination (6.5% vs 1.9%) but no violation or intervention rate. Single-agent, so E4 is also arguable. Other doubts: dataset size, number of flights/defects, seeds and error bars never given; 'field validation' is unquantified; LLM and edge hardware unnamed, no latency; Eq. (2) is labelled G_t but described as the update process; odd phrase 'in a parallel syntactic structure' suggests machine-edited text; all authors from two companies, company-funded. Abstract numbers (95.4, 93.4, 1.9) do match Tables III/IV.

title: Semantic Governance Paradigm of Heterogeneous World Models for Agentic AI Systems
venue: Proceedings - 2026 IEEE 50th Annual Computers, Software, and Applications Conference, COMPSAC 2026
evidence: "We consider multi-class node classification tasks on Person nodes, aiming to predict social or relational categories derived from graph structure and node attributes." (Section V-B, Experimental Scenarios and Tasks)
method: Design-time 'semantic governance' for heterogeneous graphs: an ontology restricts, filters and ranks metapaths (ODMD) before a heterogeneous embedding pipeline (AGHE) builds node embeddings.
evaluation: One author-made Person-Car-Pet graph, node classification, five metapath configurations: accuracy 0.8325-0.8920, MRR 0.9202-0.9441, std 0.0040-0.0169. No agent, hardware or latency.
contribution: Proposes ontology-governed selection of metapaths for heterogeneous graph embeddings, framed as world models for agentic AI, and compares metapath sets on node classification over a small Person-Car-Pet graph.
flag: Recommend exclude-E1 under the 2026-11-12 ruling: the 'world model' is a STATIC heterogeneous graph embedding; nothing predicts a future state, there are no dynamics, no actions and no agent in the experiments. 'Predictive scoring' means ranking metapaths by classification utility. The only measurements are downstream node-classification Accuracy, MRR and std (Table II); there is NO measure of world-model predictive accuracy, so it would be E2 even if it passed E1. 'Governance' here is design-time schema control, not runtime monitoring, so (a) is not met either. Text and table disagree: Section VI-C says manual designs 'consistently underperform ontology-governed configurations', but AGHE (manual) scores 0.8868, above both ODMD (filtered) rows (0.8590 and 0.8325) and within about 0.005 of the best (0.8920); differences are small relative to the claims. F1 is named as a metric but never reported; number of runs and folds not stated; single toy 'authorial' dataset with no size given. Agentic framing is rhetorical throughout. Read abstract, introduction, Sections III-C to IV opening, V, VI, VII and Table II; skimmed Section II and III-A/B.

title: Steering Uncertainty: Mean-Field-Augmented Physics-Informed Reinforcement Learning for AUV Swarm Coordination in Underwater IoT
venue: Proceedings - 2026 22nd International Conference on Distributed Computing in Smart Systems and the Internet of Things, DCOSS-IoT 2026
evidence: "The PIWM is a GRU-based stochastic latent model in the spirit of recurrent state-space architectures." (Sec. III-B)
method: Mean-field SAC for AUV swarms with soft augmented-Lagrangian SNR penalty, GRU stochastic latent world model anchored to Thorp attenuation whose prior-posterior KL is a reward penalty, and diffusion action refiner.
evaluation: Simulated 32 AUVs, 90 episodes; baselines MADDPG, Greedy, PSO, Random; 5 ablations. Relay coverage 86.1%, SNR violation rate 76.85%, max deficit 5.9 dB. RTX 4080 laptop: 0.69 ms batched.
contribution: Mean-field multi-agent RL for underwater vehicle swarms that uses the KL divergence of a physics-anchored latent world model as an uncertainty penalty, trading coverage against acoustic-link SNR violations in simulation.
flag: NO direct measure of world-model predictive accuracy: the PIWM is never evaluated as a predictor (no SNR/state prediction error, no rollout); only downstream results (coverage, SNR, violation rate, capacity) and its KL training curve. Per the maintainer's ruling that is E2, so I recommend E2. The model is predictive in form (posterior/prior latent, physics head regressing SNR) and its input includes the mean-field neighbour statistic, so (b) is nominally met, but it is used only to produce a reward penalty during training, not for prediction or planning at run time. Not (a): the constraint is a training-time penalty ('penalized rather than strictly guaranteed'); not (c) either. Doubts: removing the world model LOWERS violations (NoWM 64.78% vs Full 76.85%, said to be n.s.), and NoU+D/NoDiff/SAC have higher coverage than Full, so the 'only method with >=85% coverage and reduced violations' claim rests on chosen thresholds; violation at N=32 is 76.85% in Table II but 75.1% in Sec. IV-D; mean SNR 63.67 dB is quoted both as training min-SNR and as evaluation mean SNR, and 64.74 dB in Sec. IV-D; SAC mean SNR is exactly 60.00; Table I batched fleet inference 0.69 ms is far below the diffusion step alone (15.54 ms); MADDPG trained on one seed, baselines n=30 vs n=90. Violation rate in absolute terms is 77%. Simulation only, lossless inter-agent channel assumed.

title: Multi-Agent Sparse Interaction Modeling is an Anomaly Detection Problem
venue: ICASSP, IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing - Proceedings
evidence: "Informed by this observation, we employ the prediction loss to assess whether current states are interactive." (Sec. 3.2)
method: SIA: per-agent VAE with GRU encoder learns latent dynamics of local trajectories; next-state and reward prediction error flags interactive states and becomes an intrinsic exploration reward added to QMIX.
evaluation: Two-robot Hallway gridworld versus EITI, Max Entropy, epsilon-greedy; SMAC 3s5z, 5m_vs_6m, 10m_vs_11m versus QMIX variants, MAVEN, QTRAN, QPLEX, 5 seeds; alpha ablation. Returns and win rates, figures only.
contribution: Treats sparse multi-agent interaction as anomaly detection: states where a per-agent latent dynamics model predicts poorly are deemed interactive and rewarded for exploration, speeding cooperative learning on SMAC.
flag: NO direct measure of predictive accuracy: only downstream results (episodic reward in Hallway, SMAC win-rate curves) plus one qualitative plot of prediction discrepancy along one robot's route (Fig. 3d). Per the maintainer's ruling that is E2. (b) is borderline and E1 is also defensible: the model is predictive (decoder predicts next local state and reward) but it models each agent's LOCAL trajectory, deliberately not the joint state; multi-agent structure appears only as prediction error. Not safety: 'anomaly' here means interaction states used as an exploration bonus, not a hazard detector; nothing acts at run time. All results are curves in figures; the text gives no numeric values, no tables, no hardware, and the figure text in the extracted file is garbled. Detected interactive states are not validated against ground truth beyond the two-robot example. 4-page ICASSP paper.

title: A Graph World Model for Action-Conditioned and Multi-Step Edge Orchestration
venue: IEEE International Conference on Communications in China Workshops, ICCC
evidence: "At H = 20, GraphRSSM reaches 0.0358 MSE, compared with 0.229 for MLP, 0.304 for GAT, 0.506 for ST-GNN, and 0.395 for the action-ablated GraphRSSM." (Sec. IV-B)
method: GraphRSSM: recurrent state-space world model with node-aligned latents; action injected before edge-aware message passing; prior-driven recursive rollout; CEM-style scoring of candidate action sequences under a decision-time budget.
evaluation: Abilene/GEANT trace-derived benchmark, 11,988 transitions; baselines VAR, MLP, ST-GNN, GAT, action-ablated variant. Rollout MSE 0.0080 at H=1, 0.0358 at H=20; CPU p95 5.13 ms rollout, 1.206 s CEM.
contribution: Graph recurrent state-space world model that rolls out action-conditioned futures of an edge network over 20 steps with up to 6.39x lower error than forecasting baselines, at 5 ms per 10-step CPU rollout.
flag: Reports a DIRECT measure of world-model predictive accuracy (recursive rollout MSE at H=1..20, Table I) with four baselines and an action ablation, so the (b) minimum is met; no downstream task result at all - the authors state they do 'not train or evaluate a standalone online orchestration policy'. Method/architecture evidence only (RQ5 <= 2). Check: the action effects are synthetic - 'residual action effects are specified by diagnostic action settings rather than observed action labels from the traces' - so the model is validated against dynamics the authors designed; on the alternative-action test persistence has LOWER MSE (0.0470) than GraphRSSM (0.0657); no seeds or error bars; MSE units/normalisation not stated; graph size not stated; CPU model unnamed. Abstract's 'sub-second' holds only for H=5 CEM scoring (0.589 s); H=10 takes 1.206 s. '6.39x' is versus the best baseline at H=20 (0.229/0.0358). MSE@15 (0.0285) is below MSE@10 (0.030), non-monotone. (d) is partial: an explicit decision deadline (Eq. 9) and p95 latency, but for orchestration, not a safety decision; drop it if strict. State is a graph of edge sites under one orchestrator, not several agents, so I did not tick the multi-agent-state cell. Only arXiv id in the text is a reference (2603.17420), not this paper.

title: WHO: World Model Approach for Handover Optimization in 5G Networks
venue: Proceedings - International Conference on Computer Communications and Networks, ICCCN
evidence: "our proposed world model consistently outperforms all benchmarks, achieving the superior predictive accuracy with the lowest MAPE of 3.21% in the Industrial Zone and 2.41% in the Rural Area" (Sec. IV-C1)
method: WHO: multi-head-attention VAE encodes multi-cell handover-success states and rewards into a latent; MDN-RNN predicts 24-hour latent and reward trajectories; MAPPO agents per cell choose handover margin and time-to-trigger.
evaluation: Live 5G trial, 13 gNodeBs, 39 cells, 10 days; baselines ARIMA, Prophet, LightGBM, MAVAE-LSTM, Informer; 3 ablations. MAPE 3.21% and 2.41%; throughput +30.54%; inference 2-3 s on L40 GPU.
contribution: Latent world model over the joint handover state of neighbouring 5G cells that forecasts 24-hour success rates (MAPE 2.4-3.2%) and feeds per-cell MAPPO agents, field-tested on 39 live cells.
flag: Reports a DIRECT measure of world-model predictive accuracy (MAE/RMSE/MAPE of 24-hour handover-success forecasts, Tables III/IV) with five baselines and three ablations (Tables IX/X), plus downstream live-network KPIs; (b) minimum met, method evidence only. Many things to doubt: (1) Abstract's '19-40% higher prediction precision' and 'up to 32% improvement in KPIs' appear nowhere in the body; the body gives 30.54% throughput and 42.86% call-drop improvement. (2) Rural throughput is stated as +3.11% but Table VI gives 173.05 to 188.75 (+9.1%). (3) RMSE below MAE in the same row (Prophet 5.27 MAE vs 5.06 RMSE; MDN-RNN 4.27 vs 3.92), which is mathematically impossible. (4) Table IX: WHO RMSE 3.75 is worse than MA-VAE+RNN 3.74 although the text says the full model is lowest on all three. (5) 'RMSE is nearly 150% higher ... from 1.97 to 2.23' is a 13% rise. (6) Abstract claims gains over 'conventional DRL approaches' but no model-free DRL baseline is run. (7) Eq. 11 GRU takes only z_t, so the model as written is not action-conditioned although the text says it is. (8) Training data is 8 days of hourly samples with an 80/20 split; test set and seeds unspecified. (9) KPI comparison is before/after against earlier weeks, uncontrolled; unclear how six planners and three ablations each got live KPI rows within 10 days. (10) Duplicate equation numbers (11)-(14); claims 'near-perfect' accuracy. State is a multi-cell feature matrix with attention, not an explicit graph. Hourly cadence, seconds-scale inference: not real-time. All authors from one operator.

title: Unified Scene Graph Forecasting Considering Node Birth and Disappearance
venue: 2026 IEEE 2nd International Conference on Consumer Technology, ICCT-Pacific 2026
evidence: "The LDPU introduces the existence probability of each node as a conditional variable, which enables the modeling of node birth and disappearance." (Sec. II-D)
method: UniSGF-BD: transformer object and spatial encoders, an SDE over per-node existence probability (birth and death rates), an SDE over latent pairwise relation features, and a decoder emitting future scene graphs.
evaluation: Action Genome video, horizon 3 frames, vs SceneSayerSDE and FDSG. R@20 42.7-60.2, R@50 53.3-72.0 on AG-S; Birth Acc 82.5, Disap Acc 78.9, TCS 0.74 vs 0.66. No hardware or latency.
contribution: Forecasts future video scene graphs with stochastic differential equations over latent relation features and per-node existence probabilities, so objects can appear or vanish; beats two forecasting baselines on Action Genome recall.
flag: Meets (b) as graph-state latent forecasting; DIRECT predictive accuracy is reported (R@k, mR@k, birth and disappearance accuracy) against two baselines, so not E2. Not safety, not multi-agent (human-object scene graph from video), no interceptor. Doubts: 4-page conference paper with no ablation and no training details, seeds or code; Table I PG-AGS F=0.7 baseline rows are digit-for-digit identical to the AG-S F=0.7 rows (likely copy-paste) and the PG-AGS F=0.9 numbers jump to 88-94, so the table looks unreliable; text says it outperforms both baselines but at PG-AGS F=0.9 FDSG is higher on mR@20 (72.0 vs 70.2) and mR@50 (92.2 vs 89.7); the claimed object-category and bounding-box forecasting is never scored; Birth Acc, Disap Acc, Corr and TCS are not defined by formula; dataset citation [10] is Home Action Genome, not Action Genome. Abstract carries no numbers.

title: Network Digital Twin for Route Optimization in 5G/B5G Transport Slicing with What-If Analysis
venue: IEEE International Conference on Communications workshops
evidence: "These routes are sent to the virtual twin (6), which tests the suggestions, predicts the QoS metrics for each route, and sends the predictions to the Application layer (7)." (Sec III)
method: Network digital twin: attention message-passing GNN (RouteNet-Fermi variant) predicts per-slice latency for candidate routes on the switch graph after a failure; routes proposed by PPO or random; operator approves.
evaluation: Mininet/ONOS emulation, 8-, 16-, 30-node topologies, eMBB and URLLC slices. Predicted vs measured latency MAPE 1.67-2.28%. Routing compared with ONOS default shortest path. No predictor baseline, no inference time.
contribution: Closed-loop network digital twin in which a graph neural network predicts slice latency for candidate reroutes before deployment, with predicted-versus-measured error of about 2 percent on emulated topologies up to 30 nodes.
flag: Reports a DIRECT predictive-accuracy measure: Table III MAPE of predicted vs measured end-to-end latency (8 nodes 1.73-1.89%, 16 nodes 1.67-1.95%, 30 nodes 2.10-2.28%), so not downstream-only. BORDERLINE on the v1.6 minimum: there is NO baseline or ablation for the predictor itself (no alternative model, no component removed); the only comparisons are across three topology sizes and two route proposers, and the ONOS default route appears only in latency plots (Figs 4-5, no numbers in text). If the baseline-or-ablation rule is applied strictly this is exclude-E2 - maintainer to decide. Graph state is a network of switches and flows, not acting agents, so I did not tick multi-agent state. Prediction is action-conditioned (what-if on a candidate route) but a one-step steady-state latency estimate, not a rollout. Other doubts: abstract says it 'achieved lower MAPE values' with no comparator; Sec V says predictions are 'generated by the recommendation system' where the virtual twin is meant; number of trials per MAPE cell not given; 'physical network' is a Mininet emulation on one machine with traffic scaled down for compute limits and congestion explicitly excluded; GNN pre-trained on a public 5-8 node dataset, training details deferred to ref [15]. A human operator accepts or rejects each route (Fig 2) but this is approval of a recommendation, not a takeover study. RQ5 capped at 2.

title: Push, See, Predict: Emergent Perception Through Intrinsically Motivated Play
venue: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Development and Learning, ICDL 2025
evidence: "we use a fully connected graph neural network (GNN) as an action-conditioned transition model over slot representations" (Sec. III-C)
method: Slot Attention vision encoder plus a fully connected GNN transition model over object slots; pixel-space prediction error above a reconstruction reference is the intrinsic reward for a Double Q-learning push policy; both models then fine-tuned.
evaluation: CoppeliaSim UR5 tabletop pushing, 400 episodes per dataset. Next-frame MSE (x1e-2) 0.131 random and 0.135-0.143 heuristic test vs 0.209 and 0.235 for random-data training. No hardware or latency.
contribution: Trains an object-slot graph world model from scratch in simulation and uses its prediction error as a curiosity reward; data gathered by the resulting push policy cuts next-frame prediction error by roughly 40 percent.
flag: Meets (b) as an action-conditioned GNN world model over an object graph; DIRECT predictive accuracy is reported (next-frame MSE, Table II) with data-source comparisons (random, heuristic, intrinsic policy, with or without enhanced vision), so not E2. Borderline points for the maintainer: single robot arm, the graph is object slots not agents; the comparisons vary the training data, there is no alternative world-model architecture baseline (no non-graph model); accuracy is measured after decoding to pixels, not in latent space. Not safety, no interceptor. Doubts: the headline 'up to three times more object displacement' is stated in prose only, no table, no variance; the claim that raw prediction error and ensemble disagreement rewards are too noisy is asserted without data; single run, no seeds or error bars; simulation only, fixed push orientation; Table III of hyperparameters is referenced but not present in the extracted text. I did not read the reference list in full.

title: Decentralized Collective World Model for Emergent Communication and Coordination
venue: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Development and Learning, ICDL 2025
evidence: Sec. V.A: "the BC condition demonstrated superior coordination, followed by the EC condition."
method: Two agents each hold an RSSM world model and exchange a latent Gaussian message; collective free energy is decomposed per agent with product-of-experts regularisation and InfoNCE; policies by behavioural cloning.
evaluation: Simulated 2-D two-agent point-tracing task, 5 observation-bin settings, 3 seeds x 100 tests; baselines centralized BrainConnected, NoCommunication, with/without messages; metrics cross-correlation and RSA; no hardware or latency.
contribution: Decentralized per-agent recurrent world models that align latent messages through contrastive learning, reaching coordination second only to a centralized model on a two-agent tracing task.
flag: Borderline on minimum evaluation: no predictive-accuracy metric is reported; outcomes are coordination cross-correlation and RSA, and their numeric values appear only in figures (none stated in text). Strict v1.6 reading would be E2. Only 2 agents, toy task, no RL, no safety content. Text notes overlapping std ranges for most bin settings. No graph; state is joint latent of 2 agents.

title: Spatio-Temporal Neural Networks for Space-Time Series Forecasting and Relations Discovery
evidence: "In our approach, latent factors Z_t are learned during training" (Sec III-B Continuous Latent Factors); dynamics combine latents through relation matrices W between series.
method: STNN: per-series latent states advanced by a learned dynamics function that mixes neighbours through prior relation matrices, with linear decoder; variants refine (STNN-R) or discover (STNN-D) the relation graph.
evaluation: Google Flu, WHO GHO, Beijing traffic, wind, Pacific sea temperature; baselines Mean, AR, VAR-MLP, DFG, RNN-tanh, RNN-GRU; RMSE averaged over T+1 to T+5; no hardware or latency.
contribution: STNN forecasts related time series by rolling learned per-node latent states forward through a relation graph, lowering five-step RMSE on Beijing traffic to 0.056 against 0.074 for a GRU.
flag: Reports DIRECT predictive accuracy (forecast RMSE T+1 to T+5, Table II) with baselines and the STNN/STNN-R/STNN-D variants as ablation; no downstream task results. RMSE for STNN, STNN-R, STNN-D, RNN-GRU in that order: Flu .066/.061/.073/.074, GHO .261/.261/.288/.268, Beijing .056/.055/.069/.074, wind speed .047/.047/.059/.059, wind direction .061/.061/.073/.083, PST .095/.080/.109/.104. State is a graph of sensors/regions with latent dynamics, which fits (b) as latent prediction over a graph, but nodes are NOT agents, so the multi-agent state cell is not credited - maintainer to confirm that spatio-temporal sensor forecasting is in scope. Latents are free parameters learned transductively per training series (no encoder), so the model cannot be applied to a new sequence without re-optimising, which weakens it as a runtime building block. Predictions are decoded to observation space. STNN-D without a prior only matches RNN-GRU. DFG on PST is printed as .99, probably a typo. Record year 2018 is the arXiv date; ICDM paper is 2017. Read from arXiv 1804.08562, title matches.

title: Learning Latent Graph Dynamics for Visual Manipulation of Deformable Objects
venue: 2022 International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
evidence: Abstract: "G-DOOM approximates a deformable object as a sparse set of interacting keypoints, which are extracted automatically from images via unsupervised learning."
method: G-DOOM: unsupervised keypoints from depth images form a graph with learned soft edges; a recurrent latent graph dynamics model trained contrastively scores sampled pick-and-place actions in MPC.
evaluation: SoftGym rope and cloth tasks, 1000 seeds, plus Kinova Gen3 robot; baselines CFM, PlaNet, seven ablations; dynamics accuracy 99.8-99.9% vs CFM 44.8-61.1%; success 65.7-98.1%; no latency.
contribution: A contrastively trained latent graph dynamics model over unsupervised keypoints for deformable-object manipulation, reaching 99.9% predictive accuracy and up to 98.1% task success with sim-to-real transfer.
flag: Single robot, single object: the graph is over keypoints of one rope or cloth, not over agents, so it meets (b) on the graph limb only. Non-generative cell credited because training is contrastive (hinge) with no pixel reconstruction; maintainer may disagree. Belief state is a single global vector pooled from the graph. Predictive accuracy is a contrastive ranking accuracy, not a state error, and PlaNet has no value for it. Real-robot results are distance-based scores over 3 seeds and PlaNet is marginally better on rope 45 deg (68.52 vs 67.56). Efficiency claimed "comparable" with no numbers. No safety content.

title: TrafficBots: Towards World Models for Autonomous Driving Simulation and Motion Prediction
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation
evidence: Closely paraphrased (Sec. III, Problem Formulation): the policy is rolled out for all bot agents to predict "the joint future of all agents" given shared vectorized map and traffic-light context.
method: TrafficBots: shared scene-centric vectorized context plus per-agent CVAE personality and destination; interaction transformer over agents; action heads with unicycle dynamics roll out next states of all agents.
evaluation: Waymo Open Motion, up to 64 agents, 8 s horizon; vs SimNet, TrafficSim variants; test minADE 1.313, minFDE 3.102, collision 11.5%; about 10 ms per step on one 2080Ti.
contribution: TrafficBots rolls out the joint future of up to 64 traffic agents with a sub-3M-parameter attention model at about 10 ms per step, framed as a world model for driving simulation and motion prediction.
flag: Method evidence only. Authors frame it as 'towards' a world model: it is a closed-loop multi-agent behaviour policy in explicit state space (x, y, yaw, speed); the only latent is a 16-dim time-invariant personality, so 'latent prediction' is weak - maintainer to judge whether (b) holds. Prediction accuracy trails leaderboard baselines (test mAP 0.212, minADE 1.313, minFDE 3.102, miss 0.344 vs SceneTransformer 0.612/1.212/0.156). Ablation table: best model collision 11.5%, red-light 1.31% vs SimNet BC 33.4%/4.27%; these are simulation-realism metrics, not a safety mechanism. Latency figure is 16 parallel sims of 64 agents on a desktop 2080Ti, not edge hardware and no jitter analysis; latency cell credited loosely, drop if strict. Read via WebFetch summary in one pass.

title: Graph-JEPA: Self-Supervised Relational Inference on Heterogeneous Biomedical Graphs for Drug Repositioning
venue: 2026 10th International Artificial Intelligence and Data Processing Symposium (IDAP)
evidence: "The Embedding Alignment Loss (LJEPA) calculates the Mean Squared Error between context predictions and target embeddings." (Sec. IV-C)
method: Two-layer RGCN context encoder and EMA target encoder with curriculum edge masking on a static SemMedDB plus RepoDB knowledge graph; predictor aligns embeddings and classifies relations; drug-disease pairs scored by cosine similarity.
evaluation: Held-out 15 percent edge split, 20,560 balanced edges: test ROC-AUC 0.7840, accuracy 56.17 percent. No baseline or ablation on the same data; lung carcinoma case study of 3 drugs. Cloud GPU, no latency.
contribution: Adapts the joint-embedding predictive architecture to a heterogeneous biomedical knowledge graph for drug repositioning, reporting 0.784 ROC-AUC on held-out links but without any baseline run on the same data.
flag: Recommend E2: meets (b) only nominally (masked latent prediction over a STATIC knowledge graph; nothing is forecast over time and there is no world model or agent state, so E1 is equally defensible) and the minimum evaluation fails - there is NO baseline or ablation on the same data. The only comparison is TransE figures (0.58 Hits@10, 0.38 MRR) quoted from another paper on another graph in a different metric, yet the abstract claims 'outperforming classical baselines'. A direct accuracy measure does exist (link-prediction ROC-AUC 0.784, accuracy 56.17 percent) but 56 percent on a 1:1 balanced set is close to chance. Other doubts: abstract says collapse is avoided 'without negative sampling' while the loss includes a negative sampling term (0.5 LNeg); selection threshold stated as SCosine > 0.73 but the showcased Entrectinib scores 0.7143; Etoposide and Gemcitabine are long-established lung cancer drugs, not novel predictions, and the PubMed-count validation is circular; '62.94% average confidence score' appears only in the conclusion; garbled terminology ('Joint Embedded Estimator Architecture', 'Unified Embedding Estimation Architecture', 'gradient descent (EMA)') and a header listing 'Turkiye ... Philippines' suggest machine translation or weak editing. Abstract numbers 78.40 and 56.17 are found in Sec. V.

title: A Graph Regularized Point Process Model for Event Propagation Sequence
venue: Proceedings of the International Joint Conference on Neural Networks
evidence: "GRPP provides model interpretability by uncovering influence strengths between nodes" (Abstract); intensity evolves in a latent space with attention-weighted graph propagation over node embeddings (model section, Eq. 2)
method: GRPP: graph-regularized neural point process; latent Hawkes-style attentive intensity, graph-attention propagation over node embeddings, KL regularizer toward empirical propagation graph; predicts next event time and node.
evaluation: Synthetic Hawkes 10d and 100d, Higgs retweets, Meme cascades; baselines MHP, RMTPP, NHP, GBTPP; ablations woGP, woAT; node accuracy and time RMSE in figures; no hardware or latency.
contribution: A graph-regularized latent point process predicts the next node and time of event propagation over a learned influence graph, improving node-prediction accuracy by roughly 1.5-2% over a graph-biased point-process baseline.
flag: DIRECT predictive accuracy reported (next-node accuracy and next-event-time RMSE against four baselines plus two ablations), but ONLY IN FIGURES (Figs. 3 and 5): the text gives no numeric values except "about 1.5% to 2%" improvement over GBTPP in node prediction and a "notable margin" on time. Borderline for (b): a temporal point process forecasting the next event on a latent graph, not a world model for an acting agent and not multi-agent in the agent sense (nodes are event types/users/sites); the maintainer may judge this E1. I did not credit multi-agent state. Higgs node count inconsistent in the paper (984 vs 900). Code promised, pending company approval. Record DOI is the IJCNN version; read from arXiv 2211.11758, title matches.

title: Leveraging World Model Disentanglement in Value-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
venue: Proceedings of the International Joint Conference on Neural Networks
evidence: "We employ variational auto-encoders and variational graph auto-encoders to learn the latent representations for the world model" (Abstract)
method: VDFD: latent world model for Dec-POMDPs split into action-conditioned, action-free and static branches, VAE prior and graph auto-encoder (GALA) posterior; 3-step imagined roll-outs feed a QMIX mixing network.
evaluation: SMAC, Multi-Agent MuJoCo, Level-Based Foraging; 5 seeds; vs QMIX, MASER, SMMAE, QMIX-CIA, QPLEX-CIA. Super-Hard SMAC win rate 0.67 vs 0.56; MAMuJoCo return 36.15 vs 28.69; LBF 0.83 vs 0.42. V100 GPUs.
contribution: Disentangles a multi-agent latent world model into controllable, uncontrollable and static branches with a graph auto-encoder posterior and feeds imagined roll-outs to value decomposition, improving win rates and returns on three cooperative benchmarks.
flag: Recommend E2 under the maintainer's ruling: the paper clearly meets (b) (latent world model over the joint state of several agents, graph auto-encoder posterior) but reports ONLY DOWNSTREAM TASK RESULTS - win rates and episodic returns, plus ablations (NO-AC, NO-AF, NO-ST, VDF-SV, VDF-POST) also measured in win rate. There is no direct measure of the world model's predictive accuracy anywhere (no roll-out or reconstruction error, no KL or likelihood reported). If the maintainer accepts ablation win-rate drops as evidence it would be an include, it is the strongest (b) fit in this batch. Other notes: not safety, no interceptor; the world model is used in training (roll-outs into the centralised mixing network), not as a runtime predictor; Fig. 4 text says VDFD beats SMMAE by 7.96 percent on 2c_vs_64zg and QMIX by 25 percent on MAMuJoCo, consistent with Table I averages; Table I gives no variances; LBF has N/A for three baselines; authors admit longer run time than model-free methods with no figures; abstract carries no numbers. References skimmed only.

title: A self-supervised joint embedding predictive approach for bipartite graphs to solve linear programs
venue: 2026 International Joint Conference on Neural Networks (IJCNN)
evidence: "By predicting global embeddings from masked local views, BiJEPA enables large-scale pretraining on unsolved LPs." (Abstract)
method: BiJEPA: masks nodes and edges of a static bipartite variable-constraint LP graph, aligns view embeddings to the mean global-view embedding with a SIGReg anti-collapse term; solver heads then trained with a KKT residual loss.
evaluation: Ecole LP relaxations (4 families, n=10,50,200), results shown for Combinatorial Auction only; optimality gap vs MLP and unpretrained GNN: n=50, 5 epochs 11.2 vs 20.8 percent; final 9.9 vs 9.3. LPs solve in about 20 ms.
contribution: Pretrains a bipartite graph network on unsolved linear programs by joint-embedding prediction, then trains a label-free solver with a KKT loss; pretraining helps only at small fine-tuning budgets.
flag: Recommend E2 under the maintainer's ruling: ONLY DOWNSTREAM RESULTS are reported (LP optimality gap after fine-tuning); the latent prediction itself is never scored (no embedding prediction error), the only evidence about the representation is a t-SNE plot. Criterion (b) is met only nominally - JEPA-style latent prediction over a STATIC bipartite graph of one LP instance, no dynamics, no forecast, no agents - so E1 is equally defensible. Candid points: abstract claims 'low optimality gaps' and 'Across four LP families' but tables cover Combinatorial Auction only and gaps are 7-36 percent with very large standard deviations; the unpretrained GNN baseline matches or beats the pretrained model at full budget (authors say so), and at n=200 E=50 GNN-BL 7.1 vs GNN-FF 16.9; text lists epochs {1,2,5,10,30,50} but tables include 20; warm-starting a classical solver gave negligible benefit (authors say so); no seeds, hardware or model sizes stated; no latency figure for the network itself, the ~20 ms is the classical solver. Not safety, no interceptor. References skimmed only.

title: Robust Real-Time Motion Retargeting via Neural Latent Prediction
venue: IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems
evidence: "predictive model in the latent space is built to generate future motion sequence, which allows robot to perform future actions to reduce influence of time-delay" (Sec. I Introduction)
method: Spatial-temporal graph encoder/decoder maps human skeleton sequences to robot joints; an ST-GCNN+MLP predicts future latent frames so a P-controller tracks ahead of delay.
evaluation: Chinese sign language to ABB YuMi dual-arm, 13847 frames; baselines NLO, DMPMR, NMG, C-3PO, Ours-sl; Frechet distance, acceleration norm; 34 ms per frame on RTX 2080 Ti.
contribution: Predicts future latent frames of a skeleton graph so a humanoid tracks human sign-language motion ahead of a 34 ms compute delay; single human-robot pair, no multi-agent state.
flag: Recommend E1: the model is predictive in latent space, but its graph is the kinematic skeleton of ONE body (joints as nodes) in a single human-to-robot pair, not a relational or multi-agent state, and it is a motion forecaster with no action conditioning, not a world model. If the maintainer reads 'latent prediction over graphs' literally it would meet (b), so this is a judgement call. Predictive accuracy: a direct measure exists only as figures (Fig. 8 Frechet distance by prediction horizon 1-5 frames, Fig. 10 Frechet vs time); NO numeric accuracy values appear in the text, the only table is timing (encoder 7, prediction 6, decoder 21, total 34 ms; human sampling about 67 ms). No ablation isolates the prediction module numerically (Ours-sl removes graph and prediction together). Not safety work; self-collision is a training loss term only. Extracted text ends mid-sentence in the fault-tolerance paragraph before the references, so the last lines of Sec. V and the conclusion ordering are jumbled by two-column extraction.

title: Decentralized but Not Compromised: Modular Architecture with Refined Observation for Multi-Agent Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
venue: 2025 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: "Our world model extends the RSSM architecture from Dreamer [14], [15] by incorporating a communication module from MAMBA [3], thereby adapting it for multi-agent dynamics modeling." (Sec. III-A RSSM World Model)
method: MARO: centralized RSSM world model with cross-agent Transformer communication block, adaptive weighted loss and history-initialised rollouts; decentralized actors with dual-stream hypernetwork (DSDN) trained on imagined trajectories.
evaluation: SMAC v1/v2, 14 maps, 100K-400K steps, 3 seeds; baselines MARIE, MAMBA, MAPPO, QMIX; win rate; offline observation/reward prediction loss vs history length; agent execution 1.3 ms on i5/RTX 2080 Ti.
contribution: Multi-agent model-based RL with a centralized RSSM world model used only in training and decentralized actors; improves low-data SMAC win rates over MARIE and MAMBA on harder maps.
flag: BORDERLINE include vs E2. Predictive accuracy: the headline evidence is downstream only (win rates, Table I: e.g. corridor 86.8 vs MARIE 71.0, 3s_vs_5z 87.4 vs 78.4, 3s_vs_4z 89.4 vs 73.0). The ONLY direct world-model measure is Fig. 8, offline observation loss and reward loss curves for history length 1-4 (an ablation of one design choice); values are readable only from plot axes, none stated in text, and there is no predictive-accuracy comparison against another world model. If the maintainer requires a tabulated accuracy metric with a baseline, this is E2. The 'weighted loss' contribution is not ablated at all. MARO is not best everywhere: loses to MARIE on 3m (95.5 vs 99.5), 2m_vs_1z (90.7 vs 95.5) and 3s_vs_3z, and to MAMBA on 2m_vs_1z (96.7). SMACv2 MARIE figures have no std and are copied from the original paper; MARIE missing on 3s5z. Authors admit training collapse/divergent loss on SMACv2 and instability on short maps. World model is absent at execution, so no runtime prediction or interception; game benchmark only; 'edge devices' claim rests on a desktop timing (1.3 vs 2.3 ms), not edge hardware. Not safety work.

title: Proposal for the Implementation of Spatial Common Ground and Spatial AI using the SSCP (Spatial Simulation-based Cyber-Physical) Model
evidence: "The Spatial AI instructs WHILL to slow down or stop when a person or obstacle enters its path." (Sec. V-B Collective Agent Control)
method: SSCP: layered digital-twin architecture (IoT sensing, BIM/USD model server, game-engine simulation, MQTT) in which a space-level Spatial AI monitors and commands heterogeneous robots and mobility devices.
evaluation: Prototype demo at Common Ground Living Lab, Osaka: 7 ToF sensors, LiDAR, WHILL and Temi; no baselines; only rendering delay <=0.6 s, obstacle detection 0.3 s, control delay <=0.1 s.
contribution: Architecture proposal for a game-engine digital twin (Spatial AI) that tracks human flow and commands robots in a building; demonstrated qualitatively in a living lab without quantitative evaluation.
flag: Recommend E2: architecture proposal plus qualitative demonstrations (Figs. 8-10); no dataset, no baseline or ablation, no accuracy or safety metric. Predictive accuracy: NONE reported, neither direct nor downstream; the abstract's 'prediction of the state of the world' is aspirational - the prototype uses 'simple logic' for monitoring and remote control and the 'world model' is a hand-built BIM/game-engine digital twin, not a learned or evaluated predictive model, so (b) is not met in substance (E1 also defensible). The slow-down/stop command to the WHILL vehicle is a runtime override, hence runtime_interceptor yes, but it is described in two sentences with three unreferenced delay figures (0.6 s, 0.3 s, 0.1 s) and no measurement method. Naming inconsistency: SSCP is 'Spatial Simulation-based Cyber-Physical' in the title but 'Spatial Smart City Platform' in the conclusion. Authors state coordination methods are 'presently limited and not yet systematized'.

title: Vectorized Representation Dreamer (VRD): Dreaming-Assisted Multi-Agent Motion Forecasting
evidence: "a recurrent state-space model (RSSM) which predicts the next latent state of the world" (Sec. III, Methodology)
method: VRD: VectorNet encoder, GRU recurrent model and deterministic transition predictor form an RSSM-like world model; closed-loop dreaming in latent space trains multi-agent trajectory forecasting with ego re-planning.
evaluation: Argoverse 2 and inD; vs QML, HeteroGCN, Forecast-MAE, QCNet; test minADE1 2.19, minFDE1 5.68, actorMR1 0.36; ablation on horizon and time step; no hardware or latency.
contribution: VRD trains a deterministic vectorized latent world model by dreaming closed-loop rollouts, reaching the lowest miss rate on Argoverse 2 single-mode forecasting while displacement error trails the best baseline.
flag: Method evidence only. Mixed results: on Argoverse 2 test VRD is worst on displacement (minADE1 2.19, minFDE1 5.68 vs QCNet 1.56/3.96) and best only on actorMR1 (0.36 vs 0.55); validation 1.68/4.17/0.37 vs QCNet 1.69/4.32/0.58. Authors attribute the miss-rate edge partly to the metric. Scene latent is a single VectorNet embedding of map and all agents, not an explicit per-agent graph state at rollout. Non-generative cell credited because the transition is deterministic with a cosine latent loss and no observation reconstruction - verify against Eq. 2. No ablation removing the dreaming stage reported in what I read; ablation is only horizon T and dt. No latency or hardware. inD results (3 s: 0.14/0.37/0.07; 6 s: 0.49/1.39/0.12) have no baseline. Read via WebFetch summary in one pass.

title: V2X-JEPA: Self-Supervised Multiagent Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture for Robust Vehicle-to-Everything Perception
evidence: "the model predicts latent target embeddings for masked regions using contextual information from the agent itself and its neighbors" (Sec. III-B Self-Supervised Pretraining Mechanism)
method: V2X-JEPA: JEPA-style self-supervised pretraining where each vehicle/roadside agent predicts latent embeddings of masked BEV regions from grid-spatial-attention fusion of neighbours' features; EMA target encoder; cooperative masking.
evaluation: OPV2V (LiDAR, sim, up to 7 agents) and DAIR-V2X (camera, real); baselines V2X-ViT, CoBEVT, DiscoNet, CooPre, CoCa3D, MAE, BEV-MAE; mAP, reconstruction cosine similarity; 78 ms, 98 M params, V100 GPUs.
