evaluation: Custom 9-player Werewolf, seven-rung ablation ladder, 450 games each: full system 42.4% villager win rate, 55.0% vote accuracy, latent MSE 0.01966 versus 0.02073 random. No hardware or latency.
contribution: A master's thesis pairing JEPA latent belief prediction with planner heads, LLM speech and social-influence updates for agents in a nine-player Werewolf game, compared across a seven-step ablation ladder.
flag: Borderline include; maintainer may well prefer exclude-E2. A DIRECT predictive measure IS reported (delta-z latent MSE, Table 1) alongside downstream win rate and vote accuracy, with an ablation ladder, so the letter of the (b) minimum is met. But the measure is weak: it is MSE in a latent space whose encoder is trained jointly on the same loss (collapse not ruled out), it has no confidence intervals, and it moves only from 0.02073 to 0.01966 (about 5%); B6 random, B5 heuristic and B4 LLM-only have no JEPA yet report near-identical MSE (0.02073, 0.02066, 0.02073), so the metric barely discriminates. Multi-agent state is nominal: each agent predicts its OWN belief latent (which includes alive masks and talk statistics), not a joint or graph state. Rollouts are one step and the planner is behaviour-cloned, not search. Inconsistencies: Table 1 B1 vote-accuracy CI printed as [0.551, 0.481] (reversed); B0 win-rate CI [0.349, 0.490] asymmetric about 0.424; Section 4.3 says B1 win rate 'around 20-30%' but Table 1 gives 0.333; stray sentence fragment 'interdependent mechanisms.' at end of 4.4; title-page placeholder 'Name, Month 2025'. FEP planning is admitted to be preliminary. Unreviewed MSc thesis (VCU 2025), own environment, no external baseline. Long-file note: read abstract and Chapters 3-5 in full; did NOT read Chapter 1 introduction, Chapter 2 related work, Chapter 6 or appendices. Not safety work; RQ5 capped.

title: Interactive multi-agent world models for embodied autonomy
evidence: "This thesis builds, controls, and reasons through Interactive Multi-Agent World Models for autonomous driving." (Abstract)
method: PhD thesis of five works: InfGen (interleaved token model for long-horizon multi-agent traffic rollout with agent insertion), LCTGen, ProSim (promptable closed-loop simulation), RIPT-VLA, LCDrive (latent world-model chain-of-thought for driving).
evaluation: Waymo Open Motion and Sim Agents: 30 s composite 0.6606 vs 0.6584 (CatK), agent-count error 8.1 vs 12.0; ProSim ADE 0.288 m, 43-394 ms on A100; LCDrive ADE 1.626 vs 1.762, Coll5.0 0.836% vs 2.207%.
contribution: A doctoral thesis on multi-agent traffic world models: long-horizon rollouts with agent insertion, language and prompt control of simulation, and a driving policy that reasons over latent world-model predictions.
flag: THESIS (UT Austin 2026, 240k chars): maintainer should decide whether theses are eligible and whether the five component papers (InfGen, LCTGen, ProSim, RIPT-VLA, LCDrive) are queued separately - it largely reprints them. Meets (b) with DIRECT predictive measures against baselines: WOSAC realism likelihood scores and agent-count error for InfGen (Tables 3.3, 3.4), ADE for ProSim (Table 5.1) and ADE for LCDrive (Table 7.1). Caveats: InfGen's composite gain over CatK is tiny (0.6606 vs 0.6584) and it is worse on Map and on placement distances; ProSim is below SMART-large on the Sim Agents composite (0.718 vs 0.756); LCDrive's ADE edge over text CoT is small (1.626 vs 1.650) and its latent world-model prediction accuracy is not itself reported - only ego-trajectory ADE, off-road and collision rates (open-loop, on a logged dataset). Models are generative token predictors, so no non-generative cell; runtimes are simulator throughput on an A100, not a safety latency budget. No runtime safety mechanism. Read: abstract, Ch. 1 contributions, Ch. 3, 5 and 7 experiments, Ch. 8. NOT read: Ch. 2 preliminaries, Ch. 4 (LCTGen), Ch. 6 (RIPT-VLA, which is LIBERO manipulation, not multi-agent), method sections and appendices.

title: Learning-enabled decision-making for autonomous driving: framework and methodology
evidence: "We introduce a joint multi-agent prediction model based on Transformers, leveraging hierarchical game theory to model interactions among agents in driving scenarios." (Abstract)

flag: PhD thesis (NTU, 2023), 514k chars: read abstract, contributions, Ch.4 (GameFormer) results and results tables of Ch.5-6; did NOT read Ch.2 (RL actor), Ch.3 (IRL cost), method detail of Ch.5-6, or Ch.7. title: Hybrid intelligence systems for reliable automation: advancing knowledge work and autonomous operations with scalable AI architectures
evidence: "encoder and predictor align current-state and future-state embeddings, creating a lightweight world model usable by RL agents for dense reward shaping." (Sec. 2.4 Multimodal representation)
method: Three-tier hybrid agent platform (navigation, discrete-action, planning agents on a blackboard); a graph-based JEPA over daily satellite proximity graphs feeds a maneuver classifier and a PPO alert-prioritising agent, plus symbolic constraints.

contribution: Industrial hybrid-intelligence platform using a graph JEPA over satellite proximity graphs with RL alert prioritisation, reporting maneuver-detection F1 0.98 on about 15,000 space objects and ablations, but no direct world-model accuracy.
flag: ONLY DOWNSTREAM RESULTS: no direct measure of the JEPA world model's predictive accuracy (no embedding or state prediction error); the evidence is anomaly-detection precision/recall/F1 and alert latency, with a w/o-JEPA ablation (F1 0.92 vs 0.98; delta -0.06 in Table 5), so E2 under the maintainer's ruling. The JEPA is described in two sentences with no architecture, loss or graph-encoder detail; whether it predicts future graph state or only a PatchTST time-series embedding per object is unclear, so the graph-state claim for (b) is itself doubtful. Abstract numbers not supported in the body: 'linear scaling across 2,000 compute nodes' (Table 4 tests at most 512 nodes and 1,024 GPUs; '>2,000 GPUs' is only asserted in text) and 'secure model aggregation incurs less than 4% latency' (no experiment or table anywhere; federated learning is not described in Methods). Text cites Tables 6 and 7 for ablations inconsistently; Sec. 4.2 says symbolic rules reduce CFD failures by 86 pp while Table 3 shows 10% vs 2% for that ablation (86 pp matches the abstract's 88% to 2% for the optimiser instead). Operator study and 8-GPU edge tests are 'not shown'. No comparison with external baselines. Maneuver labels are simulated (GMAT). Company authors (MSBAI). Detection is not multi-agent hazard detection in the sense of (c): single-object maneuver anomalies, no collision or conjunction outcome measured. SDA plus CFD is not a physical plus logical pair for the same world model, so cross-domain not credited. 1,200 graphs per s per GPU and 150,000 objects per s on 64 GPUs are throughput, not a latency bound for a safety decision.

title: Predictive Intrusion Detection for Industrial IoT Using World Models and Counterfactual Safety Analysis
evidence: "The state comprises two levels, an inter-tank flow and a pump pressure; the safe envelope bounds the levels and the pressure." (Sec. 5.1)
method: PREVENT-IIoT: action-conditioned Gaussian one-step world model rolled out under observed and nominal commands; reachability risk, time-to-unsafe, counterfactual excess risk, dependency-graph residuals and network score fused into a sequential alarm.
evaluation: Simulated two-tank testbed, 9 attack families, 10 seeds; 8 classical and 4 deep baselines; AUPRC 0.674 vs 0.643, pre-impact rate 0.53, TTU-MAE 2.1 s; 0.07 ms per window on one CPU core.
contribution: An intrusion detector for one simulated industrial process that rolls a learned action-conditioned model forward to estimate risk and time-to-unsafe, alarming before physical impact in 53% of consequence-bearing attacks.
flag: Pillar-2 test fails: the world model's state is a flat 4-variable vector of ONE two-tank process, not a graph or multi-agent state; the 'dependency graph' is a separate hand-specified set of per-variable parent regressors, not the predictive model's state. Direct predictive measures ARE reported, but only for the safety head (Brier 0.047, ECE 0.056, risk AUROC 0.83, time-to-unsafe MAE 2.1 s), with no baseline for them ('No baseline produces a comparable quantity') and no state-prediction RMSE. Alarm-only: no veto, block or halt, so strict (a) is not met either; a maintainer who counts alarm-only runtime monitoring could reconsider under (a) (FA/h and baselines exist), but it is single-process (E4 risk). The paper's own ablation shows removing the world-model risk head leaves AUPRC unchanged (0.677 vs 0.674); the graph-residual signal carries detection. Evaluation is entirely on the author's own simulated testbed; Sec. 5.1 says the public datasets (HAI, SWaT, WADI) 'could not be downloaded' in 'our build environment' and refers to 'the original proposal' - phrasing that suggests machine-assisted drafting; single author, MDPI, one-month review. Table 13: target 1 FA/h realises 2.56 FA/h. Abstract numbers were found in the body.

title: Graph Spatiotemporal World-Model-Driven Rolling MPC for Low-Carbon Economic Dispatch of Industrial-Park Integrated Electricity–Heat–Hydrogen Energy Systems
evidence: "a graph spatiotemporal world model is developed to learn multi-step state transitions" (Abstract)
method: Directed device graph of an electricity-heat-hydrogen park; attention message passing plus temporal encoder trained with multi-step rollout and physics-consistency losses; embedded in hard-constrained economic MPC with quantile-based bound tightening.
evaluation: One industrial-park dataset, held-out month, hourly, 24-step horizon; baselines EMPC, DRAMPC, GRU-MPC, LSTM, TCN, Transformer, DLinear; 24-step NRMSE 4.28% vs 4.84-5.87%; cost -6.07%, -3.83%, -10.79%; violation rate 0.00%.
contribution: A graph spatiotemporal world model of a coupled electricity-heat-hydrogen park predicts 24-step device states at 4.28% NRMSE and drives a constraint-tightened economic MPC, lowering cost and constraint violations against sequence predictors.
flag: Meets (b) with a DIRECT predictive-accuracy measure and baselines: Table 4 (1-step and 24-step MAE, RMSE, R2 per variable), Table 9 (avg 24-step NRMSE 4.28% vs Transformer 4.84, TCN 5.09, LSTM 5.34, DLinear 5.87) and Table 8 ablation (6.11% without physics-consistency). Graph nodes are devices of one plant under one central MPC, not agents, so multi-agent state is NOT claimed. The quantile tightening is a constraint inside the planner, not a runtime interceptor. Doubts: dataset is a confidential industrial-park log, not available, size and site undisclosed; no hardware, solver or solve-time figures; several 'predicted states' (grid import, CHP output, electrolyzer power) are really dispatch decisions, so the model partly imitates the logged controller; the graph-vs-sequence ablation (Table 7) reports only cost, not prediction error; text under Table 6 cites 'Table 5' for robustness results; robustness repetitions count not stated. All from one month of one site; numbers in the abstract were found in the body. MDPI, 3-week review.

title: Kuramoto Object-Centric Reinforcement Learning for Robotic Manipulation Tasks
evidence: Abstract: "We design a world model that leverages these structured object-centric latents and predicts dynamics using graph neural networks, thereby incorporating an inductive bias for modeling object interactions."
method: KORL: frozen Kuramoto Slot Attention for Video encoder gives object slots; TD-MPC2-style latent dynamics, reward, value and policy are GNNs over a complete graph of slots; MPPI planning in slot latent space.
evaluation: CausalWorld, ManiSkill, Robosuite, Isaac Gym (1-3 cubes) visual manipulation; baselines SOLD, OCRL, OC-CA, OC-SA, DreamerV3, TD-MPC2, SDAC; success rate and return at 500k and 1M steps, 3 seeds; no latency.
contribution: Object-centric model-based RL agent whose latent dynamics is a graph neural network over Kuramoto slot-attention object slots, achieving the best mean normalised score among object-centric agents on four manipulation suites.
flag: Predictive accuracy: NOT reported. Only downstream task results (success rate, return, mean normalised score 0.82 vs OCRL 0.58, SOLD 0.44), so exclude-E2 under the maintainer's ruling. No dynamics-prediction error, no rollout error, and not even a quantitative segmentation metric for the KSAVi encoder (attention maps are shown qualitatively only). (b) is met in form: predictive latent dynamics over a complete graph of object slots (3-6 slots), but it is a SINGLE-agent manipulation setting - graph state yes, multi-agent no. Claims need care: the abstract says KORL 'outperforms object-centric model-free and model-based approaches', yet in Table 2 SOLD beats it on ManiSkill at 1M steps (0.95 vs 0.82), and the monolithic DreamerV3 or TD-MPC2 beat KORL on every environment at 1M steps (e.g. Robosuite return 89 vs 61). The only clear win over monolithic agents is the red-floor shift test (KORL 0.72 vs 0.00 for both), one environment, one perturbation. Only 3 seeds. No ablation isolates the GNN dynamics from an MLP dynamics on the same slots (the SlotContrast comparison swaps the encoder, not the dynamics). MDPI Technologies, 37 days from submission to acceptance. No safety content, no runtime interceptor, no hardware timing.

title: A Graph Auto-encoder Framework for Spatio-temporal Anomaly Detection of Corrosion across a Fleet of Offshore Wind Turbines Using ICCP Data
evidence: "a latent-space LSTM model which captures temporal evolution of these representations and predicts future turbine states" (Section 2, Methodology)
method: Graph autoencoder over a turbine proximity graph gives per-turbine latents; an LSTM predicts the next latent state; reconstruction, latent and observation prediction errors are summed into an anomaly score.
evaluation: Synthetic ICCP-like fleet data with injected anomalies, 30-run sensitivity sweep: best F1 about 0.76, accuracy above 0.92; GAE-only ablation qualitative; unlabeled 26-turbine real data. No hardware or latency.
contribution: Couples a graph autoencoder with a latent-space LSTM that predicts the next fleet state of offshore wind turbines, flagging corrosion-protection anomalies from prediction and reconstruction errors.
flag: Recommend exclude-E2: ONLY DOWNSTREAM results (anomaly-detection F1, precision, recall, accuracy on a synthetic set); no direct measure of the latent predictor's accuracy (no forecast MSE or similar) is reported anywhere. The model itself does fit (b) on reading (next-latent prediction over a graph of 26 turbines), so this is E2 not E1, but the nodes are passive monitored assets, not acting agents. The only baseline is a GAE-only ablation described qualitatively from Fig. 3; the 30-run table (Appendix A) is an image and not in the text, so the F1 0.56-0.59, 0.61-0.64 and 0.76 figures come from prose only. Real-data section has no labels (authors say detections are 'statistically unusual' patterns, not confirmed faults). Sloppy: Fig. 3 caption duplicates Fig. 2 caption; text says k-nearest-neighbour graph but gives a Gaussian kernel; intro says 'LSTM Autoencoder', method is a plain LSTM; called 'initial implementation'. Conference paper (PHME 2026), AI tool acknowledged for typesetting only.

title: ORION: A Hierarchical Surgical World Model for Real-Time, Multi-Agent Operating-Room Intelligence
venue: Journal of Ubiquitous Computing and Communication Technologies
evidence: "they are not the product of a new evaluation carried out in this work, but are reproduced to characterise the temporal component that ORION integrates." (Sec. 6.4 Evaluation)
method: ORION: proposed twelve-layer surgical world model stacking perception, surgical scene graph, Gaussian-splatting digital twin, SurgicalMamba phase recognition, predictive risk layer, generative SurgWorld and LangGraph multi-agent reasoning with human override.
evaluation: No new experiment. Table 4 reproduces published Cholec80/AutoLaparo phase-recognition figures (94.6%, 89.5%, 238.7 FPS) from the constituent methods. Latency targets (sub-50 ms, sub-30 ms on Holoscan) are design goals, not measurements.

The abstract and Sec. 6.4 state openly that the 94.6%, 89.5% and 238.7 FPS figures are copied from the constituent methods' publications and that 'prospective validation of the integrated system is future work'. Contribution 2 nonetheless lists SurgicalMamba as the paper's own model although it is ref [6] by other authors - check authorship claim. The predictive layer (Layer 5: remaining duration, complication probability, bleeding forecast) and the scene-graph world state are described in one paragraph each with no model. Human-in-the-loop override and consensus scoring (Sec. 10.2) and the sub-50 ms/sub-30 ms Holoscan figures, Jetson/IGX edge deployment, are design statements with no measurement, so no gap cells are credited and runtime_interceptor is no (the interrupt pauses advisory decision support, it does not gate an action, and it is not implemented). 'Roughly ninety-nine percent' information loss and 'under thirty seconds' reporting are unsupported. Several references are blogs or vendor pages; 'multi-agent' here means LLM specialist agents, not the modelled state. Reads partly as machine-assisted survey of other groups' components; could alternatively be E3.

title: Multi-Agent Embodied Autonomous Driving: From V2X Information Exchange to Shared World Models
evidence: Sec 2.1: 'This survey is a structured narrative review'; Sec 3.4 defines the shared world model as 'the intermediate representational target for multi-agent collaborative driving'.
method: Survey of about 400 publications on multi-agent collaborative driving, organised around a shared-world-model lens with three evidence criteria: cross-agent state alignment, intent/plan alignment, coordinated action.
evaluation: No original experiments; tables report setups of cited work (OPV2V, DAIR-V2X, CARLA); latency budget is schematic with no numbers; explicitly not a meta-analysis.

Topic is squarely (b) (shared world models over multi-vehicle state), so worth mining its reference list for includable primaries, but it has no method, no experiments and no predictive-accuracy measure of its own (neither direct nor downstream). Mentions an onboard fallback control path as a design principle only. Only chars 0-100000 of 276443 were read (through Sec 6.2.2); Secs 7-10 unread, but the paper type is unambiguous from Sec 2.1.

title: Cognitive World Models for Process-Level Social Influence Evaluation
evidence: Sec 3.1: CogWM 'models the user from the perspective of the assistant agent', mapping profile, task context, dialogue history and previous state to the current BDI/E state and user utterance.

evaluation: 7,563 test turns from DailyDialog, ESConv, P4G, DuRecDial; baselines zero-shot Qwen3, GPT-5.5, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Dual-LLM; E-Acc 77.6 vs 36.4, B-Sim .773, E-MAE 0.29; ablations; one A100-80GB; no latency.

It IS one-step predictive and DOES report direct predictive accuracy (E-Acc 77.6, B-Sim .773, D-Sim .705, I-Sim .458, E-MAE 0.29) with baselines and ablations, so E2 does not apply. Doubts: ground truth is LLM-generated (human check on 300 dialogues); judge model is also a baseline; abstract E-Acc 77.6 vs ablation-table Full 72.8 and Sec text 71.1; test split sizes conflict between Sec 6.1 and Table 9; the 32B scale row is empty ('pending'); Table 5 values not extractable. Read chars 0-100000 of 107649 (tail of appendix G unread).

title: BioM-JEPA: joint-embedding prediction of graph-connected gene blocks in single cells
evidence: Discussion (Sec 2): 'Graph-connected blocks are operational prediction targets rather than curated pathways'; Methods 3.2-3.5: targets are masked gene blocks of the same cell sampled by breadth-first expansion on a fixed STRING/coexpression graph.
method: JEPA for single-cell expression: student encoder sees a cell minus graph-connected gene blocks, predictor regresses EMA-teacher block-level latents; fixed STRING/coexpression gene graph; linear attention.
evaluation: Pretrained on 22.1M cells; CellBench-LS annotation (9 datasets), reconstruction, perturbation (Adamson, Norman, Dixit); nine baselines plus objective controls; mean Top-5 macro-F1 61.62 (rank 4.33); A100, 678 cells/s.
contribution: A joint-embedding predictive pretraining objective for single cells that predicts latent summaries of masked gene blocks drawn from a fixed gene-interaction graph, improving embedding rank and throughput.
flag: E1 under the 2026-11-12 ruling: masked latent prediction on a STATIC gene graph within one cell profile, no future state or dynamics in the objective; no agents. Perturbation response appears only as a downstream probe on frozen embeddings. Predictive accuracy: no numeric latent-prediction accuracy in the text (loss/teacher similarity only in Fig 2a); everything quantified is downstream (annotation F1, perturbation Top-5 MSE-LFC 10.31 vs 10.87-10.98, response-gene recovery 0.123 vs 0.115). Not best on the aggregate benchmark (Nicheformer 67.30). Inconsistency: Sec 1.2 mean F1 0.835 vs Table S8 mean about 0.829, and Sec 1.1 claims best on cortex while Nicheformer is higher (92.51 vs 90.34). Read chars 0-100000 of 107601 (Tables S11-S13 tail unread).

title: Learning and Planning Multi-Agent Tasks via an MoE-based World Model
evidence: Sec. 5.2: "Compared to other structures, M3W achieves the lowest prediction error and highest stability, along with strong long-range prediction capability."
method: M3W: multi-task multi-agent latent world model with a SoftMoE dynamics model and SparseMoE reward predictor over per-agent latents; decoder-free self-supervised latent prediction; MPPI-style planner over predicted rollouts, no explicit policy needed.
evaluation: Bi-DexHands (14 tasks), MA-MuJoCo (24 tasks); baselines MACD, HMASD, MAT, MAPPO, HATRPO; normalised return; dynamics and reward prediction error vs Transformer, Switch-Transformer, MLP; RTX A6000, 25.8 ms per step (9.8 ms early-stop).

flag: Predictive accuracy: DIRECT measure reported with architectural baselines (Appendix E.3 Table 12: latent dynamics error 0.042+-0.007 vs Switch-Transformer 0.067, Transformer 0.119, MLP 0.422; reward error 0.14 vs self-attention 0.59, MLP 0.81; also Fig. 6), plus downstream results (Table 1 Bi-DexHands average 84.1 vs MACD 72.0, HMASD 72.3). Caveats on the predictive evidence: it is a separate offline study on 6 two-robot MA-MuJoCo tasks (Cheetah and Walker2D only) with 150K random-action transitions and other modules frozen, not the world model as trained in the main runs, and it is not measured on Bi-DexHands; the error is in learned latent space (encoder is trained jointly), so values are not comparable across architectures in an absolute sense; the stated -53% and -78% reductions do not match Table 12 against the nearest competitor (0.067 to 0.042 is -37%; -53% seems to be against an unstated reference, possibly averaged) - check. Multi-agent only modestly: 2 agents (two hands) in Bi-DexHands, robot body parts in MA-MuJoCo; no graph. Latency: per-step planning time is reported (Table 14: 25.8 ms default, 9.8 ms with KL early stopping, vs 1.1-3.4 ms for policy baselines) against a self-chosen 50 ms threshold on a desktop RTX A6000; I did not tick latency/jitter aware because there is no deadline or jitter analysis and no edge hardware - maintainer may disagree. Decoder-free latent prediction, hence non-generative ticked. The '71% of tasks best is statistically significant' argument in E.2 is weak. No safety content, no runtime interceptor. NeurIPS 2025 proceedings; I read the main text and Appendices D-E, skimmed A-C and the checklist.

title: WALL-E: World Alignment by NeuroSymbolic Learning improves World Model-based LLM Agents
evidence: "The cover rate measures the percentage of LLM failed predictions that can be corrected by our world model." (Figure 6 caption, Sec. 4.4)
method: LLM world model aligned with learned symbolic knowledge (action rules, knowledge graph, scene graph) compiled to code rules; LLM agent proposes actions, world model predicts outcome, predicted failures trigger replanning (MPC loop).
evaluation: Mars (Crafter-like) and ALFWorld, single agent, GPT-4 and GPT-3.5; baselines ReAct, Reflexion, Skill Library, IfR, RAFA, AdaPlanner; Mars reward 6.7 vs 5.5, score 15.3% vs 7.4%; ALFWorld 98% success.
contribution: WALL-E aligns an LLM world model with code rules, a knowledge graph and a scene graph learned from trajectories, and uses it to check an LLM agent's actions before execution in Mars and ALFWorld.
flag: Results are essentially DOWNSTREAM ONLY (reward, score, success rate), hence E2 under the maintainer's ruling. The only direct world-model measure is 'cover rate' (share of the unaligned LLM's mispredicted transitions fixed by the code rules), shown only as a curve in Figure 6 with no numeric value in the text, no table and no baseline; no overall prediction accuracy is reported. E1 is also arguable: single agent, and the state is a text observation - the scene graph is an accumulated memory of object locations and the knowledge graph a static prerequisite graph, neither is a predicted graph state. runtime_interceptor is 'yes' only in the literal sense that the world model vetoes predicted-to-fail actions before execution and forces replanning; this is task feasibility, not safety, so (a) is not credited. Abstract says baselines are surpassed 'by 16.1%-51.6% of success rate' but the body says reward improvements of 16.1% to 51.6%; the body also says WALL-E exceeds IfR by 17.9% in reward while Table 1 averages (6.7 vs 5.5) give about 21.8%. DreamerV3 (1M steps) beats it on reward. No latency reported. This is the NeurIPS 2025 proceedings version (elsewhere circulated as WALL-E 2.0); check for a duplicate arXiv record.

title: Causal inductive biases for learning Structured World Models
venue: Oxford University Research Archive (ORA) (University of Oxford)
evidence: "we propose SPARTAN, a structured world model that jointly performs dynamics model learning and causal discovery" (Sec. 5.4)
method: PhD thesis: VCD (latent world model with learned sparse causal graph), COMET (competing reusable mechanisms), SPARTAN (sparse-attention Transformer world model learning state-dependent local interaction graphs between entities, with intervention tokens).
evaluation: SPARTAN on Interventional Pong, CREATE, Waymo traffic vs Transformer (MTR), Global Graph: prediction error 8.60 vs 8.83, 246.6 vs 265.5, 0.52 vs 0.51; SHD 1.51 vs 6.37, 1.17 vs 6.29, 6.84 vs 10.6.
contribution: A doctoral thesis on causally structured world models; its SPARTAN sparse Transformer learns local interaction graphs between entities while matching dense Transformers on prediction and adapting few-shot to unseen intervention combinations.
flag: THESIS (Oxford, 406k chars), compiled from published papers the maintainer may hold separately: VCD (TMLR 2023), COMET (preprint arXiv:2404.15109, cited in Sec. 1.2 - that id belongs to the Ch. 4 paper, not this thesis) and SPARTAN (NeurIPS 2025). Meets (b) with DIRECT predictive measures and baselines: rollout prediction error and structural Hamming distance to ground-truth or human-labelled graphs (Table 5.1), robustness to removal of non-causal entities (Table 5.2: traffic 13.9% vs 32.8% Transformer, 25.5% local attention), and VCD rollout error vs RSSM (Fig. 3.5, figure only). Caveats: SPARTAN matches rather than beats the dense Transformer on prediction (traffic 0.52 vs 0.51, slightly worse); the graph is an inferred attention graph over object or vehicle slots, and the Traffic task predicts only the ego vehicle from other vehicles' trajectories, so 'multi-agent state' is weak; Pong and CREATE use ground-truth object masks; few-shot adaptation results are in a figure only. No safety mechanism, no latency figures (training GPU only). Read: abstract, Ch. 1, Sec. 3.3.2, Ch. 5 experiments and conclusion, publications list. NOT read: Ch. 2, most of Ch. 3, Ch. 4 (COMET), Ch. 6 (RL and LLM interpretability case studies), Ch. 7 and appendices.

title: A Tool to Complement Human Intelligence: The Math Behind Human Indispensability
venue: Applied Human Factors and Ergonomics International
evidence: "we constructed a generalized model for joint task accomplishment which frames the problem as assignment of subtasks rather than seeking individual optimized plans" (Conclusion)
method: Task modelled as a directed graph of subtasks; greedy expected-cost procedure picks which subtasks run autonomously vs manually; derives robustness conditions for the chosen autonomy level.
evaluation: Physical robot sanitisation task, 7 subtasks, 25 operators; greedy plan cost 42.2 s at autonomy level 4 vs MDP solution 42.67 s (1.1% error). No latency or hardware.
contribution: Analytical conditions under which a mixed human-robot allocation of subtasks beats all-human or all-robot execution, checked on one robot sanitisation task with 25 operators.
flag: Not a world model: the graph is a static task graph of subtasks, not a predicted state, and the abstract explicitly argues AGAINST needing a world model of the human. No predictive-accuracy measure of any model; the only numbers are plan cost (downstream) and the robustness inequalities. Allocation is planned offline, not a runtime handoff, so (e) is not met either. Quality doubts: text cites 'Equation 9' as the continuous optimisation where Eq 7 is meant; Table 1 probabilities and sigma columns are unexplained (manual success probabilities 0.15-0.37 look implausible as success rates); Table 2 '% diff' row undefined; Table 4 last row is cited as the proof but its derivation is not shown; authors listed as independent researchers; 10-page AHFE paper with no baseline other than the MDP.

title: Disaster Digital Twins: AI World Models for Predicting Cascading Infrastructure Failures
venue: International Journal of Academic and Industrial Research Innovations(IJAIRI)
evidence: "Consequently, the presented results emphasize evidence anchoring and reporting formats rather than full end-to-end predictive performance." (Sec. 5.3 Limitations and research directions)
method: Blueprint for a disaster digital twin: typed dependency graph of infrastructure nodes plus an action- and hazard-conditioned latent state-space world model with a graph neural transition operator. Specified, not implemented.
evaluation: No experiment. Winter Storm Uri (Texas 2021) public impact figures tabulated as case context; Table 4.2 is a reporting schema without values. No model trained, no baselines, no metrics, no hardware.
contribution: Position-style blueprint proposing a graph-structured latent world model for forecasting cascading infrastructure failures, illustrated with public Winter Storm Uri impact figures but with no implemented model or predictive evaluation.
flag: UNEVALUATED: reports neither a direct measure of world-model predictive accuracy nor downstream task results; no model is trained or run. The only numbers are externally reported storm impacts (>4.5 million customers, 702 excess deaths, 246 official deaths, $9,000/MWh, 69,692 MW). Table 4.2 has no values. Sec. 5.3 admits no end-to-end predictive performance. Single author publishing in a journal run by his own organisation (National Education Services); conclusion calls itself a 'PhD-level, journal-ready blueprint'; reference list is largely irrelevant (antibiotics, post-quantum cryptography, hydrogels) and heavily self-citing - signs of machine-generated text. Topic fits (b) in concept (predictive, graph state) so E2 rather than E1.

title: AI-Powered World Models for Smart Governance: Integrating Traffic, Infrastructure, and Emergency Response Data
venue: International Journal of Academic and Industrial Research Innovations(IJAIRI)
evidence: "Development of a novel world model for smart governance that fuses traffic, infrastructure, and emergency data into a unified, adaptive AI framework." (Sec 6, Expected Results and Contributions)
method: Proposes, in prose only, a city-wide spatiotemporal graph world model (GCN, ST-GNN, transformer attention, deep RL) fusing traffic, infrastructure and emergency data for policy simulation with a GIS dashboard.
evaluation: None performed. Two unsourced illustrative tables (travel time 45 to 30 min, accidents 20 to 12 per month; response time 15 vs 8 min). No dataset, model, baseline or hardware.
contribution: Conceptual proposal for a spatiotemporal-graph world model of a city combining traffic, infrastructure and emergency-response data for governance simulation; no implementation or evaluation is reported.
flag: Unevaluated: (b) is met only as a stated intention. No predictive-accuracy measure is reported (MAE is named in Stage 5 as the planned metric but no value is given) and no real downstream result either: Tables 5.1 and 5.2 are introduced with 'let us take a closer look' and 'a case study' with no city, dataset, method or source, and read as invented illustrations. Sec 6 is titled 'Expected Results'. No equations, architecture details or experiments. Self-published: sole author is Research Director of National Education Services, which publishes the journal (IJAIRI), and the PDF is digitally signed by the author as publisher. Sec 5 calls itself 'This essay' and has its own 'Conclusion' - text looks machine-generated and stitched. A figure referred to as 'the following data visualization' is absent from the text.

title: Puzzle it Out: Local-to-Global World Model for Offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
venue: Proceedings of the International Joint Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems, AAMAS
evidence: "Instead of directly predicting complex global state transitions, we first predict each agent's next local observation" (Sec. 4.2, Local-to-Global World Model Construction)
method: LOGO: per-agent local predictive models whose outputs a deductive model fuses into next global state and reward; state-prediction discrepancy gives ensemble-free uncertainty for weighting synthetic offline MARL data.
evaluation: SMAC (5 maps) and MaMuJoCo (3 tasks), 4 datasets each; vs MACQL, OMAR, CFCQL, Morel, SUMO, MAMBA, MAZero, OMIGA; returns; one-step reward prediction error 0.0051 vs 0.0257 (MAZero).
contribution: A local-to-global world model for offline multi-agent RL predicts per-agent observations then deduces the joint state, cutting one-step prediction error and replacing ensembles for uncertainty at roughly 3x lower inference cost.
flag: Method evidence only, no safety claim. Predictive-accuracy metric is a single row (Table 7: reward prediction error LOGO 0.0051, MAZero 0.0257, MAMBA 0.0673, SUMO 0.0928, Morel 0.1316); otherwise returns only. Abstract says 8 scenarios, tables show 5 SMAC maps + 3 MaMuJoCo tasks. Table 5 runtime (LOGO 0.042-0.063 vs ensemble 0.225-0.247) has no stated unit; hardware, seeds and agent counts not reported. Table 4 MACQL values differ from Table 2. Rollouts are not clearly in latent space (encoder features, observation-space prediction). Uncertainty only reweights training samples, no runtime gate. Read via WebFetch summary in one pass; quote not checked against the PDF character by character.

title: Multi-Agent Model-Based Reinforcement Learning with Joint State-Action Learned Embeddings
venue: Proceedings of the 25th International Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems
evidence: Sec. 4.3: "This world model significantly enhances sample efficiency by generating imagined roll-outs without the need" (sentence truncated in my reading).
method: MMSA: VAE-based world model predicts next-step latent joint state-action embeddings (SALE); 3-step imagined roll-outs feed a QMIX-style mixing network under centralized training, decentralized execution.
evaluation: MAMuJoCo, Level-Based Foraging, SMACv1, SMACv2, 5 seeds; baselines QMIX, VDN, MAG, MAMBA, MABL and others; ablations without world model or SALE; SMACv1 win rate 0.93; wall-clock training hours only.
contribution: A multi-agent model-based RL method whose world model predicts latent joint state-action embeddings for short imagined roll-outs, reaching 0.93 mean SMACv1 win rate against 0.63 for the best model-based baseline.
flag: Borderline on minimum evaluation: no predictive-accuracy or model-error metric is reported (the paper lists model error as future work); the evidence is task return or win rate plus a no-world-model ablation whose result is in a figure (text: win rate capped around 0.5). Strict v1.6 reading would be E2. Other figures: MAMuJoCo mean return 36.94 vs QMIX 28.69; LBF 0.80 vs QMIX 0.42; SMACv2 0.81, only tied with HPN-QMIX 0.81 and behind it on Protoss (0.81 vs 0.84). Roll-outs are used in training targets only, not at execution, so nothing is predicted at runtime. Hardware not stated; training 3.7-33.3 h. Prediction is in latent space but trained with VAE reconstruction, so non-generative cell not credited. Evidence quote is cut off at the end; verify wording.

title: PCGAT-Stab: An Explainable Temporal Graph Attention Network for PCIe Protocol Behavior Modeling and System Stability Prediction in Cloud-Native Microservices
venue: Fundamental Scientific Reports in Multidisciplinary Areas
evidence: "PCGAT-Stab constructs a dynamic PCIe topology graph to represent device-level interactions, employs multi-head graph attention to learn error propagation pathways" (Sec 1)
method: Per-window PCIe device graph encoded by 4-head graph attention, GRU over time, device-to-pod mapping matrix, MLP heads for pod restart, SLA violation and latency variance; attention and SHAP for explanation.
evaluation: 32-node Kubernetes GPU cluster, 3 months, 1.2M 20 s windows; vs MLP, LSTM, Transformer, static GCN. AUC 0.94, F1 0.91, precision 0.90; RMSE 5.72, MAE 4.68. No inference latency.
contribution: Temporal graph attention network over PCIe device topology that predicts pod restarts, SLA violations and latency variance in a Kubernetes cluster, beating sequence-only and static-graph baselines on one dataset.
flag: Reports DIRECT predictive accuracy with baselines (Table 2: AUC/F1/precision 0.94/0.91/0.90 vs static GCN 0.89/0.87/0.86, Transformer 0.88/0.85/0.84, LSTM 0.86/0.83/0.81, MLP 0.82/0.79/0.77; Table 3: RMSE/MAE 5.72/4.68 vs static GCN 6.81/5.54), so the E2 rule for downstream-only results does not apply. BORDERLINE on (b), please judge: this is a supervised failure classifier over a time-indexed graph, not a world model - no action conditioning and no next-state prediction; the graph topology is fixed and only node features change. NO PREDICTION HORIZON is stated: it is unclear whether labels are for a future window or the same 20 s window, so it may be detection rather than prediction. Possible label leakage: Table 1 lists Pod_Restart_Count and P99_Latency as input features while pod restart and latency variance are targets. Text arithmetic is wrong: Sec 4.3 says RMSE is reduced 'by 1.23 compared to Static GCN (6.81) and by 1.59 compared to Transformer (6.95)' but the table gives 1.09 and 1.23 (1.59 is the LSTM gap). Table 3 is captioned as classification; two sections numbered 4.3; RMSE units not given; Precision@K is said to be monitored but never reported; SHAP and attention results are described but no figure or number shown; no ablation of the model's own components (static GCN is the nearest). No dataset release. Low-tier journal with clear citation padding (unrelated refs 12, 14-20, including the same journal issue) and duplicated sentences in the conclusion. Multi-agent state is nominal (devices and pods, not acting agents). RQ5 capped at 2 as predictor-only evidence.

title: Learning to communicate through imagination with model-based deep multi-agent reinforcement learning
evidence: "we make use of a recurrent world model that takes the form of a mixture density network LSTM (MDN-LSTM)" (Sec. 2 Background, Decision-time planning)
method: MACI: each agent rolls out a shared MDN-LSTM world model of its own future observations and rewards for K steps, encodes the rollout with a 1D-CNN into messages over a neighbour graph, then acts (PPO).
evaluation: Two 2-agent toy environments (Digit game, Invisible spread) vs IPPO, IQL, QMIX, QTRAN; mean reward learning curves over 5 runs; ablation with and without world model; wall-clock hours inset. No numeric tables.
contribution: Model-based multi-agent RL in which two agents exchange encoded imagined rollouts from a recurrent world model to plan jointly, outperforming model-free baselines on two purpose-built toy tasks.
flag: ONLY DOWNSTREAM RESULTS: no direct measure of world-model predictive accuracy (no prediction loss or rollout error reported); evidence is mean-reward learning curves in Figs 4 and 5 only, with no numeric values in the text, so E2 under the maintainer's ruling. An ablation with and without the world model exists (reward curves; benefit 'less significant' in Invisible spread). The file is the anonymous ICLR 2021 submission ('Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2021', anonymous authors) - apparently never published in a proceedings; no arXiv id appears in the text, though one probably exists and the maintainer may want to add it. Multi-agent state is weak: only two agents, and the world model predicts each agent's OWN next observation and reward (shared weights), not the joint state; joint information enters only through messages. 2-step rollouts. Method section's 'Training.' paragraph is empty (content only in pseudocode blocks). Wall-clock comparison is training hours, not inference latency. Abstract has no numbers to verify.
